items.title: Residual Allan Stability under Periodic Auxiliary Ramsey Sampling
items.summary: The timing of auxiliary Ramsey measurements can change the frequency stability associated with a drifting pulse shift at a fixed nominal Fisher-information rate for a constant shift. For periodic instantaneous observations of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck shift with causal prediction between updates, we derive the exact residual covariance averaged over the update cycle and the corresponding Allan variance at arbitrary averaging times. Relative to a continuous Kalman reference at the same information rate, periodic estimation increases the cycle-averaged estimation-error variance, reduces the short-time residual Allan variance, and increases its long-time value. Its covariance decays more slowly at the origin and has a larger integral. We extend the result to instantaneous sensing of the sum of finitely many independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck modes. Integrated observations preserve the short-time ordering for the scalar shift, and numerical calculations resolve the dependence of the crossover on window duration. A zero-order-hold comparison shows that the short-time ordering can change when the same estimator drives a different correction command. A three-level Ramsey model of coherent population trapping (CPT) maps the discriminator response to an effective information budget and illustrates how the dark times affect the choice of schedule.

items.title: Strong Epsilon-Near-Zero Confinement and Interface-Controlled Dynamics in Inverse-Designed Transparent Conducting Oxide Cavities
items.summary: Achieving optical modulation that is both strong and ultrafast remains a central challenge in time-varying photonics. Here, we theoretically demonstrate that combining inverse-designed cavities that utilize transparent conducting oxides (TCOs) operating at the epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) point with boundaries that support carrier transport can meet this requirement. This is achieved by leveraging ENZ-enhanced optical absorption and electron heating with interface-engineered carrier relaxation. A multilayer inverse-design framework, combined with a structural disorder-aware correction loop, is developed to preserve robust resonant absorption in ultrathin TCO films under realistic material disorder. Relative to conventional TCO cavity geometries, the inverse-designed structures exhibit stronger light confinement, greater electron temperature modulation, and markedly faster recovery. Beyond cavity design, interfacial barrier engineering and adjacent-layer doping emerge as effective degrees of freedom for co-designing spectral and temporal dynamics. Furthermore, our theoretical framework shows that the inverse-designed cavity supports richer oscillatory transmittance dynamics on the few-optical-cycle timescale compared to its single-film counterpart, with interfacial control enabling further temporal compression. The combined control of optical confinement and interfacial dynamics establishes inverse-designed TCO cavities as a viable platform for time-varying photonic media capable of supporting strong and ultrafast optical responses.

items.title: The role of externally-driven density fluctuations in the enhancement of beam spray
items.summary: Speckled laser beams, commonly used to ionize and heat plasma for inertial confinement fusion and high-energy-density experiments, are shown to drive long-wavelength plasma-density fluctuations that induce beam spray in other laser beams. Experiments show that a 1053 nm beam undergoes increased beam spray when 351 nm speckled heater beams are on. These observations indicate that the high-intensity speckles sustain an increased level of steady-state density fluctuations. Modeling of these fluctuations predicts amplitudes that are orders of magnitude larger than the level of thermal fluctuations. Beam propagation simulations show increased beam spray due to self-focusing and filamentation when heater-driven density fluctuations are included.

items.title: Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks
items.summary: Understanding chemical reactivity requires uncovering which pathways are accessible from a given set of reactants, how they compete, and how successive reactions reshape the mixture. Automated saddle-point searches can explore from reactants alone, but their computational cost rises sharply as competing pathways accumulate across successive steps. Machine-learning approaches to transition state generation typically require predefined products, yet identifying those products is a central goal of exploration. Here we introduce ReactNexus, a generative framework that generates transition-state candidates directly from reactant graphs without specifying products, predicts the species they connect, and refines pathways with a reactive machine-learned potential to guide network exploration. Its models were trained on a quantum-chemical database of 130 million structures from 1.1 million reaction records, spanning 11 elements and multiple charge and spin states. On held-out reactions, 93.6% of generated candidates refined to valid transition states at the density functional theory level, and 83.3% connected the supplied reactants to distinct products. Across decomposition, complex rearrangements, and organocatalysis, ReactNexus reveals how competing mechanisms shape product formation, uncovering pathways missed in previous studies. In a multisite nucleophilic aromatic substitution, ReactNexus identified diarylation products that explained initially unassigned LC-MS signals, with structural assignments supported by NMR after isolation. ReactNexus also predicted an additional product family not detected under the initial conditions; subsequent higher-temperature experiments provided LC-MS evidence supporting its formation. This work highlights the potential of generative models to extend mechanistic analysis to increasingly complex reaction mixtures.

items.title: Toward high-throughput, low-latency structural biology using light, Part I: Protein-ligand pose determination
items.summary: We demonstrate for the first time that an optical spectroscopy - electron-vibration-vibration two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy (EVV 2DIR) - has sufficient structural competence to enable the reconstruction of the three-dimensional geometries of drug-protein binding at the level needed for practical drug discovery applications. Klug et al. previously demonstrated experimental detection of drug binding to a kinase using EVV 2DIR. Here we use a quantum mechanical approach to calculate and assign elements of EVV 2DIR spectra for the spectral region 1200-1800 cm$^{-1}$ / 1100-1800 cm$^{-1}$ of 92 protein-ligand complexes. This dataset includes ligand-target poses drawn from existing crystal structures and ligand-target poses created by docking and cofolding models. We find that binding-dependent spectral features are robust, interpretable, and consistent across poses in a given binding mode, and distinct for each unique hydrogen bonding geometry. We construct a spectral distance metric to distinguish poses that conform to the ligand-target hydrogen-bonding pattern of the crystal structure from those that do not. These results show that, given a set of predicted ligand-target poses containing the correct geometry, the hydrogen-bonding pattern of the valid pose may be rapidly identified by comparing simulated and experimental EVV 2DIR spectra. Finally, we discuss the practical implications for a new, high throughput structural biology for drug discovery that will be the subject of forthcoming manuscripts, noting that the base technologies to perform EVV 2DIR quickly and efficiently already exist and will enable a novel structure to be determined in only minutes for each sample. Moreover, this can be achieved without the need for crystallization, isotopic labeling, or low temperatures, non-destructively using picogram quantities of material.

items.title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
items.summary: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

items.title: Toward chemically accurate quantum simulations on quantum hardware: A quantum-HPC hybrid approach
items.summary: We present a large-scale experimental study of quantum-computing-based molecular simulation carried out on IQM's Sirius 24-qubit superconducting processor, utilizing up to 16 operational qubits. The work employs Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) together with the Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz to estimate ground-state energies for a set of benchmark molecules, including H$_2$, LiH, BeH$_2$, H$_2$O, and NH$_3$. In addition, we introduce a Linear-CNOT variant of the Unitary Coupled-Cluster Singles and Doubles (LCNot-UCCSD) ansatz within the SQD workflow, trading higher circuit depth for reduced classical preprocessing. A comparison between these ansätze is provided, clarifying their respective strengths, limitations, and suitability for near-term quantum hardware. We further explore potential energy landscapes through 1D scans for H$_2$ and HeH$^+$ using both STO-3G and 6-31G basis sets, and for LiH and BeH$_2$ in STO-3G. Extending beyond this, we demonstrate the experimental construction of a full 2D potential energy surface for the water molecule on quantum hardware, mapped over a 32 $\times$ 32 grid in bond length and bond angle. To move beyond small benchmark systems, we combine SQD(LUCJ) with Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) to compute active-space energies for a set of ligand-like molecules, as well as the pharmacologically relevant amantadine system. Across all studies, the majority of quantum-computed energies agree with reference FCI results, as well as with DMET-CASCI energies for embedded systems, to within the chemical accuracy threshold for the chosen basis sets. These results demonstrate the reliability of sample-based diagonalization approaches and underscore the potential of hybrid embedding strategies for extending quantum simulations to increasingly complex molecular systems, while also highlighting their practicality on quantum hardware.

items.title: Electron Scattering with ASTRA: Helium and Molecular Hydrogen
items.summary: We present an implementation of electron-impact scattering in \ASTRA{}~(AttoSecond TRAnsitions)~[J. M. Randazzo {\it et al.}, Phys. Rev. Research {\bf 5}, 043115 (2023)], a general close-coupling method for the molecular electronic continuum based on transition density matrices and already employed for molecular photoionization. The scattering states are obtained with a pole-free Galerkin method with variational surface matching, which yields the scattering matrix and, from it, the elastic and electronically inelastic integral cross sections and the molecular-frame differential cross sections. For helium, \ASTRA{} reproduces elastic and inelastic cross sections over a broad energy range, resolves the $\mathrm{He}^{-}(1s2s^2\,{}^2S^e)$ Feshbach resonance in both energy and angle, and reproduces the interference features in the angular distributions for $1s^2\to1s 2\ell$ excitations observed experimentally. For molecular hydrogen, the elastic and inelastic cross sections closely reproduce the benchmark results obtained with \UKRmolplus{} for the same close-coupling expansion. We also report orientation-resolved, three-dimensional molecular-frame angular distributions for state-resolved electron-impact excitation, which are shown to depend strongly on the molecular orientation. These results validate the method in view of its application to larger molecular targets.

items.title: Kinetic study of Reaction-Control-Jet Interference in Rarefied Hypersonic Crossflow
items.summary: A 1975 wind-tunnel study at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) of a helium jet blowing from a flat plate into a Mach 11 to 12 air crossflow at three freestream densities is revisited using two- and three-dimensional Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) computations at Knudsen numbers 0.021 to 0.125. The planar slot used in two-dimensional model computations reproduces the shock topology, the sign and two-lobed structure of the interference pressure and its trend with rarefaction, and its plate-alone boundary layer is consistent with the three-dimensional one and with a similarity solution with slip and temperature jump. However, two-dimensional simulations overpredict the peak interference pressure about twelvefold at every condition and carry it farther upstream. A resolution sweep at the most rarefied condition converges the planar interference to within 1% of its extrapolated limit. Three-dimensional DSMC reproduces the measured interference pressure at all three densities, within 25% at the lobe peak and 3 mm in its position, although two- and three-dimensional simulations overpredict the plate-alone wall pressure by 50 to 75%. Continuum breakdown around the jet persists even at the lowest Knudsen number examined. Fully three-dimensional kinetic simulations are underway to extend the present validation to a comparison of jet strength and forces over wider Knudsen number ranges, and to an examination of lateral relief as a reason for the discrepancy.

items.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part II: The momentum convection term
items.summary: The two-phase Volume-of-Fluid solvers of OpenFOAM overpredict the horizontal water velocity near the crest of a water wave, and the error grows as the wave propagates. Part I of this series removed the spurious air velocities caused by the gravity term but left this error unchanged. Here we show that it is caused by the momentum convection term. Its mass flux is computed in the interface advection step from the velocity at the start of the time step, whereas the convected velocity is taken at the end of the step, because convection is discretised implicitly. In a progressive wave, where the horizontal and vertical velocities are 90 degrees out of phase, this time lag produces an upward flux of horizontal momentum, proportional to the time step, which accumulates in a spurious current near the surface. The same mismatch makes the response to a force depend on the density at the wrong time level. Explicit convection removes the lag and makes the response consistent with the gravity force, but requires the convected face velocity at the interface to be taken from the upwind cell. Only then is the new velocity of a cell a weighted average of old velocities, whatever the density ratio. We demonstrate both requirements with prescribed flows and with the full solver. For a progressive wave, explicit convection with upwind face velocities at the interface reduces the overprediction of the crest velocity from 26-31 % to within 1 % and removes the near-surface current. The resulting solver, fluxinator, is meant for maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below, where it keeps the wave height within 1.5 % over 15 periods on meshes with six or more cells per wave height. Because the spurious velocities that limit the time step are removed, it needs 34-42 % less wall-clock time than interFoam for the tested wave.

items.title: Time-Varying Medium from an Ensemble of Laser-Dressed Quantum Emitters
items.summary: We propose a minimal quantum-mechanical model of a frequency dispersive, time-modulated medium that explicitly incorporates the pumping mechanism. It consists of a homogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters dressed by a pump laser. We analyze their dispersive, time-varying response to a perturbative probe field by deriving the macroscopic polarizability of the ensemble, and then solving Maxwell's equations via the Floquet formalism. This yields a rich band structure that departs from conventional analyses in which the modulation source is neglected, arising from the interplay between the dispersive polaritonic and time-varying responses. These results shed light on the role of the modulation source in time-varying media and pave the way toward realizing dispersive time-varying media from driven quantum-mechanical systems.

items.title: Effect of a role model-based show on the STEM aspirations of primary school students
items.summary: A STEM outreach show called 'Who wants to be a Superhero' went into primary schools across England and Wales, delivered by professional science communicators. The show was structured around four female STEM role models and two male STEM role models as part of a wider narrative about scientists and engineers being real-life superheroes. The show was found to increase both boys' and girls' aspirations for a STEM career, with a bigger effect seen in the girls. The intervention also increased positive attitudes, and decreased negative attitudes, towards scientists measured through word association given by the audiences pre- and post-show. There was a larger reduction in negative stereotypes from the girls after the show, especially in the 'nerdy' and 'crazy' stereotypes. The show saw an increase in both boys' and girls' perceptions of the 'helpful' nature of science and engineering. It was also found that some students may not want to do a STEM job because of the perceived dangerous nature of the job.

items.title: Non-intrusive modal decomposition of transport-dominated data
items.summary: We derive a non-intrusive modal decomposition method for positive transport-dominated datasets. We derive our method by generalizing an optimization-centric formulation of the Proper Orthogonal Decomposition. We propose two principles as a basis for this generalization. The first is that the Wasserstein distance is a more effective measure of the approximation error for transport-dominated problems, and the second is that the smoothness of the low-dimensional trajectories must be taken into account during the reconstruction. The framework is sufficiently flexible that domain-expert knowledge, in the form of inequality constraints, can be easily included. These features are demonstrated on synthetic problems and on data from a wildland fire simulation. Our method is based on the Shifted POD, which models the data as the sum of modes undergoing different coordinate transformations, but unlike the bulk of Shifted POD literature we do not assume that the correct transformation parameters are known. For a fixed number of modes, we observe a reduction of the reconstruction error of up to $43\%$ with respect to the Shifted POD baseline, despite the fact that the baseline assumes a-priori knowledge of the coordinate transformation parameters and the proposed method does not.

items.title: Raman-induced Kerr effect and heating in diamond
items.summary: We fully characterize the polarization-dependent third-order nonlinear susceptibility in a diamond crystal using phase-sensitive nondegenerate pump-probe spectroscopy near 1~$μ$m wavelength. Measuring the frequency-domain phase shift and amplitude change of the probe pulse as a function of polarization and probe wavelength allows direct extraction of the full anisotropic $χ^{(3)}$ response, including the Raman contribution. We find that the polarization dependence of the two-beam coupling contribution for the Raman component differs from that predicted solely using one-beam selection rules. We measure a Kerr coefficient that is within the range of reported values in the literature, and our measured anisotropy parameters satisfy Kleinman symmetry, as expected. Our measured Raman polarizability agrees, after scaling for its dispersion, with a Brillouin-referenced measurement at 514.5~nm [Grimsditch and Ramdas, Phys. Rev. B \textbf{11}, 3139 (1975)], but is lower than measurements from absolute Raman cross sections. The same technique could be used to measure other materials with relatively high phonon frequencies, and it complements measurements of the Kerr contribution of low-frequency modes using impulsive stimulated Raman scattering (ISRS). When the pump-probe difference frequency matches the phonon resonance, Raman-enabled two-photon absorption occurs; we directly measure the resulting heat deposition in diamond using time-resolved beam deflection of a continuous-wave laser. The measurement technique demonstrated here is capable of precise absolute $χ^{(3)}$ measurements and will enable quantitative stimulated Raman heating microscopy, with potential extensions to thermal conductivity metrology.

items.title: A basis-set-free reference for the exact exchange-energy density and functional development
items.summary: The exact local exchange-energy density, obtained from the Slater potential of the Hartree-Fock exchange hole, is a central ingredient of Becke's B05 and B13 functionals and of many other local hybrids. It is usually evaluated in a Gaussian basis, so the local quantity retains a pointwise basis-set incompleteness error. We describe here a basis-set-free numerical code that solves the Kohn-Sham problem on real-space grids for atoms, diatomics, and polyatomics, and returns the exact local exchange-energy density together with the density, its derivatives, the kinetic-energy density, and the reverse Becke-Roussel hole quantities. Reconstructed from the published record of Becke's non-public NUMOL code, AXEL reproduces numerical atomic references through krypton, scalar-relativistic uranium orbital energies, and Becke's diatomic spectroscopic constants. We then extend the original local-density numerical framework to generalized-gradient and hybrid functionals. Comparisons with the independent adaptive-multiwavelet code MRChem give sub-millihartree agreement for Hartree-Fock and PBE0. The same calculations agree with large Gaussian-basis references to a similar level of accuracy. Atom-centred eXact Electronic Limit (AXEL) is intended as both a basis-set-free numerical reference and a platform for exchange-hole-based density-functional development.

items.title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics
items.summary: Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics are fast alternatives to physics-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Their foundational limitation is a lack of zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, which results in an expensive, custom training campaign for each new vehicle design. Similar to pretrained models in other fields, a pretrained surrogate should adapt to a new vehicle class using only a few simulations and stay accurate on its pretraining domain. No prior study has systematically tested this transfer behavior. We conduct a large-scale, controlled benchmarking study on five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets. These datasets differ from the source in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions. We find that fine-tuning these surrogates outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of the comparisons and lowers the accuracy of the surrogate on its source dataset. We introduce GeoReplay, a geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay that keeps source simulations resembling the target in training and applies their updates only when they agree with the target gradient. A risk bound separates geometric coverage from differences in the simulated physics, and we prove that every sufficiently small GeoReplay step decreases the target training objective. GeoReplay lowers the source error of fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings and matches its target accuracy.

items.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part I: The gravity force term
items.summary: The OpenFOAM solver interFoam for incompressible two-phase flows combines the single-phase PISO/PIMPLE algorithm for the pressure-velocity coupling with an interface advection step. It relies on the standard finite volume discretisation of the momentum equation, which assumes smooth fields, but across a water-air interface the density jumps by a factor of about 1000. The geometric Volume-of-Fluid method isoAdvector, used in interIsoFoam, made the advection step consistent with a sharp interface, but spurious velocities near it remain due to the momentum discretisation. This series revisits it term by term. Here we treat the gravity term, which acts only at the interface and depends on the local interface height. Both solvers crudely assign this height using the face centre positions. We show that this is a key source of the spurious air velocities. Taking the height from the reconstructed interface instead gives an exact discrete balance between pressure and gravity for a horizontal interface on any mesh. We implement this geometric gravity model in a new solver, interIsoGoam. In a tilted box of still water, where the original solvers give air speeds of metres per second, it keeps the velocity of order $10^{-9}$ m/s. This holds for density ratios up to $10^7$ and, with a hydrostatic initial pressure, on skewed and locally refined meshes. In a progressive wave, interIsoGoam has the lowest maximum velocity of the three solvers. At maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below it therefore needs up to 43 % fewer steps and up to 38 % less wall-clock time. At 0.5 the wave grows by up to 12 % over 15 periods, so we recommend 0.1 or less. One error remains, namely an overprediction of the horizontal water velocity below the wave crest. All three solvers exhibit this error, which grows steadily with time. In Part II we trace this error to the implicit discretisation of the momentum convection term.

items.title: Shedding Light on Quantum Non-Classicality: Witnessing Wigner Negativity with Free Electrons
items.summary: Certifying quantum non-classicality like Wigner negativity typically demands full optical state tomography. This work introduces a noise-resilient framework for witnessing optical Wigner negativity using phase-resolved quantum photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (QPINEM). By mapping electron coherences directly to symmetrically ordered optical characteristic functions within a coupling-limited phase-space region, the protocol bypasses full optical reconstruction. A post-measurement witness matrix is constructed via Bochner's theorem from recorded electron spectra, where negative eigenvalues certify non-classicality. To ensure reliability under realistic experimental conditions, a noise-aware selection procedure decouples discovery from statistical validation. Benchmarked across various optical preparations-including vacuum-Fock superpositions, odd cat states, and GKP states-the protocol provides a statistically bounded pathway for probing quantum features with free electrons.

items.title: xTBloom: GPU Batching for High-Throughput GFN-xTB Calculations
items.summary: Conformational searches and multiwindow free-energy sampling require large numbers of GFN-xTB energy and force evaluations across molecular conformations and sampling windows. Processing each system separately on a GPU makes it difficult to amortize memory management, host-device data transfer, and kernel-launch overhead. Here, we present xTBloom, a GPU batching library for GFN-xTB energy and force evaluations. xTBloom sorts evaluation queues by atomic orbital (AO) count before forming batches, accommodates size differences through a native ragged layout, maintains independent self-consistent charge (SCC) and failure states for each system, and selects execution paths according to data residency. We focus the quantitative evaluation on GFN2-xTB through cross-program comparisons on QM9 and OMol25, CPU-CUDA comparisons, finite-difference force checks, and controlled failure tests. On a near-size OMol25 workload, GPU execution achieved a 2.9-fold speedup over xTBloom's single-core CPU backend. A companion LAMMPS plugin integrates cross-window batching with periodic quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) simulation. In a short synchronized test with 48 windows on one GPU, the complete coupled workflow achieved an aggregate speedup of approximately 14 over sequential execution of the same windows. These results demonstrate the throughput benefits of batched GFN-xTB evaluation for repeated electronic-structure calculations and multiwindow sampling.

items.title: Design and Modeling of Graded Base III-Nitride HBTs for High-Frequency Applications
items.summary: This work analyzes the high-frequency performance constraints of AlGaN/GaN heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) and proposes a novel band-engineered graded base N-polar AlGaN/GaN HBT and evaluates the RF performances. Unlike conventional p-GaN base designs, we propose a graded base in the N-polar orientation which offers polarization-induced hole accumulation with quasi-electric field-assisted minority carrier transport. The proposed design simultaneously mitigates the longstanding current crowding, Webster effect, and conventional base resistance limitations. Using well-calibrated two-dimensional TCAD simulations, the proposed compositionally graded base HBT projects peak f_T/f_{max} of 190/200 GHz with a power density (V_{br}I_{max}/8 > 20 W/mm), offering a promising pathway toward simultaneous high-frequency and high-power GaN millimeter-wave electronics.

items.title: 4D-TEMPO: Differentiable 4D-STEM ptychography via fast Physics Optimizers
items.summary: Electron ptychography recovers atomic structure from 4D-STEM data: diffraction patterns at multiple positions of a scanned probe. Current codes reconstruct an image and read atoms off it, or fit atoms under an $L_1$ loss; neither gives per-atom uncertainty. We propose 4D-TEMPO, a differentiable physical renderer that fits the atoms, the microscope, and the detector directly to the recorded electron counts under a Poisson likelihood. The output is a list of atoms, each a Gaussian primitive with a 3D position, a thermal width, and a model-conditional error bar from the Fisher information. The Fisher information also conditions the solver, gives the dose (electrons per Å$^2$) each parameter needs, and separates calibration from imaging. On a simulated WSe$_2$ bilayer, starting from the published reconstruction, fitted atoms cut in-plane error by a third (3.2 vs. 4.8 pm) and depth error by 40-61% against its 3D peaks. Depth comes from multiple scattering into the dark field, the faint counts outside the direct beam. The two layers, $10\times$ closer than the depth of field, separate; per-atom depth then follows the layer geometry. When the model is well specified, the bars are calibrated (69% of position coordinates within $1σ$). On experimental WSe$_2$, fitted atoms predict held-out patterns better than the three published codes we test. With free probe modes where atoms are incomplete, the same likelihood predicts best on all three held-out benchmarks, matches every WSe$_2$ baseline in 5 min against up to 20.5 h, and passes torchslice at its released setting 180$\times$ sooner on PrScO$_3$. Per-atom error bars, planned doses, and fast reconstruction point to low-dose, real-time 3D imaging of beam-sensitive and dynamic materials.

items.title: Electric combined-field-only P1 Galerkin BEM for PEC scattering with scalar Helmholtz operators
items.summary: We develop a Galerkin boundary element method for the indirect electric field-only combined-field integral equation (ECFOIE) for perfectly electrically conducting obstacles with smooth surfaces. The method is free of low-frequency breakdown and of spurious resonances. It applies scalar Helmholtz operators componentwise, so that fast scalar solvers can be reused, with less memory than a Rao-Wilton-Glisson (RWG) discretization. The iteration count of the Calderón-regularized ECFOIE (R-ECFOIE) is constant under mesh refinement and, with a complex-wavenumber Calderón regularizer, grows only mildly with frequency. The discretization uses continuous, nodal piecewise-linear basis functions on flat triangular meshes, with essentially as many unknowns as an RWG discretization, and tangential and normal projections and the mean curvature of the obstacle's surface carry the vector structure. On flat meshes the curvature is concentrated on the edges, and we average the edge measure obtained from the first variation of area over vertex patches, which gives sparse curvature matrices. At low frequency, four Lagrange-multiplier constraints on the induced charge and on the longitudinal dipole moments of the far field keep the R-ECFOIE accurate in the quasi-static regime, tested on scatterers eight orders of magnitude smaller than the wavelength. Under mesh refinement, the errors decrease at about second order. A Helmholtz resonator, a rounded Fichera cube, and a smoothed Stanford bunny are compared with electric field integral equation (EFIE) solutions, and the first two also with electrostatic references at extreme low frequency.

items.title: A boundary integral formulation for microscale Marangoni surfing
items.summary: We consider a model for collections of surfactant-producing particles moving along the surface of a viscous fluid under their self-generated Marangoni flows. Such systems are challenging due to their nonlocal nature: particle motion is coupled to Marangoni stresses distributed across the entire fluid surface and to the resulting flows in the bulk. In the low Reynolds and Péclet number limit, we reduce these nonlocal effects to a system of integral equations supported solely on the particles and their boundaries. This formulation is not only computationally tractable, but also provides a framework for systematically coarse-graining many-particle systems. Numerical simulations, performed with a custom spectral method, show collective dynamics are highly sensitive to shape. In particular, among elliptical particles, we find prolate particles tend to attract while oblate particles tend to repel, and these geometric details control the stability of polarized populations. We rationalize these behaviors through a far-field expansion of the boundary integral equations and its corresponding reduced-order model.

items.title: Characterizing adsorption thermodynamics in carbon capture materials: an efficient first-principles approach
items.summary: Porous materials offer a vast design space for CO$_2$ capture, whose exploration hinges on efficient and accurate first-principles predictions of the thermodynamics governing adsorption. However, simulating isotherms and heats of adsorption using grand canonical molecular simulations is extremely computationally expensive when combined with accurate ab initio treatments of the molecular interactions, limiting screening to low-pressure uptake encoded in the Henry constant. Identifying and designing the best CO$_2$ capture materials requires a strategy that can efficiently calculate their adsorption properties using ab initio potential energy surfaces such as those now available from foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Here we develop a neural classical density functional (cDFT) framework for carbon capture processes that allows direct calculation of adsorption isotherms from low to high loading limits of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) without grand canonical simulations. We demonstrate the success of our approach by calculating the ab initio adsorption isotherms for over 5,000 experimentally reported MOFs. From our screening, we show how these materials can be characterized using four isotherm shapes, arising from their pore size and binding sites, which the Henry constant cannot distinguish. We show that these shapes, rather than the binding strength alone, decide which MOFs suit which process: small pores with strong binding sites for vacuum and temperature swings at low pressure, large pores with weakly binding walls for pressure swings. Finally, we identify the most promising candidates by weighing their working capacity against the energy needed for regeneration.

items.title: Polycentrality in Urban Socioecological Systems: A Multilayer Analysis of Social Infrastructure in Iztapalapa, Mexico City
items.summary: The spatial distribution of infrastructure and activities, along with the networks and interactions that connect them, is key to understanding the relationship between urban form, function, and sustainability from a complex systems perspective. Within this dynamic relationship, the extent to which localized social infrastructure can reinforce existing functional centralities or create conditions for the emergence of new ones remains insufficiently understood. This study examines these relationships through the UTOPÍAS program in Iztapalapa, Mexico City, where 15 public social facilities have been established across a historically underserved urban territory. We develop a multilayer network framework integrating pedestrian infrastructure, GTFS-based public transport services, and UTOPÍAS as a target layer to assess multimodal connectivity, travel-time accessibility, and spatial coverage. These conditions are examined alongside indicators of local economic centrality (PCI and wPCI) to investigate how infrastructure interdependencies relate to the functional organization of urban space. The analysis reveals spatial heterogeneity in multimodal accessibility and differences in the integration of UTOPÍAS with existing transport networks. By relating these patterns to pre-existing economic centralities, we examine whether distributed social infrastructure may reinforce established functional centers or create conditions favorable to emerging centralities, without assuming that spatial decentralization necessarily produces polycentrality. The findings contribute a relational, data-driven approach to understanding how social infrastructure and mobility shape urban functions, emphasizing accessibility and territorial integration as critical conditions for more equitable and sustainable urban development.

items.title: Instability of layered two-phase flow in a vertical plane channel
items.summary: The equilibrium two-phase flows in a vertical plane channel are explored by adopting an approximate Boussinesq-like model. The class of stationary parallel flows examined in this paper features three-layer configurations in which the central core is less dense than the peripheral layers. Such flows are considered purely buoyant, induced by the density difference between the phases. The simplified scheme leads to a formulation where the parameters driving the transition to linear instability of the equilibrium flow are the Archimedes number and the dimensionless positions of the interfaces between the phases. The analysis takes into consideration symmetric and asymmetric flows, including, as special cases, also two-layer configurations with one phase close to the left-hand boundary wall and the other close to the right-hand wall. In particular, the completely antisymmetric flow, where the equilibrium velocity profile is an odd function of the transverse coordinate, shows up as the least stable configuration among those examined in this study.

items.title: GenerativeQC: A Generative, GPU-Accelerated Quantum Chemistry Program
items.summary: GenerativeQC is an open-source, GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry program that computes energies and analytic nuclear forces from Hartree-Fock (HF) and density functional theory (DFT) to closed-shell density-fitted CCSD(T) and an MP2-assisted CCSD(T)/complete-basis-set (CBS) composite. Its scientific compiler translates symbolic equations into C++ and CUDA code and uses automatic differentiation to generate the derivative and response programs that analytic forces require. A native runtime executes these programs together with hand-written iterative solvers and integral routines. Across HF and DFT benchmarks for eight methods on water clusters of up to 96 atoms, GenerativeQC is faster than GPU4PySCF in all 128 comparisons on an RTX 5090 GPU and in all but two comparisons on an H100 GPU. For correlated wave functions, compiler-generated derivative contractions and transpose Jacobian operators enable complete density-fitted CCSD(T) and CCSD(T)/CBS analytic forces on GPUs, completing a CCSD(T)/CBS energy-and-force calculation for heptane (23 atoms) in 4.5 min on a single H100 GPU (17 min on RTX 5090).

items.title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED
items.summary: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.

items.title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy
items.summary: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves $\sim\!300$ nm lateral and $\sim\!650$ nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and $<\!60$ nm localization precision in vivo. Compared with two-photon point scanning, the lower illumination NA delivers order-of-magnitude lower peak intensity, enabling $>\!5\times$ faster volumetric acquisition (up to $3.25 \times 10^6$ voxels s$^{-1}$). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by $\sim\!2\times$ and restores volumetric resolving power by $>\!2\times$ relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

items.title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
items.summary: A physics-based reduced-order model unifies curved-meniscus inertia, viscous losses and nonsmooth contact-line stick-slip in a passive port-Hamiltonian formulation for lateral sloshing in cylindrical tanks. Dirichlet-Neumann and Jacobi operators describe inertia and restoring forces, while a convex potential combines bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line dissipation. Analytical propagation between stick-slip events supports faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft translation and sloshing. The viscous closure agrees within 5% with a reference Stokes calculation, and the model reproduces the Henderson-Miles modal measurements and the Cocciaro hysteretic decay. Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduces the root-mean-square frequency error from 24 to 4%. For flight and ground tests from the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE), frequency errors range from 0.9 to 7.1%, while ideal contact lines underestimate the damping ratios from the MODE fits by 38-87%. One hysteresis width, calibrated on the lowest orbital water excitation, predicts higher orbital excitations and the ground test with normalised force errors of 11-35%, against 149-208% for an ideal pinned line. It predicts 8.5% resonance softening against 7.3% measured, which the tested one-parameter damping laws miss. Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies motivate damping ranges in spacecraft control analyses.

items.title: Bogoliubov self-consistent $GW$ and second-order Green's function methods for attractive fermionic interactions
items.summary: Describing fermionic systems with attractive interactions, such as superconductors and atomic nuclei, beyond the mean-field level remains a central challenge. In this work, we investigate the performance of Bogoliubov fully self-consistent $GW$ (Bog.~sc$GW$) and second-order Green's function (Bog.~scGF2) methods, implemented within a unified imaginary-time and imaginary-frequency framework. Using two attractive Hubbard lattices ($4\times4$ and $2\times8$) as a model study and benchmarking against full configuration interaction (FCI), we find that, for these systems, Bog.~scGF2 provides a more accurate description than Bog.~sc$GW$. In particular, Bog.~sc$GW$ systematically overestimates the correlation energy, with errors increasing rapidly as the attractive interaction strength grows. These results suggest the importance of exchange contributions in such strongly correlated fermionic systems, even when exchange effects are included only at low order in perturbation theory.

items.title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
items.summary: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

items.title: The Structural Number of Parties: An Electoral-Outcome-Independent Baseline for Comparing Party-System Scale
items.summary: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

items.title: The Long and Winding Pore: Tuning Porosity in Templated Nanoporous Carbons
items.summary: Disordered materials pose a recurring challenge for molecular simulation: realistic structural models are often generated through thermal protocols in which several structural descriptors emerge simultaneously and cannot easily be varied independently. Nanoporous carbons constitute a particularly relevant example: pore size, wall order, curvature, and network tortuosity generally emerge as outcomes of the thermal preparation protocol, rather than being independently prescribed structural parameters. Moreover, for practical applications, models of porous materials should ideally exhibit a percolating pore network, capable of supporting end-to-end transport of adsorbed species through the material. To this end, here we introduce a hierarchy of templating strategies, built around a common melt-quench-anneal protocol driven by a machine-learned interatomic potential for carbon, that progressively separates these variables. A rigid cylindrical template interacting with the environment through a tunable Lennard-Jones potential provides independent control over pore size and local wall organization, while leaving the structural disorder of the surrounding carbon matrix essentially unchanged. Generalizing the template to a spring-connected, tortuous backbone further allows pore geometry and curvature to be prescribed without qualitatively altering the local templating mechanism established for the straight pore. Finally, making the template mobile lets the growing carbon network reshape it in turn, which sharpens pore boundaries and allows sub-nanometer pore sizes to be targeted precisely, as needed for applications such as supercapacitor electrodes. Ultimately, this approach enables systematic studies of structure-property relationships in porous materials for applications such as energy storage, desalination and gas capture.

items.title: Projection of global daily CO2 emissions in 2026
items.summary: Global fossil-fuel combustion and industrial-process CO2 emissions remain close to historical highs, yet the recent slowdown in growth is difficult to assess before conventional inventories become available. We project emissions for 2026 and examine daily departures during major climate and energy disruptions. We fit Prophet models to the latest five years of Carbon Monitor activity estimates for 47 region-sector series. We use these models to project daily emissions for October-December and combine them with activity estimates through September. Global emissions are estimated at 38.0 Gt CO2 in 2026, 34.1 Mt CO2 (-0.1%) below 2025. The hindcast-adjusted range for the annual change is -0.9% to +0.7%. Five September-cutoff hindcasts show lower mean daily errors and larger mean absolute annual biases for Prophet than for a seasonal-naive benchmark. Regional increases total 0.331 Gt and decreases total 0.365 Gt, so 95.1% of the 0.696 Gt gross movement cancels in the global sum. China contributes the largest reduction (-0.243 Gt), concentrated in industry and ground transport, whereas India contributes the largest increase (+0.222 Gt), led by power and industry. Heat-period power anomalies differ among countries and can be muted by summer averaging, while aviation and shipping show different disruption and recovery profiles. Resolving the near-zero global change reveals where reductions are concentrated and where continued growth offsets them, providing a timely basis for assessing the breadth of mitigation progress.

items.title: Scalable Non-Parametric Bayesian Inference of Free Energy Landscapes and Emission Functions from Observations
items.summary: Free-energy landscapes govern processes from protein conformational change to climate oscillations, but are typically observed only indirectly, through observables such as FRET intensity or optical-tweezer transmittance. Neither the landscape shape, nor the emission function mapping latent state to signal, is usually known, and distinct states may produce the same signal. We therefore infer landscape and emission function jointly and non-parametrically, using the exact non-linear Bayesian filtering likelihood, to fully use the information contained in observable trajectories that are often noisy, scarce and costly to acquire. A novel parallel-in-time algorithm makes this tractable: it is up to 27 times faster than sequential filtering on one GPU, scales near-ideally across GPUs, and, given enough resources, has runtime independent of trajectory length. We demonstrate the method on a single-protein optical tweezer recording, where distinct conformations produce the same signal, and beyond biology on the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and financial market volatility.

items.title: Physics-based Tabulation Approach for Rotating Detonation Engines
items.summary: High-fidelity simulations of rotating detonation engines remain computationally expensive due to the strong coupling between compressible flow dynamics and stiff chemical kinetics. The coexistence of deflagrative and detonative combustion, along with shock interactions and rapid thermodynamic changes, further challenges conventional reduced-order chemistry models. This work presents a multi-mode tabulation framework that replaces detailed chemical kinetic integration with precomputed thermochemical states and source terms while accounting for variations in the local thermodynamic state. The key novelty lies in a unified treatment of distinct combustion regimes, wherein homogeneous reactor solutions describe deflagrative combustion and post-detonation reactions up to the Chapman-Jouguet (CJ) point, while an equilibrium isentropic expansion model captures supersonic relaxation beyond the CJ state. The framework is evaluated against detailed chemistry across progressively complex configurations, including homogeneous ignition, one-dimensional detonations, and a two-dimensional rotating detonation engine (RDE). The tabulated model accurately reproduces ignition delays and captures the initiation and sustained propagation of detonation waves across varying mixture compositions. Furthermore, the framework reconstructs the complete thermodynamic evolution along an RDE streamline, including post-injection expansion, detonation, post-detonation expansion, and oblique shock interactions, directly from conserved flow variables. These results demonstrate the capability of multi-mode tabulation to represent coupled combustion, shock, and expansion processes within a single thermodynamically responsive framework, offering a promising route toward computationally efficient simulations of detonative combustion across a broad range of applications.

items.title: Optical readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors with SiPMs
items.summary: Scintillation light readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) is used for imaging and track reconstruction applications including in optical Time Projection Chambers (TPC). Typically, high resolution CCD or CMOS imaging sensors are used and PMTs can be employed to obtain auxiliary timing information. We report on the optical readout of MPGDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) which enables limited spatial resolution. Arrays of SiPMs were used to read out Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) and Glass Micromegas amplification stages. Center of gravity reconstruction of hit positions yields a spatial resolution of approximately 1.35 mm for signals shared across multiple SiPMs. High gain of the amplification stage as well as the SiPMs enables good signal sharing and is advantageous for position reconstruction.

items.title: Modelling population distribution across cities on spatial networks using the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems
items.summary: We investigate the urban population distribution of the Italian region of Sardinia through the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems on spatial networks, interpreting cities both as agents and vertices of a graph, and representing interurban links as edges. We consider various emigration rules to model the interactions between agents, obtaining two main results: the bimodal lognormal fit of the total population distribution among cities and the Pareto fit of the tail. Overall, our model provides results consistent with the actual distribution derived from ISTAT data of Sardinia; furthermore, the bimodal lognormal fit generally follows the distribution tail more accurately than the Pareto one, although the two coincide in the first half.

items.title: Generation of neutron Bessel beams
items.summary: Matter waves can exhibit structured wavefields analogous to those of light, offering new means of controlling the spatial and angular-momentum degrees of freedom of massive particles. Bessel beams are a fundamental class of structured waves that exhibit non-diffracting propagation, self-healing, and well-defined orbital angular momentum (OAM). Here, we experimentally realize neutron Bessel beams by imprinting a nanoscale conical phase gradient onto a neutron wavefront. By incorporating azimuthal phase gradients, we generate zeroth-, third-, and sixth-order Bessel beams, demonstrating direct control of both the OAM and radial structure of a massive particle. We also propose a neutron Bessel-grating interferometer, complementary to established optical and electron interferometric methods, in which varying the radial grating period by approximately 100 nm yields a controlled Gouy phase shift of $π$. These results establish neutron Bessel beams as a new platform for diffractive neutron focusing and provide an experimental foundation for theoretical studies of Bessel beams in neutron scattering, decay, and OAM characterization.

items.title: The state of nuclear data for fusion activation simulations
items.summary: This report compares decay-heat calculations made with four nuclear data libraries, TENDL-2025, ENDF/B-VIII.1, JEFF-4.0 and JENDL-5, against the JAEA FNS decay-heat benchmark. The main comparison uses the 2000 campaign, in which 73 foils were irradiated for five minutes in a mostly 14 MeV neutron field and their decay heat was measured for about an hour. The 1996 seven-hour campaign, with 29 foils and cooling times of up to 400 days, is compared separately and is not included in the rankings. Over the 69 elemental foils solved by all four libraries, the median deviation from the measurement (the mean absolute C/E deviation of each foil) is JENDL-5 17 percent, TENDL-2025 19 percent, JEFF-4.0 22 percent and ENDF/B-VIII.1 44 percent. No library is best everywhere: JENDL-5 on 24, JEFF-4.0 on 18, TENDL-2025 on 17 and ENDF/B-VIII.1 on 10 of the foils. For each element the report breaks the heat down by product and lists the nuclear data on which the libraries differ, and the final sections propose measurements, including enriched-isotope irradiations, that would resolve the largest differences.

items.title: Attosecond soft X-ray pulses generated by chirp-dispersed manipulation in an XFEL reveal nonlinear core-electron dynamics in neon
items.summary: Free-electron lasers deliver intense attosecond X-ray pulses, which are the key to studying electron dynamics in specifically targeted electronic states, but come at the expense of complicated generation schemes and stochastic pulse shapes. Here, we demonstrate a novel and simple operation concept based on dispersive manipulation of the lasing electron bunch and capable of working with the full 4.5 MHz repetition rate at the European XFEL in Germany. Using a high-fidelity single-shot temporal characterisation, we detect X-ray pulses with durations of down to 200 attoseconds and peak powers reaching into the terawatt regime at ~1 keV photon energy. As a direct application, we present simultaneous measurements of nonlinear X-ray-matter interaction via time-resolved electron spectroscopy. Using the pulse duration retrieval and restricting the durations to a regime where individual X-ray pulses are shorter than the single-core-hole life time in neon atoms, we reveal an otherwise hidden peak-intensity dependence in the nonlinear dynamics of double-core-hole formation. Our results shed light on highly transient intermediate steps in complex electronic dynamics of systems driven far off their equilibrium state, and thus promise to help build the conceptual bridge between fundamental physics processes and real-world photo reactions.

items.title: Hydrodynamics of robotic micro-swimmers in confinement
items.summary: Inspired by seminal work by E.M. Purcell, we discuss the problem of predicting and optimizing the performance of autonomous robots swimming in confinement. Our approach is based on the explicit numerical resolution of the fluid flow induced by the swimmer, and it is validated experimentally on a cm-size prototype composed of a cargo head and a rotating propulsive tail. Using hydrodynamic scaling, we predict the performance of replicas of our prototype scaled down to mm- and sub-mm-size to test the feasibility of autonomous micro-robots navigating in narrow vessels. The main result of our theoretical, computational, and experimental analysis is that, while hydrodynamics seems to place no fundamental obstruction to the vision of autonomous micro-robots navigating in narrow lumens inside the human body, it does provide useful and strict guidelines for rational design at different length scales.

items.title: Early spectra of AT2017gfo from scaled 3D merger ejecta: mass--velocity distribution, 3D structure, and treatment of line opacity
items.summary: We present ARTIS radiative transfer calculations for neutron star merger ejecta with line-by-line opacities, wavelength-calibrated lanthanide data, and time-dependent r-process compositions and thermalisation, testing how the early kilonova depends on the mass-velocity distribution, dimensionality, and line treatment. We rescale 3D dynamical ejecta from a merger simulation in density and velocity to approximate AT2017gfo. Mass scaling alone provides good agreement with the bolometric light curve but inconsistent spectra. With velocities additionally halved, the model also reproduces the observed spectra at 1.4, 2.4, and (albeit less accurately) 3.4 days. The Sr II triplet contributes most to the 10500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ peak, and La III and Gd III to the 13500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ shoulder. Although hydrodynamically not fully self-consistent, this model is to our knowledge the first kilonova model based on calibrated atomic data that reproduces the light curve and main spectral features of the early AT2017gfo, suggesting that total (dynamical plus post-merger) ejecta with higher mass, lower velocity, and similar composition compared to our dynamical ejecta could explain AT2017gfo. A 2D azimuthal average mixes lanthanide-poor with lanthanide-rich regions, smooths the density, and makes the averaged model three times fainter at 1 day and redder throughout than the 3D model, highlighting the importance of 3D modelling. We compare the line-by-line macroatom treatment with expansion-opacity and line-binned schemes with thermal redistribution, using identical atomic data. Luminosities agree to $\lesssim 10$ per cent after 1 day, but the expansion-opacity scheme, unlike converged line-binned schemes, overestimates the spectral flux by up to 20 per cent, which can bias inferred abundances.

items.title: Computational regimes in matrix-product-state-based quantum trajectory simulations
items.summary: Efficient simulation of open quantum systems is central to modeling noisy quantum hardware and many-body dynamics. In trajectory-based tensor network methods, cost is often associated with trajectory-level quantities such as entanglement growth or bond dimension. However, the total cost of a fixed-accuracy simulation also depends on statistical sampling and on how many trajectories can run in parallel. Here we characterize computational regimes in matrix product state (MPS)-based quantum trajectory simulations by separating memory per trajectory, runtime per trajectory, and sampling effort. Two dimensionless ratios compare the bond dimensions and trajectory counts required by physically equivalent unravelings to reach the same target accuracy. When memory limits parallel execution, a smaller trajectory representation reduces the work per sample and allows more samples to run concurrently. Our scaling model predicts when this additional benefit reverses the preferred unraveling between execution limited by workers and execution limited by memory. Benchmarks across several noise channels illustrate how physical and numerical parameters change the bond dimension and sampling requirements. As an application, a pilot protocol estimates the inputs to this regime classification for a specified problem. These results show how the computational cost of an unraveling depends jointly on trajectory complexity, statistical convergence, and available hardware resources.

items.title: Data-driven impeller model for efficient large eddy simulations of metastable von Kármán flows
items.summary: The von Kármán turbulent swirling flow exhibits intriguing large-scale metastable dynamics, including low-frequency state switching. The study of state switching demands long-duration high-fidelity simulations at high Reynolds numbers that capture the flow generated by the impellers. Blade-resolved Large Eddy Simulations (LES) are computationally prohibitive, limiting access to these slow dynamics. Here, we develop a model for the action of the impellers on the flow using experimental data from Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and torque measurements of the von Kármán flow. The impeller-region velocity is parametrized via B-splines and coupled to the LES through momentum forcing. An initial set of B-spline coefficients is inferred using the Optimizing a DIscrete Loss (ODIL) framework constrained by the Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations, PIV measurements in the optically accessible portion of the device, and impeller torque measurements. The coefficients are then refined by the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), which minimizes the discrepancy between the LES time-averaged velocity and torque and their experimental counterparts. Using the data-driven impeller model, we perform long-duration LES of the von Kármán flow. We find that the simulation reproduces the mean flow in the bulk and displays metastable state-switching dynamics. We further show that these metastable states are not axisymmetric and consist of an alternating four-cell flow pattern that slowly rotates around the axis of the cylindrical vessel. The proposed approach provides a practical and computationally efficient route to investigating large-scale dynamics in impeller-driven turbulent flows.

items.title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
items.summary: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

items.title: Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic
items.summary: The frequent static failure of CMOS logic gates at ultra-low voltages has historically been perceived as a strict barrier to extreme voltage scaling: this paper introduces a statistical circuit law proving this intuition wrong. We discovered a universal power law connecting gate and circuit static failure probabilities, revealing that circuit failure requires the simultaneous breakdown of an entire gate cluster rather than a single component. Because the required cluster size increases rapidly as voltage drops, low-voltage \textit{sub-digital} logic exhibits surprising inherent resilience to static failure. This insight stems from new theoretical tools we developed to quantify static failure, extending well beyond conventional voltage-margin analysis. Consequently, sub-digital processors could potentially offer a viable, near-term solution to drastically reduce the energy demands of AI.

items.title: Numerical study of nitrogen oxides chemistry during plasma assisted combustion in a sequential combustor
items.summary: Plasma Assisted Combustion (PAC) is a promising technology to enhance the combustion of lean mixtures prone to instabilities and flame blow-off. Although many PAC experiments demonstrated combustion enhancement, several studies report an increase in NOx emissions. The aim of this study is to determine the kinetic pathways leading to NOx formation in the second stage of a sequential combustor assisted by Nanosecond Repetitively Pulsed Discharges (NRPDs). For this purpose, Large Eddy Simulation (LES) associated with an accurate description of the combustion/NOx chemistry and a phenomenological model of the plasma kinetics is used. Detailed kinetics 0-Dimensional reactors complement the study. First, the LES setup is validated by comparison with experiments. Then, the NOx chemistry is analyzed. For the conditions of operation studied, it is shown that the production of atomic nitrogen in the plasma by direct electron impact on nitrogen molecules increases the formation of NO. Then, the NO molecules are transported through the turbulent flame without being strongly affected. This study illustrates the need to limit the diatomic nitrogen dissociation process in order to mitigate harmful emissions. More generally, the very good agreement with experimental measurements demonstrates the capability of LES combined with accurate models to predict the NRPD effects on both turbulent combustion and NOx emissions.

items.title: Mid-Infrared Integrated Acousto-Optic Phase Modulation on GaAs/AlGaAs
items.summary: We demonstrate a mid-infrared (7.5-10 um) integrated acousto-optic phase modulator operating at 460MHz based on a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure. The combination of broad mid-infrared transparency and piezoelectric properties of GaAs based structures allows monolithic integration of all the device functions (electro-acoustic transduction and acousto-optic interaction) on a single material platform. Addressing the challenge presented by comparable mid-infrared and acoustic wavelengths, simultaneous propagation and confinement of surface acoustic waves and guided light is achieved using a deep-etched sub-wavelength grating. We develop a comprehensive and quantitative simulation framework to design the modulator devices, characterize their acoustic properties in a heterodyne vibrometer and perform a full, quantitative analysis of the device performance by inserting them in an integrated Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Remarkable agreement with simulations validates the proposed design flow, and opens the way to improved integrated acousto-optic devices operating in the longer end of the mid-infrared.

items.title: Machine-learned potentials for iron oxides at extreme conditions
items.summary: Reliable phase stability requires accurate relative free energies, which small force errors alone do not guarantee. We develop atomic-cluster-expansion potentials for five iron oxides from Fe$_2$O to Fe$_2$O$_3$, covering crystalline and liquid states at 140--260\,GPa and 1000--11000\,K, with electronic and ionic temperatures matched. Force-dominated training leaves systematic energy offsets between structure families of up to 41\,meV/atom that persist despite additional training data. Stronger energy weighting and weaker regularization largely remove these offsets, while converged k-point sampling prevents further composition-dependent biases. The final potentials achieve held-out energy errors of 2.0--5.5\,meV/atom and first-order free-energy errors within 3.4\,meV/atom for liquids at 5000--9000\,K. However, an untrained NiAs-type FeO phase exhibits a free-energy error of 57\,meV/atom despite a low extrapolation grade. These results show that reliable phase-diagram calculations require control of relative energy offsets and explicit free-energy validation of every competing phase.

items.title: Fundamental-derivative criticality of ion-acoustic solitons in fluid-Poisson plasmas with general equations of state
items.summary: Non-ideal ion compressibility modifies the nonlinearity of ion-acoustic waves. In a fluid-Poisson plasma with Boltzmann electrons and a barotropic ion equation of state, we relate the quadratic KdV coefficient to the fundamental derivative of the effective acoustic pressure. Its vanishing marks loss of genuine nonlinearity. Higher derivatives of the equation of state determine whether the cubic reduction is focusing or defocusing and govern the quartic-flux reduction at simultaneous criticality. The exact Sagdeev formulation resolves compressive and rarefactive soliton branches and their Gardner unfolding. Exact continuation identifies an equation-of-state-controlled rarefactive double-layer boundary distinct from both the cubic critical point and an orbitwise pressure-slope threshold. As they approach this boundary, solitons develop a logarithmically widening flat top, and the exact Sagdeev quadrature quantitatively captures the standard saddle-passage law. Along the boundary toward the acoustic codimension-two point, exponential localisation lengths diverge while the amplitude vanishes. Full fluid-Poisson simulations confirm finite-time propagation of selected exact stationary profiles. Our results connect acoustic criticality, exact orbit admissibility, and equation-of-state-controlled solitary waves in dispersive plasmas.

items.title: Electrostatic interactions drive the self-assembly of secondary coat-protein layers around wild-type MS2 particles
items.summary: The protein capsids of many icosahedral RNA viruses can self-assemble in vitro in the absence of any host cell factors. For bacteriophage MS2 and related viruses, previous studies have focused on the role of specific RNA-protein interactions in driving the assembly process. However, the contribution of electrostatics remains unclear. We show that MS2 coat protein dimers can assemble into additional capsid layers around intact wild-type MS2 particles, even in the absence of free RNA. We characterize the size and morphology of the particles through transmission electron microscopy, gel electrophoresis, and dynamic light scattering, and we use binding and infectivity assays to determine how the maturation protein affects layer formation. Our results are consistent with a heterogeneous nucleation-and-growth assembly pathway, in which the nucleation barrier is controlled by the protein concentration, and electrostatic attraction between the positively charged coat proteins and negatively charged capsid drives growth. Interestingly, the secondary layers rarely fully encapsulate the wild-type particles, suggesting that elastic energy may limit their growth. These results highlight the importance of electrostatics in the assembly of protein shells, even in systems such as MS2 that are known for their strong, specific RNA-protein interactions.

items.title: OmniFish: A Bioinspired, Modular, Reconfigurable Soft Robotic Fish Enabling Multi-Modal Swimming
items.summary: In this work, we introduce OmniFish, a bioinspired modular soft robotic fish designed to emulate the full spectrum of body and/or caudal fin (BCF) locomotion modes within a single robotic platform. The design combines morphology averaging across representative fish species with a tendon-driven compliant segmented spine whose effective stiffness can be reconfigured through progressive mechanical jamming.
