items.summary: Unlike periodic field-intensity patterns, which can be generated by interference of coherent beams, periodic material structures are usually created by periodic modification. In contrast, we show here that a millimeter-long bundle of four conventional side-coupled optical fibers with a slowly varying transverse arrangement can support a nearly periodic array of whispering-gallery-mode microresonators, whose period can be tuned mechanically down to about $100\,μ\mathrm{m}$.

items.title: Online reduced-order modeling from primal solver trajectories for PDE-constrained optimization
items.summary: Repeated high-fidelity state and gradient evaluations make large-scale PDE-constrained optimization computationally expensive. Reduced-order modeling provides a natural way to reduce the cost of these repeated high-dimensional computations. However, existing reduced-order modeling approaches often rely on converged high-fidelity states for model construction or updating, while their reduced spaces may lose accuracy as the design moves beyond the region represented by the available data. To address these limitations, we present Reduced-order Trajectory-based Optimization (RETO), an online framework that constructs local reduced-order models (ROMs) directly from unconverged primal solver trajectories. Each local ROM is built from snapshots collected during a finite number of high-fidelity primal iterations, without requiring full-order convergence, and supports multiple low-cost state evaluations, adjoint-based gradient evaluations, and design updates. New solver trajectories are generated at updated design points to reconstruct the local ROM and continue the optimization. Across the Poisson inversion and logistic resource-allocation problems, RETO achieves solution quality comparable to that of full-order optimization, with speedups of 14.7 times and 8.49 times, respectively. Even for the more challenging airfoil inverse-design problems, RETO retains speedups of 2.52 to 3.13 times under subsonic and transonic conditions. These results demonstrate the value of unconverged primal solver trajectories as an online information source for reduced-order optimization, allowing the reduced basis to evolve with the design rather than requiring a basis that covers the entire design space in advance.

items.title: Optimisation of importance sampling implementation in rare-event shielding simulations using Geant4
items.summary: Rare-event search experiments demand ever-lower backgrounds, and the resulting radio-pure materials and suppressive shielding make related background simulations computationally expensive without event biasing. We present a method for optimising the widely used importance splitting and Russian roulette technique for rare-event searches, in which a whole number of equal-width importance layers fill the shielding geometry. Balancing relative uncertainty against execution time, we optimise the layer thickness for both $γ$-rays and neutrons, and across different shielding materials and thicknesses. Expressed as a multiple of the primary particle's mean free path, the optimal thickness generalises across energies for a given particle type and yields a physics-based prediction applicable to any shielding design. The same trend reveals that over-biasing is possible, with relative uncertainty worsening at high layer counts for fixed execution time. The optimal configuration gives an $\mathcal{O}$(20) gain in computational efficiency over the unbiased case.

items.title: Temperature Flips the Sign of the Hydrogen Response in Nanogranular Palladium Networks
items.summary: In nanogranular palladium networks, hydrogen uptake has two opposing effects on electrical resistance. Absorbed hydrogen scatters electrons within the particles, raising their resistance, while particle expansion narrows the gaps between them and lowers the junction resistance. Such networks are widely studied as resistive hydrogen sensors, and the sign of their net response is usually treated as a fixed property of the architecture. In networks grown by atomic layer deposition on macroporous silicon, we show that changing the operating temperature can reverse this sign at a fixed hydrogen concentration. A thermodynamic model indicates that scattering contributes less as temperature rises, allowing sub-angstroem changes in gap width to dominate. Where the two effects cancel, the network absorbs hydrogen yet gives the same reading as in hydrogen-free gas, so a leak could escape detection. Between 25 and 40 degrees Celsius, this cancellation point is predicted to rise over tenfold, crossing reported leak-alarm setpoints. At 55 degrees Celsius, the measured response stays negative but passes through a minimum, so a concentration above a setpoint can mimic one below it. Annealing at 200 degrees Celsius alters the calibration and turns the room-temperature response negative at the lowest concentration tested. Quantitative sensing therefore requires a defined thermal pretreatment and an operating temperature giving distinct signals across the intended concentration range. Response polarity becomes an operating parameter rather than a fixed property. More broadly, any nanoparticle network whose particles deform on sorption may show the same temperature-dependent competition between transport within and between particles, with implications for sensors and switches beyond palladium-hydrogen.

items.title: A Jump-Diffusion Model of Home Price Dynamics and Neighborhood Change
items.summary: We develop a dynamical model that links the fluctuations of individual home prices to changes in the full distribution of home prices in an urban area. We model the price of an individual home as a jump-diffusion stochastic differential equation. To capture the dynamic and hyper-local economic conditions that drive the residential real estate market, we allow all parameters to depend on both time and neighborhood. In the mean-field limit, we derive the associated Fokker-Planck partial integro-differential equation (PIDE) governing the evolution of the home price distribution in a neighborhood. We quantify spatial heterogeneity within a city by using the Wasserstein-2 distance to compare home price distributions across the city's neighborhoods. We validate our model using data from Boston, Massachusetts as a case study.

items.title: Cancellation of cryocooler-induced vibration in trapped-ion systems
items.summary: Mechanical cryocoolers offer numerous benefits for the operation of vacuum systems containing trapped atomic ions. However, the fidelity of laser-based gates can be degraded by phase noise induced by the cryocooler vibrations. We present a feed-forward vibration-cancellation system that directly measures inner shield displacement with an auxiliary interferometer and applies a compensating phase correction to the laser drive. The interferometer signal is demodulated, and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) system unwraps the displacement measurement signal, computes the required correction phase, and updates the RF drive of an in-line acousto-optic modulator (AOM) to correct for the vibration-induced dephasing. With cancellation active, the qubit coherence time improves from $3.0\pm0.4$ ms to $35\pm5$ ms, consistent with a simulation based on the measured vibration spectrum. We further validate the cancellation by artificially increasing the mechanical coupling of the cryocooler to the vacuum chamber. The vibration-induced decoherence rate is suppressed by a factor of approximately 70 at an RMS (root mean square) displacement of 0.65 $\mathrmμ$m.

items.title: Surrogate-assisted beam distribution shaping at the CERN Proton Synchrotron and Super Proton Synchrotron
items.summary: The Super Proton Synchrotron at CERN delivers protons to the North Area experimental facility at 400 GeV/c. The extracted beam is split twice vertically in the transfer line with Lambertson septa to serve three fixed-target experiments simultaneously. A significant fraction of the beam is lost during these splitting processes, driving radioactive activation of the Lambertson septa. This contribution investigates reducing the splitting losses by optimising the vertical beam distribution before extraction. The developed method relies on resonant excitation with the transverse damper, reshaping the Gaussian vertical profile into a uniform and ultimately bimodal distribution, with the excitation amplitude acting as a single continuous control knob. A loss reduction of up to 23.5 % was measured. In simulations, the vertical amplitude detuning is established as a second knob that reduces the resulting beam envelope. This technique was verified with measurements at the CERN Proton Synchrotron. Surrogate models based on generative deep learning were developed for efficient real-time validation and Bayesian system identification.

items.title: Mechanically induced self-propagating reactions within the realm of mechanochemistry: Fundamentals, overview, in situ monitoring and perspectives
items.summary: Mechanically induced self-propagating reaction (MSR) represents a promising but rather underexplored phenomenon within mechanochemistry, a solvent-free alternative to classical solution-based chemistry. In contrast to the gradual mechanochemical reactions, MSRs are sub-second combustive-like processes bringing about substantial benefits such as faster product formation, time efficiency, and lower energy consumption. Despite the fact that the mechanochemical field is in the research spotlight, MSR investigation remains on the periphery. This review aims to catalyze a renaissance in MSR fundamentals investigation by reviewing the current state-of-the-art. This is done via systematically reviewing the reaction systems that were reported to react via a MSR in the past twenty years, such as metal-metalloid ones (carbides, borides, silicides, and carbonitrides), metal chalcogenides, metal oxides, and other specific types of reactions. A couple of case studies are briefly reviewed for each system, and the comprehensive table follows afterward. The review also revisits the factors impacting the MSR course from milling conditions and reagent's properties point of view, showing either a direct or inverse relationship with MSR ignition time. The recent development in the in situ monitoring of mechanochemical reactions allowed to obtain some mechanistic insights into the MSR process, which are summarized in the last chapter.

items.title: Axion electrodynamics and the advection-diffusion structure of TEM modes in hollow-conductor waveguides
items.summary: We present a systematic investigation of transverse electromagnetic (TEM) modes in hollow-conductor waveguides filled with a dielectric medium described by axion electrodynamics. While such modes do not propagate in conventional single-conductor waveguides, the coupling of the axion field to an external magnetic field enables their propagation. We show that the resulting TEM modes are governed by an advection-diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential, establishing a direct mathematical connection between axion electrodynamics and advection-diffusion phenomena. We illustrate this connection through explicit solutions and field profiles for cylindrical waveguides, considering uniform and rigid rotational drift fields, both individually and in combination, as well as different values of the parameter controlling the advection-to-diffusion ratio (Péclet number). These results establish a transport-based framework for understanding how spatial variations of the axion-electrodynamics background shape the transverse electromagnetic fields in hollow-conductor waveguides.

items.title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
items.summary: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

items.title: Oblique incidence and non-commuting limits: a remark on the convergence of Fresnel integrals
items.summary: The Gaussian integrals of quantum mechanics and of paraxial optics are oscillatory and only conditionally convergent. Textbooks usually make them converge by adding a small imaginary part to the time or by analytic continuation. We point out that the one-dimensional Fresnel integral converges by itself, while in two dimensions the result depends on the shape of the expanding domain: over squares it converges, over discs it oscillates for ever. The second case is the field of a uniformly excited plane of dipoles, which Feynman uses to explain the refractive index. Lai, Lau and Wong showed that at oblique incidence the integral converges and that normal incidence is recovered in the limit; we note that the two limits do not commute, and that this provides a transparent introduction to the regularization of the time-sliced path integral, where the ordering of the integrations in time plays the role of the physical prescription.

items.title: Topological Control of Polaritonic Flatbands in Anisotropic van der Waals Metasurfaces
items.summary: Anisotropic van der Waals (vdW) materials exhibit direction-dependent optical and electronic properties, making them valuable for tailoring directional light-matter interactions. Rhenium disulfide (ReS$_2$) stands out for its strong in-plane anisotropy and its thickness-independent direct-bandgap excitons, which can hybridize with light to form exciton-polaritons. In parallel, metasurfaces, engineered arrays of nanoscale subwavelength resonators, can support ultra-sharp photonic modes in the form of quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs). Topological transformations of photonic modes can give rise to flatbands, i.e., dispersionless states with quenched kinetic energy and vanishing group velocity. Intrinsic material anisotropy offers an unexplored route to robust far-field flatband formation and control. Here, we demonstrate how structuring an intrinsically anisotropic excitonic material into a resonant metasurface fundamentally transforms its photonic topological features and light-matter coupling behavior, allowing us to drive and topologically control extended far-field flatband formation. To this end, we fabricate C$_4$-symmetric metasurfaces directly from bulk ReS$_2$. The intrinsic anisotropy lifts the initial double degeneracy of the qBIC mode and yields two distinctly polarized resonances. It also reshapes the topological landscape: the integer topological charge of the qBIC mode splits into momentum-separated half-integer singularities, thereby flattening the far-field photonic dispersion. The resulting topologically-controlled photonic flatbands are then tuned in resonance with the linearly polarized excitonic transitions of ReS$_2$, resulting in two distinct, directionally hybridized exciton-polariton flatband regimes. These findings establish anisotropic vdW metasurfaces as a new platform for topologically engineered flatbands and flatband-driven light-matter coupling.

items.title: Reconstructing the Probability Measure of a Multi-group Curie-Weiss Model with Interacting Groups
items.summary: We study the problem of reconstructing the probability measure of a multi-group version of the Curie-Weiss or mean-field model of ferromagnetism from a sample of the voting behaviour of the population. While originally used to study phase transitions in statistical mechanics, the Curie-Weiss model has been applied to study phenomena where many agents interact with each other, in particular in case of a heterogeneous population with identifiable subpopulations. The degree of social cohesion within social groups manifests in the way the members of the group influence each others' decisions as well as how they behave under outside influence from voters belonging to another group. While the maximum likelihood estimator of the coupling parameters has desirable statistical properties in theory, computational challenges make applications to larger populations impractical. Therefore, we analyse an estimator based on asymptotic approximations to the behaviour of the Curie-Weiss model valid for large populations. Due to the wide application of models such as Curie-Weiss, the estimator is potentially useful in disciplines such as political science, sociology, automated voting, and preference aggregation.

items.title: Revisiting structured-light propagation in screw-dislocation geometries: Landau dynamics and gradient-induced polarization textures
items.summary: We derive the propagation of finite electromagnetic beams in the effective metric of a continuous distribution of screw dislocations from gauge-invariant, minimally coupled Maxwell theory with $F=dA$. The Burgers flux fixes the metric profile through $σ(ρ)=f'(ρ)/(bρ)$, which separates true density gradients from coordinate factors. In geometric optics, both polarizations share one light cone, and a uniform density rotates the polarization uniformly relative to the geometry-adapted frame; laboratory polarimetry also requires matching at the interfaces. At leading paraxial order, the orbital motion is of Landau type, with a closed propagator for arbitrary inputs, and for a uniform density the polarization evolution factorizes exactly. For an arbitrary smooth axisymmetric density, the polarization texture initially grows in proportion to the standard deviation of the density weighted by the beam intensity; the local-phase coherence is the characteristic function of that distribution. For a coherent transverse Jones field, an exact relation links the linear-Stokes texture and the local circular polarization to spatial--polarization nonseparability. For linearly polarized, real axisymmetric input beams, diffraction produces local circular polarization at second order in the propagation distance, while the integrated circular Stokes component is conserved in the lossless leading-paraxial theory. Exact Maxwell eigenmodes, analytic results for a saturating profile, and numerical propagation test the approximation. We propose a full-Stokes measurement that compares uniform and graded samples with the same mean twist, with a closed-form criterion for the beam waist. These predictions apply to the ideal metric-Maxwell model or to a transformation-optics medium that realizes it, not to natural dislocated crystals without further constitutive modeling.

items.title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
items.summary: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.

items.title: Terahertz emission from $α$-W/CoFe epitaxial spintronic emitters
items.summary: We report efficient terahertz (THz) generation in epitaxial $α$-W/Co$_{60}$Fe$_{40}$ spintronic emitters. Two types of emitters have been investigated; epitaxial $α$-W$(110)$/Co$_{60}$Fe$_{40}(110)$ and $α$-W$(001)$/Co$_{60}$Fe$_{40}(001)$ deposited on single crystalline Al$_{2}$O$_{3}$($11\bar{2}0$) and MgO($001$) substrates, respectively. First principle calculations of the electronic band structure at the W$(001)$ surface reveal Dirac-type surface states, similar to that reported previously for the W$(110)$ surface. The generated THz radiation is about $10\%$ larger for $α$-W$(110)$/Co$_{60}$Fe$_{40}(110)$ grown on single crystalline Al$_{2}$O$_{3}$($11\bar{2}0$), which is explained by the fact that the $α$-W$(110)$/Co$_{60}$Fe$_{40}(110)$ interface for this emitter is more transparent to the spin current due to the presence of Ångstr\" om-scale interface intermixing at the W/CoFe interface. Our results also reveal that the generation of THz radiation is larger when pumping with the laser light from the substrate side, which is explained by a larger part of the laser light due to interference effects in the film stack being absorbed in the ferromagnetic Co$_{60}$Fe$_{40}$ layer in this measurement configuration.

items.title: One dimensional high-order moment models with realistic collisions for nonequilibrium ion transport in weakly ionized plasmas
items.summary: Ion-neutral collisions are fundamental in the transport of partially ionized plasmas. When collisional scales are comparable to the system scales or the electric field is strong, nonequilibrium conditions for the ions arise that are beyond classical transport models due to large drifts, strong heat flux, and temperature anisotropy. In this paper, we propose the resolution of non-linear high-order moment closures for simulating nonequilibrium ion dynamics in one-dimensional weakly ionized plasmas. We compare a four-moment anisotropic Maxwellian model (mass, axial momentum, and axial and perpendicular energies), a five-moment hyperbolic quadrature-based model (first five axial moments), and a novel six-moment hyperbolic quadrature-based model (first five axial moments + perpendicular energy). We derive analytical collision source terms from the Boltzmann operator for ion-neutral scattering with arbitrary differential cross sections. This formulation generalizes the Chapman-Cowling theory for arbitrary drift velocities, temperature anisotropies, and heat flux, ensuring strictly realizable distributions. The models are validated via non-linear simulations benchmarked against kinetic solutions for argon plasmas with realistic cross sections (0.05-500 mTorr). We test a bounded plasma between floating walls and a direct-current discharge. The six-moment model robustly captures ion dynamics, particularly under strong nonequilibrium, where anisotropy and heat flux are non-local. It reconstructs the distribution function with high fidelity, without noise, and at a cost comparable to fluid models in a self-consistent manner.

items.title: Altermagnetism-induced magneto-optical effects
items.summary: Altermagnets break time-reversal symmetry despite their zero net magnetization, enabling time-reversal-odd responses while retaining the advantages of antiferromagnets. However, magneto-optical (MO) effects are not universal among altermagnets because MO effects typically arise from magnetic dipole order (ferromagnetism), which is generally absent in altermagnets. In this work, we address this limitation by establishing octupolar MO effects, which arise from magnetic octupole order through spatial dispersion. Owing to this distinct origin, octupolar MO effects do not necessarily require spin-orbit coupling even in collinear magnets and can arise without an external magnetic field in antiferromagnets where conventional MO effects are symmetry-forbidden. Such antiferromagnets include $d$-wave altermagnets such as RuO$_2$ and KV$_2$Se$_2$O, certain $g$- and $i$-wave altermagnets, including CrSb, as well as noncoplanar antiferromagnets such as MnTe$_2$ and pyrochlore iridates with all-in-all-out magnetic order. From an experimental perspective, octupolar MO effects can reach detectable magnitudes and offer potential for magnetic-domain imaging, as supported by numerical calculations showing $μ$rad-scale Faraday rotation for a 100-nm-thick sample in the visible-light range and a sign reversal between opposite domains. Furthermore, octupolar MO effects are linked to an $f$-sum rule, enabling a quantitative estimate of the spin magnetic octupole moment from optical measurements. These results extend the scope of MO effects to a broad class of antiferromagnets, including altermagnets, and open a field-free optical route to exploring magnetic octupole order.

items.title: Spin-Adapted Neural-Network Backflow Wavefunctions for Excited States of Strongly Correlated Open-Shell Systems
items.summary: Building on the success of neural-network quantum states (NQS) for molecular ground states, multi-state frameworks such as natural excited states (NES) [Pfau et al., Science 2024, 385, eadn0137] extend NQS to chemically important excited states. However, without control over total spin, such calculations can require the inclusion of many intervening states of other spins, particularly in strongly correlated systems with dense low-energy spectra. We therefore generalize our previously developed spin-adapted neural network backflow (SA-NNBF) ansatz [Li et al., arXiv:2604.06841 (2026)] to improve its variational flexibility for excited-state calculations within a prescribed spin sector. We establish the universality of this extended ansatz within the chosen orbital space and spin sector, and use numerical benchmarks to assess how parameter allocation affects the ansatz's accuracy. With the spin-adapted ansatz, we are able to directly optimize the first excited state (a singlet) of $O_2$ without using any multi-state frameworks. Combining the extended ansatz with NES, we obtain low-lying triplet states of $O_2$ and singlet states of the $[\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{S}_2(\mathrm{SCH}_3)_4]^{2-}$ cluster without including intervening states of other spins. Both the single-state and NES calculations achieve chemical accuracy relative to the exact energies. Our work provides a practical NQS framework for targeting excited states of prescribed spin in strongly correlated systems.

items.title: Geometric encoding of turbulence for end-to-end quantum simulation
items.summary: Simulating multiscale turbulence in engineering remains challenging. Any quantum advantage for such simulations requires efficient initial-state preparation. Yet exact loading of an arbitrary classical snapshot requires exponential quantum resources. We introduce "turbuloscope", a physics-informed geometric method that generates statistically representative turbulent initial states in a gate-based register from a parameterized Pauli-spinor multiscale distribution. Scale invariance renders conditional rotations approximately affine in Gray-code space, enabling linear-depth, ancilla-free preparation. The generalized Madelung transform and Hopf fibration map the encoded Pauli spinor to fluid observables and vortex tubes. The qubit count scales logarithmically with the Reynolds number, yielding an exponential reduction in preparation overhead relative to full-grid classical spectral synthesis. We classically emulate a 30-qubit preparation circuit and generate a turbulent field over one billion grid points at a scale-inferred Reynolds number of 35,000, exhibiting Kolmogorov's five-thirds energy spectrum, tangled vortex tubes, and intermittency. This method provides scalable initial states for quantum simulation of turbulence and multiscale systems.

items.title: Optical rectification and Pockels effect in the organic nonlinear crystal MBI for quasi-discrete THz time-domain spectroscopy
items.summary: Organic nonlinear optical (NLO) crystals offer efficient nonlinear frequency conversion for broadband THz spectroscopy. Unfortunately, only a subset of NLO crystals is compatible with the telecom (~1.5 $μ$m) pump wavelength region, where convenient MHz-rate femtosecond fiber lasers are available. Here, we present ultra-broadband (1-30 THz) THz generation and detection using a benzoindolium iodide (MBI, C$_{24}$H$_{24}$NOI) crystal illuminated by a 1.5 $μ$m MHz-rate fiber laser. At 200 mW of average pump power, the crystal delivers ~1 $μ$W of THz radiation as quasi-discrete peaks covering the whole emission region with a prominent peak at 11.8 THz. High-dynamic range (>40 dB) time-domain spectroscopy is demonstrated within minutes of integration.

items.title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

items.title: LH$μ$C Concept: Energy-Frontier Antimuon-Proton Collisions at CERN
items.summary: The concept of the LH$μ$C, an energy-frontier antimuon-proton collider based on the HL-LHC, is presented. After recalling why energy-frontier lepton-hadron colliders are indispensable as QCD explorers and reviewing the history of muon-proton collider proposals, two ways of realising $μp$ collisions at the LHC are compared: with muon-collider beams and with ultra-cold $μ^+$ beams as proposed for $μ$TRISTAN. For the latter, a $μ$TRISTAN-type booster and the re-use of the LHeC energy-recovery-linac tunnel are discussed; colliding 1 TeV antimuons with 7 TeV protons gives $\sqrt{s}=5.3$ TeV and peak luminosities of $8.8\times10^{33}$ and $7.2\times10^{33}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, respectively. The detector concept and the physics potential, including searches for colour-octet muons and R-parity-violating squarks, are discussed together with the main challenges.

items.title: On the velocity range limitation of DBSCAN for event-based particle tracking and a proposed solution
items.summary: Event-based cameras offer new opportunities for particle tracking in fluid mechanics by providing asynchronous, sparse measurements with high temporal resolution and no fixed acquisition frequency. Processing such data requires algorithms capable of fully exploiting these distinctive features. A natural first approach to perform particle tracking on event-based data is to apply a clustering algorithm, in particular DBSCAN, as it does not require specifying the number of clusters a priori. In this paper, we show, using a simplified synthetic two-particle system, that this classical algorithm is severely limited in terms of the accessible velocity range vmax/vmin. To address this limitation, and to take advantage of the absence of a fixed acquisition frequency in event-based cameras, we propose a new two-dimensional, two-component (2D2C) particle-tracking algorithm based on clustering. The method relies on a recursive application of DBSCAN with multiple temporal normalizations, retaining only clusters that satisfy a set of validation criteria. A key feature of the proposed algorithm is that it does not assume any characteristic time scale or typical velocity. The algorithm is evaluated on realistic synthetic datasets generated from numerical simulations of turbulent flows, and the influence of key parameters is systematically investigated. Particular attention is given to the definition of evaluation metrics adapted to clusters of events for particle tracking. Finally, the proposed algorithm is applied to experimental data acquired in a turbulent flow generated by a von

items.title: Thermal and Acoustic Measurements of Hybrid Bonding Stacks
items.summary: Thermal and structural characterizations of hybrid bonding structures are essential for understanding heat transport in three-dimensional integrated circuits (3D-ICs). In this work, we investigate the effective thermal conductivity of the Cu/dielectric HB layer using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) combined with picosecond ultrasonic technique. Shallow-angle polishing enabled depth-resolved thermal measurements by exposing hybrid bonding layers with different remaining thicknesses, while acoustic echoes were used to identify buried interfaces and determine the thickness. The distinct waveform of the bonding interface echo compared with the Cu/dielectric interface echo suggests that its acoustic response may also reflect the interfacial bonding conditions. The extracted thermal conductivity ranges from 1.14 to 1.75 Wm-1K-1 for the bottom pad layer and from 1.76 to 4.34 Wm-1K-1 for the top pad layer. The difference in thermal conductivity is consistent with the different Cu area fractions of the two layers. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity of the top pad layer increases significantly with the remaining thickness, possibly due to the thermal boundary resistance at the bonding interface, low thermal conductivity of SiCN interlayer, and increased electron scattering in thin Cu structures. Our work demonstrates a practical approach to investigate the thermal properties of buried hybrid bonding layers, providing experimental data for thermal design and modeling of 3D-ICs.

items.title: Magnetic Flux Eruptions in Magnetically Arrested Disks: Magnetic Reconnection and Bubble Expansion
items.summary: Using a high-resolution GRMHD simulation of a magnetically arrested disk, we investigate the physical mechanism driving magnetic-flux eruption. The horizon-threading magnetic flux declines mainly in off-equatorial regions, whereas localized hot spots associated with magnetic reconnection appear near the equatorial plane around the onset of flux decline. A non-axisymmetric, magnetically supported low-density structure, which we identify as a magnetic bubble, expands radially and azimuthally within a pre-existing low-density channel in the filamentary accretion flow. Based on these findings, we propose a physical picture linking reconnection, bubble expansion, and horizon magnetic flux decline. The reconnection occurs in the pre-existing low-density channel, and may reconfigure the field and promote bubble expansion. Magnetic-pressure gradients provide broadly distributed outward support for the expansion, while magnetic tension contributes a localized outward force near the equator. Bubble expansion may limit gas replenishment, helping to maintain the low-density region and reduce the total pressure near the equator. This pressure reduction may facilitate equatorward electromagnetic energy transport. In the simulation, the polar electromagnetic energy flux reverses from poleward to equatorward near the onset of the horizon-flux decline. The equatorward transport is concentrated in the bubble sector and carries electromagnetic energy from the off-equatorial magnetosphere to the equatorial region. This energy supply may sustain localized reconnection and plasma heating as the eruption develops.

items.title: Quadrature-Free Radial Intracule Densities: A Bessel-Harmonic Formulation for Gaussian Basis Sets
items.summary: The radial intracule density $I(R)$, the probability distribution of the interelectronic distance, is a compact and physically transparent picture of electron correlation, but its evaluation for molecules has always relied on a numerical angular quadrature over the orientation of the interelectronic vector. We show that this quadrature can be removed altogether for Cartesian Gaussian basis sets and arbitrary second-order density matrices. Starting from the Hermite Gaussian expansion of the products of basis functions, the coupling exponential $e^{2μ\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{T}}$ that links radial and angular variables is expanded in modified spherical Bessel functions and real spherical harmonics, and the expansion terminates rigorously at $l=p_x+p_y+p_z$, where the $p$'s are the Cartesian powers arising from the Hermite expansion. The angular average is then exact, the atomic limit reduces to a finite sum of terms $C_iR^{n_i}e^{-μR^2}$, and the radial moments $\int_0^\infty R^nI(R)\,dR$ are given in closed form through the confluent hypergeometric function ${}_1F_1$. The scheme is exact in principle and fails only arithmetically: we identify the catastrophic cancellations in the angular-momentum coupling that ruin binary64 evaluations for heavy atoms and remove them by elevating the cancelling chain to binary128. Sum rules for the total, Coulomb and exchange-correlation intracules are recovered to seven to eight significant digits for systems from LiH to Kr$_2$, whereas Euler-Maclaurin and Lebedev quadratures err by up to 22% for stretched or multicenter molecules.

items.title: Measurement and Modeling of Structure-Induced Surface Scattering on Terahertz Channel
items.summary: As terahertz (THz) frequencies emerge as promising candidates for next-generation wireless networks, accurate characterization of propagation mechanisms in indoor/outdoor environments becomes essential for system design and performance optimization. This article presents an experimental and theoretical investigation of structure-induced indoor surface scattering on THz channels, examining how material properties and structural configurations jointly govern channel power and angular distribution. Six representative indoor surfaces are characterized, revealing that intrinsic structural inhomogeneity - particularly the quasi-periodic earlywood-latewood arrangement in pine wood - induces measurable angular scattering whose dominant lobes and angular shifts are reproduced by a beam-propagation modeling (BPM) framework. Material-covered surface configurations are further investigated, demonstrating that thin dielectric covering layers can substantially modify reflection characteristics through thickness- and frequency- dependent thin-film interference effects. Wide-angle bistatic measurements in a conference room show that folded curtains broaden the measured angular distribution of detectable received power. These findings suggest that structure-induced surface scattering mechanisms may provide scattering-assisted propagation opportunities for indoor non-line-of-sight THz scenarios.

items.title: Sub-electron noise with a buried-channel DePFET: characterisation of novel DePFET concepts
items.summary: Depleted P-channel Field Effect Transistor (DePFET) pixel sensors combine Fano-limited energy resolution with fast, low-noise readout and are used in instruments ranging from particle tracking to X-ray astronomy. In this work, two novel DePFET technologies that address the two factors of the signal-to-noise ratio through fundamental changes to the intrinsic design are characterised: a buried-channel design aimed at reducing the limiting low-frequency noise by weakening the coupling between the channel and Si/SiO$_2$ interface traps, and a super-$g_q$ design intended to increase the charge gain by reducing the effective internal-gate capacitance. Their noise and energy resolution were mapped across the transistor bias space, over a wide temperature range (100-260 K) and for integration times of 0.4-9 $μ$s (readout times of 2-19.2 $μ$s per row), and compared with standard DePFETs as developed for the NewAthena Wide Field Imager (WFI). All three variants reach their lowest noise at about 155 K. The buried-channel device achieves an excellent equivalent noise charge (ENC) of 0.96 e$^-$ (at most 0.83 e$^-$ after subtracting the readout-electronics noise), demonstrating sub-electron noise over a complete 64$\times$64 DePFET matrix in a single readout, alongside a power consumption reduction of more than 50%. The super-$g_q$ DePFET shows a 2.6-fold increase in charge gain (about 1100 pA/e$^-$) but exhibits higher total noise due to an excess noise contribution. The results highlight the potential of the novel DePFETs, with the buried-channel technology offering immediate benefits for low-noise applications such as the WFI.

items.title: Giant and sign-tunable spin Hall effect of light in a nonlocal nonlinear Rydberg medium
items.summary: We demonstrate that long-range Rydberg atom interactions provide a tunable mechanism for generating the giant spin Hall effect of light (SHEL) in a cold atomic medium. For a coherently driven 87Rb medium with Rydberg S states, we derive the linear, local, and nonlocal Kerr susceptibilities for the two orthogonal probe polarization components and evaluate the resulting spatial and angular SHEL shifts. The nonlocal third-order susceptibility reshapes the complex birefringence of the medium, and drastically enhances the y-polarized SHEL shift by about one to two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, it can reverse the direction of both the spatial and angular shifts relative to the predictions of linear response. The effect is controllably tuned by the laser detuning, the quantization-axis orientation, the atomic density, and the principal quantum number of the Rydberg state. In the 87Rb medium, we find that the spatial and angular shifts reverse sign when the principal quantum number of the Rydberg state are around n=40 and 60, respectively. At high-lying excited Rydberg states, the spatial shift can be enhanced to several tens of micrometres-a magnitude that should be directly observable in experiment. These results demonstrate that Rydberg-mediated nonlocal optical nonlinearity is an efficient mechanism for spin-dependent light transport and for future photonic sensing applications.

items.title: Generating Circularly Polarized and Chiral Cathodoluminescence from a Single Plasmonic Nanoantenna
items.summary: The generation and control of circularly polarized and chiral light is important for a wide range of applications, from sensing to optical communication and catalysis. Generally, the generation of chiral light emission from plasmonic nanostructures relies on the use of nanoantennas with predefined chiral shape, which requires complex nanofabrication. In this work, we show how localized electron excitation controls the generation of circularly polarized- and chiral cathodoluminescence from a single achiral plasmonic nanoantenna. We exploit the $π$/2 phase difference between the transverse and longitudinal components of the electric field that is carried by 30 keV electrons, to coherently excite degenerate dipolar modes of which the far-field radiation interferes in the far field, thereby creating a strong optical spin-Hall effect. Using angle-resolved cathodoluminescence polarimetry we measure the angle-resolved Stokes parameters for selected positions of the electron beam near the nanoparticle and show how the precise location of the electron beam controls the generation of the circularly polarized and chiral electric field components. Our findings represent an elemental form of generation of circularly polarized light, by synthesizing the circularly rotating electric fields characteristic for CPL from interference of orthogonal dipolar modes with controlled phase lag.

items.title: Statistical State Dynamics of Couette MHD Turbulence
items.summary: The roll streak structure (RSS) is ubiquitous in shear flow turbulence and is fundamental to the dynamics of the self-sustaining process (SSP) maintaining the turbulent state. The formation and maintenance of the RSS in wall-bounded shear flow suggest the presence of an underlying instability that has recently been identified using statistical state dynamics (SSD). Due to the parallelism between the Navier-Stokes equation and the induction equation, it is reasonable to inquire whether the RSS in wall-bounded shear flow has a counterpart in the MHD equations formulated as an SSD. In this work we show that this is the case and that an analytic solution for the composite velocitymagnetic field RSS in the MHD SSD also arises from an instability, that this instability equilibrates to either a fixed point or to a turbulent state, that these turbulent statistical equilibria may be self sustaining, and that both the fixed point and the turbulent states may correspond to large scale coherent dynamos.

items.title: Non-Intrusive Rubin Substructuring for Geometrically Nonlinear Structures via Nonlinear Manifolds
items.summary: Component mode synthesis enables modular reduction of large structural models, but its extension to geometrically nonlinear systems remains challenging. This work generalizes the Rubin method by introducing a cubic displacement manifold that statically condenses high-frequency free-interface modes onto the retained low-frequency modes and residual attachment modes. The reduced equations of motion, with cubic polynomial restoring forces, are derived by Galerkin projection onto the manifold tangent subspace. The consistency of the reduced forces is guaranteed by the cubic expansion of the component-level reduced manifold. We further present a non-intrusive procedure that combines elastic-force identification with finite-difference estimates of tangent-stiffness derivatives, which allows the reduced model to be constructed from the linear Rubin model and tangent-stiffness evaluations. In the proposed numerical tests, the reduced assembled models accurately reproduce the nonlinear responses of the full finite-element models, including internal resonance and modal coupling. Scalability and significant computational gains are demonstrated with an industrial scale model of a wing-box tip tank assembly, for which an online speed-up of about 24,666 was obtained.

items.title: Collisional lineshapes of an N$_2$-perturbed electronic transition in O$_2$ from first principles of quantum theory validated by accurate experimental spectra
items.summary: We demonstrate the feasibility of predicting the lineshape of an electronic molecular transition collisionally perturbed by another molecule from first principles of quantum mechanics. We consider an N$_2$-perturbed O$_2$ $A$-band transition, which is relevant to spectroscopic observations in Earth's atmosphere. This approach simultaneously incorporates the electronic structure, quantum scattering and lineshape effects required to accurately predict pressure- and temperature-dependence of observed lineshapes. The $\textit{ab initio}$ lineshapes reproduce measurements to better than 0.6%. Theory also provides new physical constraints on beyond-Voigt lineshape parameters in fits of high-precision data, yielding fit residuals at the 0.08% level. This work motivates advances in molecular electronic structure calculations and demonstrates the potential to generate comprehensive spectroscopic reference data from first principles.

items.title: A regime dependent parameterization of the refractive-index structure parameter $C_n^2$
items.summary: Vertical profiles of the refractive-index (RI) structure parameter, $C_n^2$, are required in atmospheric-optics calculations. The Hufnagel--Valley (HV) model is a useful reference profile and it is widely used however, it is difficult to say that it produces consistent results at the observed altitude, magnitude, and thickness of all turbulent layers and it can diverge from realistic measurements in particular height ranges, sites, and stability regimes. This study develops a regime-dependent RI structure parameter considering meteorological conditions and, more importantly, it provides a structure that can be calibrated against measured $C_n^2$ throughout the surface layer (SL), atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and free atmosphere. The formulation combines SL including distinct unstable, near-neutral, and stable limits; convective ABL; and free-atmospheric turbulence when kinetic-energy and temperature-variance dissipation rates are available. The $C_n^2$ is formed by weighting the contribution of different layers. We use representative, physically plausible meteorological profiles to examine the model's limiting behavior, transitions between atmospheric regimes, continuity, sensitivity to its parameters, and propagation-related differences from the HV 5/7 model. The intended outcome is a measurement-calibrated model that remains physically interpretable across meteorological regimes.

items.title: Energy calibration of bulk events in the BULLKID detector
items.summary: BULLKID is a cryogenic, solid-state detector designed for direct searches of particle Dark Matter candidates, with mass $\lesssim 1$ GeV/c$^2$, and coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering. It is based on an array of dice carved in 5 mm thick silicon crystal, sensed by phonon-mediated Kinetic Inductance Detectors. In previous works, the array was calibrated with bursts of optical photons, which are absorbed in the first hundreds nanometers of the dice and give rise to surface events. In this work, we present the reconstruction of bulk events through the 59.5 keV $γ$-ray generated by an $^{241}$Am source, which emulates more closely the interaction of Dark Matter and neutrinos. The peak resolution is $5\%~(σ)$ and its position is shifted by less than $10\%$ with respect to the optical calibration. We observe that the resolution is further improved by a factor $2$ combining the signal from neighboring dice. These results confirm the performance of the detector in view of the physics goals of the BULLKID-DM experiment for dark matter search.

items.title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows
items.summary: The effectiveness of neural networks in solving partial differential equations depends not only on their approximation capability but also on the suitability of their representations for the underlying solutions. Motivated by stochastic integral representations of incompressible fluid flows and the associated Biot--Savart kernel, we propose a Biot--Savart-informed (i.e. physics-informed) neural network (BS-PINN) for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations. By extracting a rational profile from a regularized Biot--Savart kernel, we construct a smooth activation function with fixed and learnable kernel scales. Both variants retain the conventional velocity--pressure formulation and physics-informed training framework, allowing the influence of the activation function to be examined independently. We evaluate the method on five benchmarks, including Kovasznay flow, cylinder wake, three-dimensional Beltrami flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and double shear layer. Across 21 benchmark--architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduce the combined velocity error relative to the conventional $\tanh$-based PINN, achieving mean relative error reductions of 31.7\% and 33.2\%, respectively. Improvements are also observed in reported pressure and vorticity errors. Notably, the double-shear-layer experiments demonstrate improved resolution of localized shear structures and, for BS-PINN-F, qualitatively clearer vortex-roll-up patterns in the long-time simulation. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating analytical flow structures into neural-network representations for incompressible flow simulations.

items.title: Improving Eddy Detection from Wide-Swath Altimetry with Multimodal Data-Driven Models
items.summary: Physically-based eddy detection algorithms usually rely on hard-coded thresholds and constraints that make the detected structures sensitive to small variations in the underlying fields. One way to relax such conditions is the use of machine-learning methodologies that transform the full problem into an optimization process. We present a multimodal, multi-task, data-driven eddy detection framework based on a shallow convolutional U-Net, trained to jointly segment eddy structures and reconstruct the co-located spatial sea surface temperature (SST) anomaly using a dynamically-based reconstruction as target. Two model variants are developed: NADIRnet, trained on conventional nadir altimetry, and SWOTnet, trained through a curriculum that incorporates SWOT-enriched maps. Both models achieve high pixel- and structure-wise detection scores against the ground-truth, with most residual disagreement attributable to boundary placement rather than missed or spurious detections. The coupled SST regression task, enforced through boundary-coupling and gradient-matching loss terms, is shown to sharpen and regularise the detected eddy boundaries. Compared to the dynamically-based reference, both models recover a substantially larger and finer eddy population; notably, SWOTnet's higher-resolution training signal transfers to conventional nadir altimetry thanks to the higher-resolution SST channel, detecting more eddies than a nadir-trained model on the same data. The framework further generalises, even without retraining, to altimetry products and processing levels unseen during training, including SWOT L3 wide-swath retrievals and an independent gridded product. Together with its low computational cost, this framework is thus promising for near-real-time operational deployment and further downstream applications.

items.title: A variational multiscale rotational pressure-correction method for incompressible flows with open boundaries
items.summary: Rotational pressure correction improves pressure accuracy near open boundaries in incompressible flow simulations, but equal-order finite element discretizations can still develop spurious pressure oscillations. We develop a residual-based variational multiscale rotational pressure-correction scheme (RPCS-VMS) that stabilizes both the pressure-increment and pressure-recovery equations. By constructing stage-specific momentum residuals using a common intermediate-velocity acceleration, the scheme retains four sequential linear solves per time step. For a reduced BDF1 Oseen model with frozen stabilization coefficients, we establish augmented-energy decay and a conditional bound on the pressure gradient. Manufactured-solution tests demonstrate suppression of pressure oscillations at small time steps and reduced near-boundary pressure errors. With \(P_1/P_1\) and \(Q_1/Q_1\) elements, the observed spatial \(L^2\) convergence rates are 2 for velocity and approximately \(1.5\) for pressure, while first- and second-order backward differentiation formulas attain their expected temporal orders. Branched-pipe and two- and three-dimensional cylinder benchmarks assess outlet flow partitioning, transient forces, and pressure differences, with results agreeing closely with reference solutions. In the three-dimensional cylinder test, RPCS-VMS achieves a 2.41-fold wall-time speedup over the tested monolithic VMS solver.

items.title: Quantum differential interference contrast microscope
items.summary: Optical sensing and imaging of transparent unstained biological and material specimen makes use of optical interference to translate phase shifts into intensity measurements, that are readily available in the optical domain. This is the case of Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopes. However, environmental disturbances such as acoustic vibrations, air currents, temperature shifts, and mechanical drifts cause random phase noise that degrades the precision attainable in the estimation of the unknown phase shift. Although there are tools to compensate for these random phase drifts, such using common path interference techniques or phase stabilization systems, these are not always an option and its introduction is generally at the expense of device simplicity and robustness. Here we introduce a quantum version of Differential Interference Contrast microscopy (qDIC), that makes use of quantum interference for polarization analysis. When compared with standard schemes that make use of coherent light, our approach shows that the transfer of classical DIC microscopy into the quantum domain offers a route towards quantum-enhanced resilience to environmental disturbances, allowing the enhancement of phase sensitivity without sacrificing the simplicity and robustness of the optical setup.

items.title: Targeted material doping to enable the formation and coherent propagation of Laser Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LIPSS): the ZnO paradigm
items.summary: This work explores how the initial free carrier density governs the formation and coherent propagation of Low Spatial Frequency Laser-Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LSF-LIPSS). As a paradigm we have analyzed the behavior of ad-hoc-doped ZnO films. ZnO is a multifunctional Transparent Conducting Oxide (TCO) with many scientific and technologic uses including applications in biomedicine, photonics, sensing or photocatalysis. Many of them would benefit from the use of large area, electrically anisotropic surfaces. By introducing small amounts of Yb3+ as donor dopant in ZnO films grown by Pulse Laser Deposition (PLD), we have substantially improved its carrier density at room temperature (RT) and its electrical conductivity while preserving the functional properties of pure ZnO. For RT carrier densities ne > 1019 cm-3, coherent propagation of LSF-LIPSS has been successfully achieved upon irradiation with 350 fs laser pulses at 1030 nm at high repetition rate (500 kHz) and for laser scanning speeds well above 1 m/s. However, the ablation mechanism (ZnO sublimation at the LIPSS valleys) and the large melting temperature of ZnO, make the thermal conductivity of the substrate, the film thickness and the irradiation pulse duration to play a crucial role in determining the morphology of the LSF-LIPPS propagated over large areas, especially in avoiding film cracking. The results achieved upon optimization fully confirm the role of free carrier density in the large-scale propagation of high quality LSF-LIPSS in doped ZnO and enable using these structures to easily generate large electrical anisotropies over macroscopic regions with conductivities along the LIPSS several times larger than transversally.

items.title: Nonreciprocal Hopfield nets for angiogenesis
items.summary: During sprouting angiogenesis, endothelial cells dynamically reorganize among three relevant phenotypes (glycolytic, stalk and tip) to form new blood vessels, with cells transitioning from one phenotype to another. These cell-state transitions may involve intrinsic nonequilibrium dynamics that go beyond relaxation of the conventional Waddington landscape. We investigate this possibility using a nonreciprocal Hopfield network inferred from single-cell RNA sequencing and RNA velocity data for 1896 endothelial cells on a panel of 1873 genes. We encode the three experimentally identified phenotypes as correlated memory patterns and introduce an asymmetric mixing matrix describing their effective interactions. A dynamical mean- field reduction yields a three-dimensional system for the overlaps with these phenotypic memories, whose parameters are fitted to RNA-velocity-derived trajectories. The nonreciprocal model outperforms its reciprocal counterpart on held-out testing data. Remarkably, its long-time dynamics exhibit either stationary attractors or sustained cycles connecting phenotypic states, depending on the inference timescale. These results suggest that angiogenic cell fate decisions may involve directed, non-relaxational dynamics that cannot be captured by a conventional energy landscape. This approach may also provide a useful framework for investigating how perturbations constrain cellular differentiation.

items.title: Overcoming configuration bottleneck: Modular pathways to stable semiconductor spin-qubit arrays
items.summary: Over the past decade, semiconductor spin qubits have progressed from few-qubit demonstrations toward larger-scale devices fabricated in increasingly reproducible academic and industrial processes. This progress marks an inflection point: the central challenge is no longer to demonstrate high-fidelity operation in carefully tuned devices but to discover, verify, and maintain stable operating conditions reliably across many interdependent controls, varied device geometries, and disparate material platforms. In this Perspective, we frame spin-qubit operation as a modular automation problem. We decompose the workflow into five modules: bootstrapping from minimal prior information, configuration tuning, virtualization of physical gates into effective control axes, qubit-level tuning, and an operation layer with drift-aware maintenance. Using recent demonstrations from our work and the broader community, we argue that scalability will depend on explicit interfaces between modules, standardized intermediate data products, and workflow-level metrics such as throughput, success probability, stability time, recovery time, and robustness. We close by outlining the infrastructure needed to move beyond isolated tuning demonstrations toward sustained operation: qubit-performance-aware feedback, reusable software and benchmark tasks, and tight collaboration among experimental, theoretical, and software efforts.

items.title: Spin-free potential-energy curves, spectroscopic constants, and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 CO states correlating with the first atomic asymptote
items.summary: We report ab initio potential-energy curves and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 spin-free adiabatic electronic states of $^{12}$C$^{16}$O correlating with the lowest dissociation limit, C($^3$P)+O($^3$P). Our state-averaged CASSCF/icMRCI(+Q) calculations with the aug-cc-pV5Z basis cover the complete set of singlet, triplet, and quintet manifolds. For the ground state, we examine basis-set convergence using the aug-cc-pV$n$Z series ($n=T,Q,5,6$) and extrapolate to the complete-basis-set limit. The resulting potential-energy curves reproduce the established topology of the low-lying CO states, including the double-minimum structure of the 2$^{1}Σ^{+}$ state and pronounced adiabatic mixing in several excited states. We determine rovibrational levels and spectroscopic constants for bound states and selected local minima, assess uncertainties, and compare our results with experiment and previous calculations. We find good agreement with experiment for the ground state and well-characterized low-lying singlet and triplet states. For the $1^1Σ^+$ ground state, $R_e=1.131~Å$ and $ω_e=2161.04$~cm$^{-1}$ are both within $0.5\%$ of experiment. The dissociation energy is $D_0=89473\pm141$~cm$^{-1}$. The most strongly bound quintet, $1^5Π$, has $D_e=6401$~cm$^{-1}$ and $ω_e=982~$cm$^{-1}$. The $1^5Σ^+$ state has a shallow long-range well with $D_e=849$cm$^{-1}$, while $2^5Σ^+$, $2^5Π$, and $1^5Δ$ are predominantly repulsive. Variations in the permanent dipole moments with bond length indicate changes in electronic character and charge redistribution, particularly where adiabatic states interact strongly. These data provide a basis for interpreting rovibrational spectra and for future studies of nonadiabatic effects, spin--orbit coupling, and collision dynamics.

items.title: Coordinating integration of multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation codes with design structure matrices
items.summary: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.

items.title: Crowd model with anticipation and interactions: an exclusion process based mean-field game
items.summary: Mean-field games (MFG) is a powerful framework to describe competitive optimization processes. A natural field of application is crowd dynamics, where pedestrians are considered to optimize their path, while interacting with the others. Despite its success to incorporate anticipation in describing pedestrian behavior, the mean-field games framework neglects microscopic granular effects, rendering its results less realistic in various applications (bottlenecks, evacuations etc.). In this work, we consider an explicitly interacting microscopic model, namely an asymmetric simple exclusion process and derive the corresponding mean-field game. This mean-field game is applied to an evacuation setting and the differences from the standard MFG based on non-interacting Langevin dynamics, as well as the correlations induced by the granular interactions are discussed.

items.title: Efficient targeting of arbitrary excited states with quantum inverse power iteration through filtering polynomials
items.summary: In this work, we introduce a quantum inverse power iteration (QIPI) algorithm based on the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) to target arbitrary excited states. Given an energy shift $ω$, QIPI prepares the target excited state by iteratively applying an approximation of the shifted inverse Hamiltonian $(H-ωI)^{-1}$ to a trial state. Prior quantum inverse power approaches typically relied on Fourier decompositions of the inverse Hamiltonian, with numerical quadrature used to reconstruct the transformation, but such methods are highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and have been observed to be numerically unstable, effectively restricting their use to ground-state preparation. To enable robust excited-state targeting, we investigate two alternative transformation techniques: a Chebyshev decomposition of the inverse (Cheb-inv) and an eigenstate filtering (EF) approach based on QSVT. We find that EF-based QIPI is substantially more robust than Cheb-inv and other decomposition-based approaches due to the symmetry of the applied filtering polynomial, avoiding divergence with respect to the choice of $ω$ and efficiently suppressing off-target eigenstates even in closely spaced spectra. Numerical simulations for molecular Hamiltonians of H$_2$, LiH, and BeH$_2$ show improved convergence and enhanced access to higher excited states relative to other quantum power methods. Assuming standard oracle access to the Hamiltonian, we further provide logical resource estimates in fault-tolerant settings in terms of T gate counts, and conclude that QIPI can achieve high target state amplification with modest polynomial degrees, thereby making it a promising candidate for scalable excited-state preparation in fault-tolerant quantum chemistry applications.

items.title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
items.summary: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry. On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

items.title: Burgers vectors from Voronoi topology
items.summary: Automated dislocation analysis is standard in atomistic simulations, yet current tools are limited to a handful of crystal structures. We introduce an algorithm without adjustable parameters, based on Voronoi topology, that identifies dislocations in a broad class of crystals. Each face shared by two cells that match the ideal crystal is taken as a step in it, and summing these steps around closed circuits of such cells yields exact Burgers vectors, without geometric templates. Tested on dislocations inserted into all 9,610 Materials Project structures whose Voronoi cells are stable with a wide margin, the algorithm finds every dislocation with its correct Burgers vector. In raw molecular-dynamics snapshots, including eleven dislocation types in $θ$-Al$_2$Cu and bcc iron up to its melting point, every Burgers vector it returns is correct, although near melting the dislocations merge into one cluster. Voronoi topology thus provides a natural language in which a crystal, its defects, and their Burgers vectors are all described.

items.title: A branchless single-precision Voigt approximation for spectral synthesis
items.summary: The Voigt function is evaluated repeatedly in spectral synthesis, and several widely used implementations carry an absolute error floor. We construct QLG, a family of branchless, single-precision approximations, separable in the damping parameter $a$. QLG is named for its three ingredients: Lorentzian and Gaussian generators $L$ and $G$, and an envelope $q$ that multiplies every fitted correction and vanishes at both endpoints. The leading Lorentzian wing amplitude is fixed analytically. Three members reach observed maximum full-profile relative errors of $6.5\times10^{-3}$, $9.2\times10^{-4}$, and $7\times10^{-5}$ over $a\in[10^{-9},10^{9}]$ and $|v|\le10^{5}$. Extended-domain and randomized checks support these error levels. For the tested SIU, MOOG, and Humlicek w4 implementations, the relative error instead approaches 100% towards small values of the damping parameter. We compare synthesis-weighted costs on an Apple M1 and an AMD EPYC 9554 using gfortran 15, and propagate errors through solar-dwarf, red-supergiant, and M-dwarf syntheses. The least expensive member costs 0.98-1.05 times as much as the tabulated Synspec kernel on the M1 and 1.11-1.20 times as much on the EPYC, with a maximum flux error smaller by a factor of 3.6. The intermediate member costs less than every tested arithmetic kernel and holds the flux error below $10^{-3}$. The most accurate member costs 1.6-3.0 times less than w4 and gives 3.4-5.0 times smaller maximum flux errors in the tested syntheses.

items.title: Orbital differentiation in a rare earth ion near half filling
items.summary: In the electronic structure of rare earth ions, details can be crucial for understanding the origin of correlated states. Currently, state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods (e.g. CASSCF) can capture single-ion properties of molecular magnets and some band insulating systems, but are expensive to perform, and cannot be applied to metallic systems. Here, we carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty. The calculated experimental observables from our model agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density also agrees with DFT predictions. By tuning the crystal field parameters, our full multiplet-derived wavefunctions reveal the presence of orbital differentiation of the ground $J=\frac{5}{2}$ manifold into two groups, which are distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness. This violation of Hund's rule, observed with a fast and inexpensive calculation tool, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may provide support for the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

items.title: Modeling of basic physics issues in toroidal pinches and tools for performance control
items.summary: Nonlinear modelling has improved significantly in dealing with physics issues encountered in magnetically confined toroidal pinches, such as the Reversed Field Pinch and Tokamak configurations. Here, recent results relevant to the understanding of helical self-organization processes are presented: formation of internal transport barriers, temporary loss of operational point, relaxation-reconnection events, excitation of Alfvèn waves, and a possible fundamental mechanism for ion heating in plasmas. Starting from physics processes in Reversed Field Pinch plasmas, several similarities with Tokamaks are presented. In addition, data analysis tools, machine learning autoencoding techniques, are here trained for the first time on a RFP data analysis case.

items.title: Controlling Mode-Locking in Liquid Light
items.summary: Mode-locking is the process by which the phases of many cavity modes organize collectively into a stationary state. In lasers, mode-locking originates from the interplay of gain, loss, dispersion and nonlinearities, most commonly resulting in the emission of short pulses. However, pulse formation is prevented when the gain recovery is fast enough to suppress amplitude fluctuations. Mode-locking then produces an extended state of nearly constant intensity, whose dynamics is governed by the phase. Yet, a general framework for designing the phase of such extended photonic states remains lacking. Here we introduce a hydrodynamic approach to designing extended photonic states, in which the phase dynamics are understood and controlled as a flow of liquid-like light. The intensity, clamped by fast gain, plays the role of a constant density, the instantaneous frequency that of a flow velocity, and the programmable radio-frequency modulation applied to the laser acts as a potential landscape that controls the flow. We derive analytical solutions connecting the applied modulation to the instantaneous frequency and hence to the spectrum emitted by the laser. We further provide experimental evidence for the liquid light shaping framework by measuring the frequency comb spectra emitted by a fast-gain semiconductor laser around 1.6 micron under the control of a programmed modulation, and comparing them to the ones predicted by the analytical solution. The hydrodynamic picture of mode-locking provides a predictive design principle for frequency combs, pointing toward a programmable synthesizer of light, and establishes fast-gain lasers as an accessible, electrically driven platform for nonequilibrium fluids of light.

items.title: Site-selective preparation of two-dimensional dipolar quantum gases in an optical beat-note lattice
items.summary: High-resolution microscopy of two-dimensional dipolar quantum gases requires selecting individual atomic layers, a task complicated for strongly magnetic lanthanide atoms by the limited applicability of standard magnetic-gradient techniques. We present an all-optical method for the deterministic spatial selection of single- and bilayer samples of cold dipolar atoms using spatially selective parametric heating within a beat-note superlattice. By utilizing a high-resolution microscope objective as a common retroreflector for both optical frequency components, the lattice planes are passively stabilized. This renders their positions exceptionally robust against experimental drifts and structure-borne vibrations, even eliminating the need for active laser stabilization over millimeter-scale separations from the reflecting surface. We validate this approach by demonstrating the robust isolation of one or two atomic layers in precise coincidence with the focal plane of our objective. This enables future single-atom-resolved studies of long-range interacting systems.

items.title: FlowMLLab: An open-source framework for reproducible computational-fluid-dynamics and scientific-machine-learning experiments
items.summary: FlowMLLab is an open-source Python framework for scientific machine learning in thermal-fluid and aerospace engineering, covering incompressible, compressible and rarefied flows. Its 22 weeks comprise 51 notebooks and 35 lectures. Solvers and molecular sampling underpin field prediction, uncertainty quantification and reduced-order modeling. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and deep operator networks (DeepONets), including POD-DeepONet, connect operating conditions to flow fields alongside Fourier neural operators. Physics-informed neural networks infer solutions and constitutive coefficients. Geometry-conditioned models, including the point-cloud DeepONet variant Geom-DeepONet, handle changing domains. Aerospace applications address airfoil shock/vortex identification, rarefied-gas modeling, nozzle flow prediction and supersonic body design. Complementary thermal-fluid examples cover unsteady wakes, hydrofoil vapor clouds and noisy particle observations.
