PRIS moves screening from a pass-or-fail verdict to a chemical reason for failure, showing that autonomous agents can discover, by active refutation, physicochemical laws that guide calculations and experiments.

items.title: Language Model Security Modules: Turning LLM Interpretability into Runtime Defense
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are served behind layered defenses such as alignment and guardrail models, yet jailbreaks still get through. Interpretability research looks inside the model, where methods such as probes and sparse autoencoders expose signals of harmful content during generation. A signal alone, however, is not a defense. To become one, the serving system must tie each signal to the right request, apply the policy as declared, and release output only when the policy allows. Today, defenses built on such signals handle these duties on their own, so every new detector needs its own integration. Yet none of these duties depends on how a signal is computed. We present Language Model Security Modules (LMSM), which adapts the design of Linux Security Modules to LLM serving and carries out these duties once in a shared mediation path. The path hosts pluggable backends that turn model internals into evidence and policies that decide what that evidence allows. Each policy declares the evidence and evaluations it needs, and LMSM provides exactly these for each request and verifies that they took place, so a failure is never mistaken for permission. Protection therefore remains cheap and correct under common serving optimizations. We evaluate LMSM in vLLM, with both eager and compiled execution, on Qwen3-4B and Gemma-3-4B with fitted probes, a released transcoder, and a released sparse autoencoder. With vLLM's default optimizations on, every backend keeps at least 96% of native throughput, and all of them share the same mediation path. On Qwen3-4B, a representative probe-based policy cuts HarmBench attack success from 39.4% to 3.3% while XSTest false refusals rise from 0.8% to 3.1%. LMSM lets existing and future interpretability methods become runtime defenses without rebuilding the serving path.

items.title: Do Egocentric Video-Language Models Capture Both Hand- and Object-Centric Cues?
items.summary: Recognizing hand-object interactions (HOIs) requires capturing both hand dynamics and object transformations, which provide complementary information for distinguishing visually similar manipulations. However, Video-Language Models (VLMs) trained solely on egocentric videos tend to over-rely on hand appearance, struggling to distinguish interactions with similar visual appearances but different dynamics (e.g., taking vs. kneading dough). To better utilize complementary hand- and object-centric cues, we propose a learning paradigm with (i) hand-object masked training to encode both hand- and object-centric cues and learn their relationships through cross-cue reconstruction, and (ii) an HOI-dynamics-aware decoder that grounds each cue through auxiliary location and semantic predictions. To assess how effectively models leverage hand- and object-centric cues for action recognition, we introduce Cue-Isolated HOI (CI-HOI), which independently evaluates recognition performance based on each cue. To enable this evaluation, we curate the DEHOI testbed using video inpainting to selectively remove either hands or manipulated objects, allowing us to evaluate action recognition with each cue isolated. DEHOI reveals that existing VLMs trained only on egocentric video rely more on hand-centric cues than VLMs trained on more non-egocentric video data. We show that our training paradigm mitigates this hand-centric bias, outperforming VLMs trained on the same egocentric data across DEHOI, standard action recognition, and object state recognition benchmarks.

items.title: Assessing the robustness of heterogeneous treatment effects in survival analysis under informative censoring
items.summary: Dropout is common in clinical studies, with up to half of patients leaving early due to side effects or other reasons. When dropout is informative (i.e., dependent on survival time), it introduces censoring bias, because of which treatment effect estimates are also biased. In this paper, we propose an assumption-lean framework to assess the robustness of conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates in survival analysis when facing censoring bias. Unlike existing works that rely on strong assumptions, such as non-informative censoring, to obtain point estimation, we use partial identification to derive informative bounds on the CATE. Thereby, our framework helps to identify patient subgroups where treatment is effective despite informative censoring. We further propose a novel model-agnostic meta-learner, called SurvB-learner, to estimate the bounds that can be used in combination with arbitrary machine-learning models, and that has favorable theoretical properties such as double-robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. We finally demonstrate the effectiveness of our meta-learner across various experiments using both simulated and real-world data.

items.title: Hull variation of algebraic geometry codes under divisor twists
items.summary: The hull $\mathrm{Hull}(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{C}^{\perp}$ of a linear code $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ interpolates between linear complementary dual (LCD) codes, with trivial hull, and self-dual codes. Its dimension is preserved by coordinate permutations but not by scalings $\mathcal{C}\mapsto\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathcal{C}$, $\mathbf{x}\in(\mathbb{F}_q^*)^n$. This governs the complexity of Sendrier's support-splitting algorithm and decides whether an equivalence class contains LCD codes. We study this hull-variation problem, formalised by Chen, for algebraic geometry codes $\mathcal{C}(D,G)$ over a function field $\mathcal{F}/\mathbb{F}_q$ of genus $g>0$, where scalings are twists of $G$ by principal divisors; as a natural relaxation, we allow twists $G\mapsto G+L$ by arbitrary divisors. Writing $\mathcal{C}(D,G)^{\perp}=\mathcal{C}(D,H)$, with $H=D-G+W$, $W$ canonical, a twist acts by $(G,H)\mapsto(G+L,H-L)$. Whenever $\gcd(G+L,H-L)$ is non-special, the hull dimensions of $\mathcal{C}(D,G+L)$ and $\mathcal{C}(D,G)$ differ by exactly $\frac12(\mathrm{deg}|G-H|-\mathrm{deg}|G-H+2L|)$. For a genuine scaling, $L=-(z)$, this variation is bounded by $2[\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{F}_q(z)]$. Under the same hypothesis, we obtain an upper bound on the hull dimension depending only on $D$ and $W$, and characterise exactly when it is attained by a scaling of it. These bounds shed new light on Chen's maximal hull dimension; explicit scalings on Kummer extensions show that the first is sharp. We construct explicit twists that raise, respectively lower, the hull dimension by prescribed amounts, one unit at a time, and apply them to two classical families. Starting from known LCD codes, we reach every hull dimension in an explicit range; starting from a self-dual code ($q$ even) or a code of maximal hull dimension ($q$ odd), we descend to $0$, yielding LCD codes of various dimensions.

items.title: Two Principles for Autoregressive Language Modeling
items.summary: We investigate the functional differentiation learned by RoPE Transformers to derive principles for autoregressive language modeling. We introduce two intervention-based metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS) measures how removing a frequency contribution changes a head's full attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD) isolates the effect of rotary modulation. In Qwen3 and Llama3.1, these metrics distinguish retrieval from positional modeling, while individual heads can exhibit both functions. A mid-low-frequency Global Positional Band (GPBand) separates their frequency dependencies and tracks the training sequence length in controlled experiments, suggesting that global positional fitting can hinder zero-shot length extrapolation. These findings motivate two principles. (1) Functional Organization: retrieval and positional functions should be assigned separately and mixed within layers with layer-specific allocation; and (2) Positional Dependence: positional modeling should operate only locally, while global access should rely on position-independent retrieval. Matched pretraining from scratch and targeted architectural ablations at 380M and 1.4B parameters support both principles and highlight the importance of mechanism choice in realizing each function. Together, these findings suggest a promising route toward architectural innovation grounded in the functional requirements of autoregressive language modeling.

items.title: Hydrogen reaction rate modeling based on convolutional neural network for large eddy simulation
items.summary: This paper establishes a data-driven modeling framework for lean Hydrogen (H2)-air reaction rates for the Large Eddy Simulation (LES) of turbulent reactive flows. This is particularly challenging since H2 molecules diffuse much faster than heat, leading to large variations in burning rates, thermodiffusive instabilities at the subfilter scale, and complex turbulence-chemistry interactions. Our data-driven approach leverages a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), trained to approximate filtered burning rates from emulated LES data. First, five different lean premixed turbulent H2-air flame Direct Numerical Simulations (DNSs) are computed each with a unique global equivalence ratio. Second, DNS snapshots are filtered and downsampled to emulate LES data. Third, a CNN is trained to approximate the filtered burning rates as a function of LES scalar quantities: progress variable, local equivalence ratio and flame thickening due to filtering. Finally, the performances of the CNN model are assessed on test solutions never seen during training. The model retrieves burning rates with very high accuracy. It is also tested on two filter and downsampling parameters and two global equivalence ratios between those used during training. For these interpolation cases, the model approximates burning rates with low error even though the cases were not included in the training dataset. This a priori study shows that the proposed data-driven machine learning framework is able to address the challenge of modeling lean premixed H2-air burning rates. It paves the way for a new modeling paradigm for the simulation of carbon-free hydrogen combustion systems.

items.title: Two $(2+ε)$-Approximation Algorithms for Minimum Spanning Tree Interdiction
items.summary: Minimum spanning tree interdiction asks for edge deletions within a budget that maximize the weight of a remaining minimum spanning tree. We give two deterministic $(2+ε)$-approximation algorithms for every fixed $ε>0$, improving the previous best factor of $4$. Both algorithms respect the original budget and run in $N^{O(1/ε)}$ time for $0<ε\le1$, where $N$ is the binary input size. The first algorithm uses two weight thresholds to choose initial deletions that force every remaining spanning tree to contain edges at or above these thresholds. It then uses the remaining budget to further increase the MST weight through Lagrangian rounding. The second algorithm achieves the same guarantee through a different decomposition: it enumerates vertex partitions and heavy trees connecting their parts, then approximates a bounded-weight interdiction problem within the parts. An objective-preserving reduction from Maximum Components shows that, assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis and $\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time $(2-δ)$-approximation exists for any fixed $0<δ<1$, even on simple graphs with weights in $\{0,1\}$. Thus, our approximation guarantee is conditionally tight up to an arbitrarily small additive constant. Finally, the MST guarantee yields a $(4+ε)$-approximation for metric-TSP interdiction.

items.title: GA-VINO: A Geometry-Aware Variational Physics-informed Neural Operator for Mindlin-Reissner Plates
items.summary: Plate and shell structures are widely used in engineering fields. Rapid response prediction for such structures under complex geometries, heterogeneous materials, and varying loads is important for engineering design, but conventional numerical methods usually require repeated modeling and solution when the physical configuration changes. To address this issue, this study proposes a geometry-aware variational physics-informed neural operator (GA-VINO) for Mindlin-Reissner plates. GA-VINO represents the plate geometry using boundary point clouds and incorporates a material encoder, a load encoder, and a scalar-parameter branch to handle spatially random material fields, spatially varying pressure loads, and sample-level uniform parameters. Through multi-branch point cloud encoding and cross-attention, GA-VINO fuses geometric, material, loading, and query point information, and predicts the transverse deflection and rotations at arbitrary query locations. Unlike conventional data-driven neural operators, GA-VINO requires no labeled solution data during training. Instead, it minimizes a variational physics-informed loss constructed from the discretized total potential energy of the Mindlin-Reissner plate. Compared with grid-based neural operators, GA-VINO directly processes irregular point clouds and allows different physical fields to be discretized on different point sets, avoiding forced interpolation onto a common grid. The method is validated on multiple examples involving different geometries, material fields, and load distributions. The results show that GA-VINO achieves promising accuracy in deflection, rotation, gradient-sensitive, and energy-based metrics, completes full-field inference for new samples within milliseconds, and exhibits promising cross-geometry generalization capability.

items.title: SCRiD: Spatial and Contextual References for Generalizable AI-Generated Video Detection
items.summary: Generalizable AI-generated video detection remains challenging because natural motion and content variations can resemble synthesis artifacts, making isolated video discrepancies unreliable indicators of authenticity. To address this challenge, we propose Spatial and Contextual Reference-informed Detection (SCRiD), a framework that interprets video variations through complementary spatial and contextual references. Specifically, we introduce Matched-Coordinate Residual Response (MCR) to characterize temporal residual associations under motion and coordinate references with matched subpixel sampling conditions. We further develop Real-Conditioned Score Adaptation (RCSA), which learns a content-conditioned denoising reference from authentic videos and probes its responses across multiple noise scales and quality views to guide feature adaptation. To integrate these complementary sources of evidence, we design Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) to enable information exchange through reversible symplectic updates. We train SCRiD using synthetic videos from only 4 generators and evaluate it across 88 generator or task subsets spanning 6 benchmarks. Our method achieves average ACC and AP of 72.72% and 74.23%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.24 and 0.81 percentage points.Ablation and robustness experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and the stability of SCRiD under common post-processing operations.

items.title: MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity Linking
items.summary: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a "divide-and-conquer" strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.

items.title: RAID: Representation Autoencoder for Intrinsic Decomposition
items.summary: Single-image intrinsic decomposition is an inherently ill-posed problem, requiring the disentanglement of strongly coupled appearance factors from a single RGB observation. Recent methods address this ambiguity with diffusion priors, at the cost of large, iterative, and often stochastic models. We show that accurate decomposition does not require a large generative model. Our key idea is to decouple reconstruction from decomposition on top of a strong pretrained representation. First, an $X \rightarrow X$ teacher learns to reconstruct each intrinsic map from DINOv3 features using a shared decoder, without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision. Then, a DINOv3-based student predicts the corresponding teacher representations from RGB through lightweight, modality-specific projections, enabling training on partially annotated datasets and predicting all intrinsics in a single forward pass. \textbf{RAID}, predicts intrinsic properties in the structured latent space, enabling a compact 165M-parameter model, 100x faster than diffusion-based methods. Despite its compact size, it achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, with improved robustness to input resolution. Additionally, our learned projections yield interpretable, modality-specific feature spaces.

items.title: Towards Online Adaptive LLM-based Semantic Filtering
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) enable semantic filtering over unstructured documents using natural language predicates, but invoking an oracle LLM on every document incurs prohibitive monetary cost and online latency. Existing model-cascade approaches reduce this cost by using a lightweight proxy model to score each document and forwarding only uncertain documents to the oracle. However, their proxy models have limited generalization capability, and they typically adopt fixed sampling budgets for proxy training and threshold calibration, which insufficiently adapts to diverse online queries. To address this, we present OASIS, an online adaptive framework for LLM-based semantic filtering. OASIS combines a query-agnostic document similarity prior with query-adaptive online learning and sampling. In the offline phase, OASIS utilizes query-agnostic document similarity as a prior and constructs a document navigating spread-out graph (NSG) over document embeddings. For each online query, OASIS trains a query-conditioned graph attention network over the document NSG to obtain proxy scores through semi-supervised node classification. To allocate labels effectively, OASIS adopts density-aware active learning to explore uncertain score regions, selectively annotate informative documents, retrain the proxy, and stop early when additional labels are unlikely to improve the cascade. During threshold calibration, OASIS progressively samples an adaptively sized calibration set, adapting calibration cost to the query's score distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OASIS achieves a 1.75x-5.42x reduction in online latency and reduces the number of LLM-processed documents by 35%-75% relative to the state-of-the-art methods at an achieved accuracy of 0.9.

items.title: ABSClaw: From Invented Worlds to Reality-Grounded Social Simulation
items.summary: LLM-based artificial societies exhibit rich behavior but often lack scientific grounding: personas and environments are assumed, interaction networks are synthetic, and simulators are generated as free-form code, making results difficult to tie to real populations and sensitive to the backbone model. We argue that simulated worlds should be sampled from observed data, while simulation logic should be implemented by composing operations from a shared, task-independent vocabulary. In this paper, we introduce ABSClaw, a zero-code agent that compiles natural-language requests into executable, reality-grounded social simulations. ABSClaw grounds who acts, where they act, and with whom they interact in survey and census data, geospatial sources, and real networks. It expresses state transitions through 26 atomic operations. To support an open and extensible ecosystem, ABSClaw further allows capabilities to be added as lifecycle-scoped skills without modifying its core. Furthermore, we propose ABSBench, a benchmark of 193 real-world social-simulation tasks. On ABSBench, ABSClaw achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated social simulators. Three real-world case studies show that grounding personas, environments, and interaction networks each improves agreement with observed outcomes. With one runtime skill, ABSClaw executes 13 population-scale simulations, collectively involving 25 million agents. Together, these results demonstrate ABSClaw's real-world fidelity, extensibility, and scalability.

items.title: FOCUS: Active Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Model Agents
items.summary: Sparse outcome rewards make it difficult for long-horizon language-model agents to assign credit to earlier actions. Learned critics provide value estimates for intermediate states, but these estimates can be inaccurate, while estimating intermediate values with repetitive continuation samples from points within a trajectory incurs substantial costs. To mitigate these issues, we introduce FOCUS, an RL method that uses selective branching to help the critic network learn its value estimator. The rollout controller facilitates active learning for the critic by sampling continuations from states that are expected to most reduce the critic's estimation error. These refined value estimates then score the segment between consecutive states with a TD($λ$) advantage, while the sampled evidence supplies training targets for the critic. FOCUS supports long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning through a modular context-management interface that decouples context management from rollout allocation. Our experiments show that using compaction-induced segment boundaries for value estimation and credit assignment, FOCUS outperforms GRPO and VinePPO with matched per-step generation budgets on legal reasoning, deep search, and code localization benchmarks, improving held-out accuracy at Qwen3.5-9B scale by 7.2 points over the strongest baseline on BrowseComp-Plus (55.4 vs. 48.2) and by 4.1 points on DeonticBench (56.5 vs. 52.4).

items.title: Symplectic Hulls over a Non-Unital Ring
items.summary: This paper presents the study of the symplectic hulls over a non-unital ring $ E= \langle κ,τ\mid 2 κ=2 τ=0,~ κ^2=κ,~ τ^2=τ,~ κτ=κ,~ τκ=τ\rangle$. We first identify the residue and torsion codes of the left, right, and two-sided symplectic hulls, and characterize the generator matrix of the two-sided symplectic hull of a free $E$-linear code. Then, we explore the symplectic hull of the sum of two free $E$-linear codes. Subsequently, we provide two build-up techniques that extend a free $E$-linear code of smaller length and symplectic hull-rank to one of larger length and symplectic hull-rank. Further, for free $E$-linear codes, we discuss the permutation equivalence and investigate the symplectic hull-variation problem. An application of this study is given by classifying the free $E$-linear optimal codes for smaller lengths.

items.title: Comparing Each Generation with Independent Siblings Gives Video World Model Post-Training a Proper Objective for Outcome Frequencies
items.summary: Video world models are used as simulators, so when a first frame leaves several physical outcomes open, repeated generations should produce each outcome as often as it occurs in the data. Physics post-training scores every generation against the single recorded future of its history, which makes single videos more faithful, but the expected score is linear in the model distribution and is maximized by always producing the most likely outcome. The log-likelihood of the recorded outcome is maximized by the data distribution, and its gradient weights agreement with the record by the inverse of how often the model produces the generated outcome, a frequency that other generations of the same history with independent noise, its siblings, can estimate. To train with this weight from a finite group, we propose SibPO, which performs Sibling-paired Policy Optimization: siblings estimate a truncated inverse-frequency weight for agreement with the record, and a second term subtracts the same weight times the agreement with the siblings, which makes the expected objective a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells at every group size. On PisaBench, SibPO lowers the KS distance to simulated landing times by 9.1-10.2% relative to the strongest method outside its reward family on three of four video models without degrading single videos, and it lowers the error of estimated robot policy success rates by 13%.

items.title: Coordinate-Free Corridor Reconstruction and Field-of-View Framing Attribution for 3D Bilateral Coronary Artery Trees in CT Angiography
items.summary: Bilateral coronary tree extraction from cardiac computed tomography angiography (CCTA) must transfer from cropped benchmarks to uncropped scans without territory swaps or lattice staircases. Using 35 training scans, we fix a coordinate-free three-dimensional network (597,032 parameters) and a flush-admissible 8.0 mm corridor solver refined by a learned medial offset. We evaluate once on 50 ImageCAS scans against Lee94 thinning skeletons and zero-shot on 40 ASOCA scans (20 healthy, 20 diseased; 80 trees) against Vascular Modeling Toolkit (VMTK) Voronoi consensus centerlines. On uncropped pericardial ASOCA scans, our method leads all comparators on per-artery Chamfer distance (6.90 mm automatic despite 14.22 mm ostium error; 7.05 vs. 9.11 mm seeded, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.0047$). It also leads 1 mm centerline F1 (51.42% and 51.56%, +13.21 to +29.08 percentage points [pp], $p_{\text{Holm}} \le 9.0 \times 10^{-4}$) at $1.66 \pm 0.07$ s/scan on an NVIDIA L4 graphics processor. In cropped ImageCAS boxes, it leads F1 (76.98%) while trailing 18--22 mm bridgers on mean distance (3.37 vs. 2.72--3.20 mm; none significant after Holm). Pitch-matched 1.19 mm zero-clutter controls show coarse pitch degrades matched U-Nets whereas fixed-frontend distance reversal requires pericardial clutter. Flush collar gating rescues 30/32 seeded ASOCA stubs (-7.97 mm), and the learned medial offset raises node (+2.72 to +5.11 pp; bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence interval [+2.42, +3.01] on ImageCAS) and curve (+1.87 to +4.40 pp) F1. Short corridors curb pericardial chaining while learned offsets lift centerlines off the lattice.

items.title: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes
items.summary: While the notions of sphere packing and sphere covering underlie the most widely used criteria for space-filling design in computer experiments, namely, the maximin and minimax approaches, they suffer from major drawbacks in high dimensions. First, when the dimension $d$ is very large, deploying a space-filling design requires an extremely large number of design points, making the very notion of a space-filling design questionable. Second, these two design characteristics are highly sensitive to boundaries, particularly when the design domain is a hypercube (the case considered in this paper), and especially to its vertices. This sensitivity is particularly acute when the design size is less than $2^d$. Instead of considering the maximin or minimax criterion, we consider here the quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube. This error has three key advantages: it accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point $U$ to the design, is less sensitive to boundary effects than the maximin and minimax criteria, and, thanks to Zador's celebrated theorem, enables a smooth and natural transition to uniform designs as the design size tends to infinity. Building on recent results on the construction of optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772) we propose a method to generate random designs of a given target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error. The support of the resulting distribution is then used to construct designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$. We demonstrate that, for moderate $n$, designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well---and significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube. We also explain how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.

items.title: Targeted Synthetic Control Method
items.summary: The synthetic control method (SCM) estimates causal effects in panel data with a single-treated unit by constructing a counterfactual outcome as a weighted combination of untreated control units that matches the pre-treatment trajectory. In this paper, we introduce the targeted synthetic control (TSC) method, a new two-stage estimator that directly estimates the counterfactual outcome. Specifically, our TSC method (1) yields a targeted debiasing estimator, in the sense that the targeted updating refines the initial weights to produce more stable weights; and (2) ensures that the final counterfactual estimation is a convex combination of observed control outcomes to enable direct interpretation of the synthetic control weights. TSC is flexible and can be instantiated with arbitrary machine learning models. Methodologically, TSC starts from an initial set of synthetic-control weights via a one-dimensional targeted update through the weight-tilting submodel, which calibrates the weights to reduce bias of weights estimation arising from pre-treatment fit. Furthermore, TSC avoids key shortcomings of existing methods (e.g., the augmented SCM), which can produce unbounded counterfactual estimates. Across extensive synthetic and real-world experiments, TSC consistently improves estimation accuracy over state-of-the-art SCM baselines.

items.title: Extending the hybrid fictitious domain-immersed boundary method for Reynolds-averaged turbulence modeling
items.summary: Engineering practice often calls for shape or topology optimization (TO) of fluid defining components, while the ever-increasing computing power allows the optimized cost functions to be based on computational fluid dynamics (CFD). However, a common bottleneck in CFD-based TO frameworks is the requirement for frequent remeshing. In order to alleviate this bottleneck, we propose an adaptation of an immersed boundary (IB) method variant, the hybrid fictitious domain-immersed boundary method, to leverage Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations and wall function. The main contribution of the present work lies in the design and open-source implementation of the IB-aware steady-state solution of the RANS equations via the SIMPLE algorithm in the OpenFOAM library. For the most common two-equation RANS models, Reynolds numbers from $10^1$ to $10^6$, and several benchmarks, such as flow over a backwards facing step or an Ahmed body, the framework gives results consistent with the standard body-fitted CFD. Furthermore, given the intended application in TO, special emphasis is placed on the robustness and applicability of the approach to general geometries, which is tested on a real-life engineering application in simulation of coolant flow in a die-casting die core.

items.title: Single-Controller Teleoperation and Multimodal Dataset Generation for a Mobile Manipulator
items.summary: Robot learning systems require synchronized, high-quality demonstrations that combine visual, proprioceptive, and action data. However, collecting such datasets with mobile manipulators is often slowed down by fragmented teleoperation interfaces and manual post-processing workflows. This paper presents an integrated framework for teleoperated multimodal data collection on a Clearpath Dingo-O mobile base equipped with a Kinova Gen3 Lite manipulator and an Intel RealSense RGB-D camera. The framework combines single-controller operation of the base, arm, and recording process with an automated ROS-based pipeline for data capture, image-quality filtering, temporal synchronization, visualization, and export to machine-learning-ready Zarr datasets. We validate the system on a pick-and-place mobile-manipulation task in which the robot transports a bottle between two surfaces. The results show that the unified controller supports complete task execution and recording without external commands, while the data pipeline produces synchronized datasets for short demonstrations and identifies corrupted visual frames. The proposed framework provides a practical basis for producing structured demonstrations for robot-learning research.

items.title: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation
items.summary: Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is. This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel obfuscators, and we hope that obfsgen and the rationale behind its design help make such obfuscators practical and deployable.

items.title: The Largest Tractable Subclass of Multi-Scale Allen Temporal Reasoning
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a novel model for temporal reasoning over multi-scale intervals. We show that this model yields a complete reasoning framework and exhibits other particularly interesting properties. Furthermore, we identify the maximal tractable subalgebra for this model, as well as for the other complete model, in the qualitative scales context, which exhibits weaker properties but whose results can be derived by transfer from our new model.

items.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
items.summary: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

items.title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
items.summary: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.

items.title: RECLAIM: Robot-Vision-Informed Adversarial Patch Defense via Embodied Attention Feedback
items.summary: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.

items.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
items.summary: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.

items.title: Mitigating fix reversal: Counterfactual constraints for function-level vulnerability detection
items.summary: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4\%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15\%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8\% to 48.4\%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.

items.title: Study and Improvement of Search Algorithms in Stochastic Perfect-Information
items.summary: In this article, we generalize Unbounded Minimax, the state- of-the-art search algorithm for deterministic zero-sum two- player games with perfect information to the framework of stochastic zero-sum two-player games with perfect informa- tion. We experimentally show that this generalized algorithm achieves better performance than the main stochastic search algorithms.

items.title: Inferring Neural Activity Changes under Recording Uncertainty with Transformers and Variational Inference
items.summary: A difference in recorded firing rate across days may reflect a change in neuronal activity, missed spikes or recording a different neuron. We present a statistical approach that combines neuron tracking with Bayesian estimates of stationary mean recorded firing rates. Bounds under assumed differences in spike detection connect recorded rates to biological rate changes. We assess recording loss and uncertainty in rate changes in simulations, and count-model fit in recordings. We also compare two transformer estimators with Gaussian and flow variational inference under a shared temporal negative-binomial model. Flow variational inference agrees most closely with reference posteriors, while predictive performance varies across mice. Rate-change intervals contain true simulated changes less often than intended. In UnitMatch recordings from five mice, some inferred changes remain supported when spike detection is allowed to differ between days; others depend on equal detection. These interpretations require a correct neuron match. The approach identifies which inferred rate changes remain supported under specified recording assumptions and where uncertainty limits interpretation.

items.title: Chemotactic aggregation as cue-mediated adaptation toward Nash equilibrium in a spatial patterning game
items.summary: Chemotactic cells generate their own chemical gradients to form spatial patterns that support collective functions ranging from cooperative metabolism to immunity. Despite progress in understanding the optimality of chemotaxis in imposed chemical gradients, it remains unclear how close decentralized cell populations can come to maximizing the population-wide benefit of spatial organization through individual movement and local modulation of chemical gradients. We employ mean field game theory to characterize efficient spatial patterns achievable by decentralized populations as Nash equilibria: each agent optimizes its positioning given the spatial density of the other cells, whereas the population density is determined by the positioning of all individuals. We derive coupled dynamics of population movement and cue modulation that drive adaptation toward these equilibria and verify its structural correspondence to established phenomenological models of chemotactic pattern formation. We apply our framework to self-organized aggregation and numerically demonstrate that the dynamics can form multiple equilibrium patterns, some of which are comparable to the population-level optimum under moderate incentives to aggregate. We also show that the relative timescales of cue modulation and movement influence pattern selection and population-level efficiency: slower cue modulation can yield more coherent and efficient equilibrium patterns. Our framework thus highlights fundamental limits on collective optimization in decentralized cell populations, and suggests a functional role for timescales in self-organized coordination through environmental feedback.

items.title: A multilayer network-based modelling framework for epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus transmission in France
items.summary: Epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 (EHDV-8) emerged in France in September 2023 but its transmission dynamics remain poorly characterised. We adapted a stochastic, spatially explicit compartmental model developed for bluetongue to reconstruct the 2023-24 EHDV-8 epidemic in cattle in mainland France. The model represented transmission across cantons, incorporating cattle demography, pasture cover, relative Culicoides abundance and temperature-dependent vector processes. Three networks represented between-canton spread through short-range vector dispersal (pasture network), non-commercial cattle movements between pastures of the same farm (farm network), and cattle trade (trade network). Using approximate Bayesian computation with sequential Monte Carlo (ABC-SMC), we calibrated the model to canton-week seroprevalence estimates derived from bulk-tank milk measurements. Calibration narrowed the plausible range of the baseline vector-mediated transmission parameter and favoured higher movement intensities through the farm network, although movement intensity remained uncertain. Simulation-based parameter recovery showed that calibration generally identified parameter regions capable of reproducing epidemic patterns comparable to the pseudo-observed data, although predictive performance varied among datasets and was typically lower than that obtained with the generating parameters. When applied to observed data, the calibrated model captured several features of the observed weekly median seroprevalence across sampled cantons, although discrepancies remained at some sampling times and predictive uncertainty was substantial. These results demonstrate how bulk-tank milk surveillance can inform the reconstruction of EHDV-8 epidemic patterns within a national-scale transmission framework. This framework provides a basis for future evaluation and optimisation of vaccination strategies.

items.title: Biases and Limits of AlphaFold Predictions for Non-Globular Proteins
items.summary: AlphaFold has transformed protein structure prediction, making structural models accessible across the life sciences. We explore experimentally validated cases of non-globular proteins to uncover where predictions diverge from biologically relevant structural states and how molecular context shapes these discrepancies, guiding a more informed interpretation of AlphaFold models.

items.title: Persistent Homology as a Morphological Signature of Fibrin Networks
items.summary: We present an investigation of the applicability of topological data analysis (TDA) to the study of high-resolution confocal microscopy images of fibrin network structures from patients with oesophageal cancer undergoing intended curative surgery. Investigation of clot structure brings new knowledge about blood coagulation, risk of bleeding, and thrombosis in this group of patients. Images of fibrin network formation in the collected blood samples were captured by confocal microscopy and three-dimensional z-stacks were analysed. Each z-stack was cropped to a centre region for analysis, the validity of which is assessed in detail. Overall, we found no significant differences in fibrin network topology across the perioperative period, and no consistent differences in network structure between the standard and intervention groups.

items.title: Are You Learning Biological Signal or Shortcuts? Auditing and Mitigating Bias in Protein-Protein Interaction Datasets
items.summary: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) databases do not faithfully reflect biological realities. Instead, they are influenced by study and technical biases that distort certain protein and interaction attributes. Machine learning models can exploit these as learning shortcuts if the negative dataset is not constructed with care. So far, the shortcuts introduced during PPI dataset construction have only been examined in isolation. Here, we systematically characterize both reported and, to our knowledge, previously unreported biases in PPI datasets that lead machine learning models to learn shortcuts instead of biological signal. We analyze HIPPIE, IntAct, and STRING, dedicated PPI databases, as well as two datasets derived from 3D-structural information in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We show that random data splitting introduces strong topological shortcuts. When train-test protein overlap is removed, the resulting datasets still retain usable shortcuts stemming from self-interactions, taxonomic identity, and functional relatedness, whose prevalence interestingly depends on the data source. We further show that sampling negatives from a set of highly replicated non-interactions, an intuitively appealing choice, can amplify the shortcut stemming from functional relatedness. To detect and mitigate these biases, we provide an open Nextflow pipeline that combines similarity-aware, data-loss-minimizing dataset splitting with bias-minimizing negative sampling, both formulated as integer linear programs. Its key concept of quantifying biases to minimize them through optimization-based negative sampling can, in principle, be extended to any machine learning problem where the pool of negative candidates is much larger than the positives and is thus of interest also beyond PPI prediction.

items.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
items.summary: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

items.title: Micrograph B-factor estimation via Wilson statistics
items.summary: The single-particle cryo-electron microscopy imaging process is known to cause exponential decay in the amplitude and power spectra of proteins. This decay is modeled by the B factor and is currently corrected as a post-processing stage of the 3D reconstruction. As a consequence, all experimental images in the dataset are assumed to share the same B factor. In this paper, we suggest a novel approach wherein the B factor is determined and corrected as a preprocessing step to the reconstruction. We show such an approach can improve reconstruction resolution.

items.title: SCOPE: Single-Cell Omics Prediction from Histology via RNA-Protein Prior Enhancement
items.summary: Predicting the RNA and protein content of cells from routine H&E images could extend spatial molecular profiling to existing slide archives. However, both H&E-spatial proteomics and H&E-spatial transcriptomics paired datasets are limited by the number of available markers and the insufficient availability of high-quality, cell-resolved data. We present SCOPE (Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA-protein prior Enhancement), a unified framework that leverages biologically complementary information between RNA and proteins to address the limited availability of single-omics supervision. Our key insight is that, although RNA and proteins represent distinct molecular modalities, their biological relationships provide valuable shared knowledge that can benefit single-omics prediction tasks. To this end, SCOPE introduces biologically informed biomarker priors to enhance shared gene-level representations, enabling knowledge transfer across RNA and protein modalities through gene-protein correspondence and molecular associations. By exploiting these complementary relationships, SCOPE enables both prediction tasks to benefit from a shared backbone enriched with cross-omics biological knowledge. Furthermore, its biomarker correlation design facilitates the prediction of unseen markers, extending spatially resolved molecular profiling beyond directly supervised targets. Across test datasets spanning 16 organs, SCOPE improves the average RNA Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 8.8%. On two external protein cohorts, it improves the average Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 9.7% for seen markers and 11.9% for unseen markers.

items.title: The Shape of Individual Fitness Distributions and the Dynamics of Ecological Communities
items.summary: Developing a mechanistic understanding of biogeography and biodiversity that predicts species abundances, distributions, and fluctuations is a central goal of community ecology. We develop a model, that can be seen as an extension of Hubbell's neutral theory, in which a focal species competes with the aggregate of all other species in a local community of fixed size. Each individual has its own competitive ability, and the shape of the distribution of these abilities is incorporated in the model, represented by distributions rather than single species-level values. Under complete mixing, symmetric competitive encounters without ties recover Hubbell's neutral model. We further incorporate immigration from a larger metacommunity and derive a diffusion approximation for the focal species' relative abundance. The model shows that competitive ability distributions with the same mean and variance can nevertheless yield different patterns of local abundance. Thus, species that appear equivalent when summarized by trait statistics need not be ecologically equivalent. Our framework links individual-level variability to population-level persistence and abundance and provides a way to examine how competition and immigration jointly shape ecological outcomes.

items.title: MitoWorld: A Stochastic World Model of the Single-Cell Cycle under Genetic Perturbation
items.summary: A cell observed after a gene knockdown has an uncertain future, both in how its appearance will evolve and when it will divide. Existing approaches predict endpoints or population-level changes without jointly modeling individual trajectories and division timing. In this work, we present MitoWorld, a stochastic world model that generates these future appearances as continuous evolution in a Gaussian reference latent, terminated by a division hazard and converted into images by a conditional diffusion renderer. The ordinary transition provably preserves its Gaussian reference, tying its noise to its dynamics; paired observations identify its discrete transition where stationary marginals cannot. The hazard turns division timing into a survival likelihood that can be tested against real cycle lengths. On 325 held-out MitoCheck tracks spanning 17 knockdowns and a control, MitoWorld lowers FID by 34.6\% and the video metric JEDi by 45.6\% relative to the strongest baselines. Its latent-space prediction intervals achieve near-nominal 90\% coverage, are 35\% narrower than those of a model with freely fitted noise. The hazard also yields cell-cycle length distributions with KS distance close to the model-based finite-sample reference. Testable single-cell stochastic dynamics thus offer a generative tool for time-lapse perturbation screens.

items.title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
items.summary: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

items.title: A Dual-SOM Learner Model of Instructional Efficiency within Cognitive Load Theory
items.summary: This paper presents a novel methodological framework, integrating a dual self-organising map (SOM) neural network architecture with Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), for assessing instructional efficiency within learning environments. By representing curriculum content as a directed acyclic graph of topic dependencies, the proposed model captures collective learning behaviour across two core dimensions: academic performance and subjective/introspective mental effort. During SOM training, representative data sets of successful learner trajectories are compressed into two topologically ordered, identically structured neural networks: PSOM (performance space) and ESOM (mental effort space). By pairing these behavioural maps, the model serves as a decision-support tool that enables instructors to simultaneously pinpoint structural instructional design defects, such as hidden topic prerequisites, and evaluate collective cognitive load profiles. The implementation and performance of the PSOM component (and, by extension, its symmetrical twin, ESOM) is linked to an earlier modelling study employing a SOM with identical structure and encoding semantics situated in the same domain (i.e., a learning environment). This paper combines the study of behavioural phenomena with theoretical work on human cognitive architecture via SOM neurocomputational cognitive behavioural modelling.

items.title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data
items.summary: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

items.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
items.summary: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

items.title: GramStatTexNet: Efficient, Interpretable, and Neuro-Inspired Texture Analysis-by-Synthesis
items.summary: Deep networks achieve high realism in texture synthesis but often rely on opaque, over-parameterized representations that have limited direct connection to biological vision. Neuroscience-informed pyramid models are interpretable, compact, and biologically inspired, but rely on small, hand-curated statistics sets that are difficult to generalize or extend. We introduce GramStatTexNet, a hybrid analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines the multi-scale Gabor filter structure of classical models with the flexibility of Gramian-based correlations, organized into structured filter families. This structured representation enables analyses that are challenging for deep-feature methods: each statistic carries a named filter-family identity, allowing us to decompose synthesis fidelity into per-family contributions and to learn an interpretable, low-dimensional embedding that preserves perceptual texture content. We compare our framework to classical and deep texture-synthesis baselines across diverse texture categories, and on multiple perceptual metrics, highlighting the compactness and interpretability advantages of this hybrid representation, alongside competitive synthesis quality. This same framework extends naturally to peripheral textures via spatial pooling, and to dynamic textures using a spatiotemporal filter bank. GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for analyzing and modeling visual information with natural extensions across space, time, and eccentricity. Project page: https://vdutell.github.io/gstn

items.title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
items.summary: ProteinGeoBench is a set of 131 tasks that give an agent protein structure files and ask it to look up recorded facts, check sequences, calculate geometry from atom coordinates or reason about structures. We ran four frontier models on every task several times (4,249 runs) and 26 models on a subset. A single overall score hides two different skills. Three of the four frontier models are best at looking up facts and worst at calculating from coordinates: Claude Opus 5 scores 0.907 on lookup and 0.716 on calculation. Gemini 3.1 Pro is the exception. Geometry is overrepresented among the hardest tasks. Half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail are calculations, although calculations are a fifth of the suite, and eight of the twelve were solved by none of the 26 models. The three leading models are within 0.031 of one another, too close to order, and with one run per task a different model ranks first in 24% of bootstrap resamples. Reports should therefore give scores by task type and the number of runs per task. They should also state the agent harness, the software that runs the model, and its network access, because both change scores. On a 15-task subset, blocking eight structural databases lowered scores, and removing network access lowered them more. Replacing our harness with each provider's own command-line agent moved scores by up to 0.09 in either direction. Across the 26 models, those that scored higher on the other tasks also scored higher on calculation.

items.title: An information-geometric framework for mapping maximum potential biodiversity
items.summary: Biodiversity measures are often used descriptively: one computes a diversity index from an observed or estimated community composition and maps the resulting values across space. Conservation planning, however, also requires a site-specific benchmark against which the observed community can be compared. This chapter develops an information-geometric framework for such \emph{potential diversity} and the associated \emph{diversity gap}. The central object is a pair of probability vectors on the species simplex: an observed or realized composition \(p^{\mathrm{obs}}\), and a potential composition \(p^{\mathrm{pot}}\) obtained by a constrained variational principle. The gap is then defined by comparing a diversity functional at these two compositions. The framework is developed for both Hill-type diversity, which measures abundance and evenness, and Rao's quadratic entropy, which incorporates trait, phylogenetic, or ecological dissimilarities among species. A spatial point-process interpretation clarifies how local ecological capacities can be defined before passing to the simplex. Escort constraints, capacity constraints, and divergence projections then provide a unified way to define nontrivial benchmarks beyond the uniform distribution. The resulting formulation separates two distinct questions: how diverse a community is, and how far it is from a locally admissible potential benchmark. It also connects the ecological idea of dark diversity with a continuous, abundance-weighted comparison on the probability simplex. We also outline a dynamic extension in which capacities, species migration, and climate-driven shifts vary over time. Empirical implementation with large-scale citizen-science biodiversity data and trait databases is left for future work.

items.title: Hebbian self-organization of monosynaptic reflexes in a biologically realistic multiarticular limb
items.summary: Spinal monosynaptic reflexes depend on patterns of connectivity between muscle spindle afferents and motoneurons that should reflect musculoskeletal dynamics. One possibility is that the details of these circuits are specified genetically, but this requires an unlikely coevolution of musculoskeletal and neural elements. Here we show how biomechanical structure can determine the connectivity of self-organized spinal circuits. Using a neuromechanical model combining a multi-joint limb, proprioceptive feedback, and Hebbian plasticity driven by motor babbling, we find that biologically realistic connectivity emerges spontaneously when babbling is neither too sparse nor too frequent. This results in strong homonymous projections, weaker heteronymous projections among functional synergists, and very weak connections among antagonists. This outcome also depends on musculoskeletal morphometry. Heteronymous synergies form when proximal muscles are strongest---the characteristic gradient of mammalian limbs--whereas excessively strong biarticular muscles lead to unphysiological antagonist coupling. The mechanisms differ: homonymous connections arise from direct sensorimotor correlation during fusimotor coactivation by beta motoneurons, while heteronymous connections depend on multi-joint dynamics that emerge only after homonymous reflexes stabilize and increasing muscle strength generates multisegmental motion. Overall, this study provides a mechanistic basis for fetal sensorimotor development and generates testable predictions about the consequences of naturally occurring and experimentally induced variations.

items.title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Rat Locomotion
items.summary: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.

items.title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
items.summary: We present the first complete implementation of $β$-reduction in the untyped $λ$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $θ$--$γ$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.

items.title: Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
items.summary: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

items.title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
items.summary: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement.
