A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.

items.title: Who Is the Regression About? Auditing AI-Labeled Treatments When Effects Differ
items.summary: Researchers increasingly regress outcomes on treatments labeled by large language models. When effects differ, OLS averages the effect on the treated (ATT) and on the untreated (ATU), weighting the smaller group more. A label's bias then has two parts: classical attenuation from misclassification, and a selective term when its errors are correlated with the outcome. In LinkedIn postings, the model misses better-paid remote jobs: a precision check passes, yet the remote pay gap is understated by nearly 40 percent, a bias that more data cannot remove. A stratified, blind audit of both labeled groups corrects it and recovers both effects.

items.title: Deterministic Uniformization for Estimation and Latent Trajectory Inference in Interval-Censored Multistate Transition Models
items.summary: Interval-censored multistate data arise when subjects are observed at irregular visit times, leaving transition times and intermediate states unobserved. Likelihood-based inference for continuous-time Markov models often requires computationally intensive matrix exponential evaluations. We propose a deterministic uniformization expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm for parameter estimation and latent trajectory inference. By representing the continuous-time process through an embedded Markov chain indexed by latent Poisson event counts, the method enables deterministic E-step calculations without repeated matrix exponential evaluations. The M-step reduces to transition-specific Poisson regressions with exposure offsets, accommodating covariate-dependent transition intensities. We establish uniform truncation error bounds and show that the procedure is an asymptotically monotone generalized EM algorithm. Under standard regularity conditions, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Simulations demonstrate accurate estimation and computational advantages over direct likelihood optimization, particularly for complex transition structures. We also develop an exact dynamic programming method to calculate posterior probabilities of candidate latent pathways and identify the most probable pathway between observations. Posterior expected transition counts and state occupancy times provide additional subject-specific summaries, while expected-count ratios offer a computational shortcut for classification in simple mutually exclusive pathway structures. The framework supports both population-level inference and individualized characterization of disease progression.

items.title: Transfer Learning for High-dimensional Quantile Regression with Distribution Shift
items.summary: Information from related source studies can often enhance the findings of a target study. However, the distribution shift between target and source studies can severely impact the efficiency of knowledge transfer. In the high-dimensional regression setting, existing transfer approaches mainly focus on the parameter shift. In this paper, we focus on the high-dimensional quantile regression with knowledge transfer under three types of distribution shift: parameter shift, covariate shift, and residual shift. We propose a novel transferable set and a new transfer framework to address the above three discrepancies. Non-asymptotic estimation error bounds and source detection consistency are established to validate the availability and superiority of our method in the presence of distribution shift. Additionally, an orthogonal debiased approach is proposed for statistical inference with knowledge transfer, leading to sharper asymptotic results. Extensive simulation results as well as real data applications further demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed procedure.

items.title: Summary Sufficiency in Simulation-Based Inference via Mutual Information
items.summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated from the model. For high-dimensional or variable-length data, SBI methods typically rely on low-dimensional summary statistics as conditioning inputs for posterior estimation, making their sufficiency crucial for accurate inference. Mutual information (MI) provides a natural information-theoretic characterization of sufficiency, quantifying how much parameter information a summary retains. However, these MI quantities are generally intractable in likelihood-free settings. Sui et al. (2026) estimate MI from a trained neural posterior using the Barber--Agakov (BA) lower bound, while discussing, but not computing, a Fisher-information upper bound. This makes the estimate ambiguous: a small lower bound may indicate either an insufficient summary or an inaccurate density estimator. We address this limitation with a tractable diagnostic that estimates the BA gap and reveals what the difference between bounds has actually measured. We extend the resulting sufficiency metric to observation-centered restricted data spaces, allowing simulations to focus on a neighborhood of the data while preserving the target posterior and enabling valid sufficiency comparisons between summaries. We illustrate the use of this diagnostic tool on a temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence model by comparing learned and hand-crafted summary statistics for variable-length earthquake catalogs.

items.title: An Adjusted Ersatz Discrepancy for Global Sensitivity Analysis: Theory and Benchmarks
items.summary: In given-data sensitivity analysis, the analyst holds only a fixed sample of model inputs and outputs. We revisit the ersatz discrepancy of Puy, Roy, and Saltelli (2024), a grid-occupancy statistic read from the scatterplot of an input against the output, and propose two modifications: a rank transformation of the output and a deterministic Moore-neighbourhood fill of isolated empty cells. We derive the asymptotic theory of the resulting adjusted ersatz under simple random sampling. Without the fill, the rank-transformed statistic is exactly a histogram estimator of Borgonovo's moment-independent measure ($δ$). At its resolution, however, it converges to $e^{-1}$ plus a different $f$-divergence, so that its value under independence is $0.37$. With the fill, the limit lies between $δ- 0.141$ and $δ+ 0.048$ for every dependence structure, and its value under independence drops to $0.047$. The theory explains the type I errors observed at screening thresholds of $0.01$, $0.05$, and $0.10$, the dominant role of the grid resolution, and when rankings by $δ$-type measures and by total-order Sobol' indices agree. In replicated benchmarks, Becker metafunctions and the HYMOD model, a degree-adaptive polynomial chaos expansion estimates total-order indices most accurately, whereas the adjusted ersatz differs from $δ$ by $0.02$-$0.08$ on average, as the theory predicts, and improves markedly on the original measure. It is best used as a fast, assumption-free screening statistic.

items.title: A Hybrid NUTS-Gibbs Sampler with State Space Marginalization for Estimation of Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Binomial Outcomes
items.summary: Dynamic structural equation models (DSEMs) are widely used for analyzing intensive longitudinal data (ILD). Although many ILD have categorical (Bernoulli or binomially distributed) responses, currently available algorithms for estimating DSEMs are limited to using the probit link and the Bernoulli distribution, i.e., the response can only be success or failure for a single trial and not the number of successes in multiple trials. They also scale poorly with increasing model complexity and sample size. Here, we present a hybrid sampler---alternating between one step of the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) and one Gibbs step---which solves both of these problems: the Gibbs step naturally handles Pólya-Gamma distributed latent variables arising from binomially distributed responses with a logit link, and the NUTS step utilizes a Kalman filter to exactly marginalize over latent states, making models with dynamics defined in terms of latent traits more computationally feasible. We demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed sampler in simulation experiments, and also study conditions under which it fails. We finally illustrate its use in an example application of predicting panic attacks.

items.title: Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
items.summary: Regularization-based continual learning reduces catastrophic forgetting by penalizing changes to parameters that mattered for earlier tasks. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), a standard instance, weights its quadratic penalty by the empirical Fisher, usually justified as approximating loss curvature. We instead derive the penalty from what training on a new task should preserve. In this formulation, Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC), new training must keep chosen functionals of learned behavior unchanged, and the local approximation of this constraint is the stored penalty. We show that EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each old sample's loss. The derivation exposes a flaw: EWC weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so samples the model fits well barely contribute, although later training can still forget them. Improved EWC (IEWC) instead penalizes how far each old output moves off its loss level set, rather than how much its loss changes, which removes this weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR, a classification-specific correction. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, removing this weighting alone raises ImageNet-R accuracy over EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07). More broadly, CLOC turns the design of continual-learning penalties into a choice of what to preserve, from which a principled penalty follows by derivation.

items.title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
items.summary: Self-supervised objectives such as VICReg learn representations by making related inputs similar, while variance and covariance penalties prevent collapse. These penalties are statistics over a batch of samples, so layer-local variants, too, are typically local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), which optimizes a VICReg-style objective one sample at a time with purely local updates: each update uses only the current activity of its own and the preceding layer and a fixed-size running state. Temporally adjacent inputs serve as positive pairs, which makes the objective a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis (SFA). Running estimates of each neuron's mean and variance, together with one lateral matrix per layer, replace the batch statistics; held fixed during differentiation, they turn the gradient into a Hebbian feedforward update and an anti-Hebbian lateral update. We show that a two-layer network trained with batch size one on an MNIST stream of class-homogeneous chunks reaches 96.48% linear-probe accuracy, above random features (95.09%) and classical SFA, and that the temporal order and each loss term contribute to this result. With both locality constraints relaxed, the same objective matches supervised backpropagation. TeReL thus shows that the collapse-preventing statistics of modern self-supervised learning can be held as running state at each neuron, which brings these objectives closer to what brains and neuromorphic hardware can implement.

items.title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
items.summary: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

items.title: Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases for Amortized Conditional Interpretability
items.summary: Gradient-based attribution provides input-specific information about model parameters, but computing it via backpropagation for many samples is expensive, while static importance scores discard input dependence. We derive KPSA (Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlas) from a block decomposition of the empirical neural tangent kernel. It measures normalized parameter-group sensitivity, embeds those sources in an explicit query space, and uses a lightweight kernel to estimate sensitivities for unseen inputs. We derive bounds that separate finite-source from irreducible representation error and give margin-based top-$k$ recovery. This paper studies two interpretability applications. Firstly, KPSA identifies parameter groups with high susceptibility to perturbations across vision, forecasting, and protein-modeling setups. Across a fivefold range of parameter budgets ($0.02$-$0.1\%$), its selected groups attain $39$-$85\%$ of the perturbation susceptibility of a first-order backpropagation oracle. In vision and forecasting, these parameter groups form sparse sensitivity circuits that extend across depth and vary systematically with the input. Secondly, we use KPSA on an activation-attribution problem for MLP features in transformers. It retains $81\%$ of the gap between a backpropagation oracle and a constant-sensitivity baseline on vision while increasing batched query-time throughput from 551 to 2,041 images/s and reducing peak GPU memory from 4.55 to 0.44GB. On the protein-modeling task, it recovers $68\%$ of this gap. An ablation of KPSA's kernel aggregation shows that nearest-neighbor retrieval in KPSA space can remain competitive. The empirics show that compact kernel atlases can store useful input-dependent parameter sensitivity while amortizing repeated gradient attribution, a step toward scalable conditional interpretability. Code can be found at https://github.com/Axym-Labs/kpsa .

items.title: Parameter-Free and Group Conditional Online Conformal Prediction
items.summary: Quantifying the uncertainty in predictions made by machine learning models is challenging in online settings where the characteristics of the data and labels change over time. Online conformal prediction (OCP) methods tackle this problem by producing intervals for each observation and guaranteeing that a proportion of them contain their labels, a property known as marginal coverage. OCP methods, however, may systematically miscover observations belonging to groups defined by attributes like age or race, raising fairness concerns. Group-conditional OCP (G-OCP) methods address this by producing intervals that provide coverage for multiple groups. Existing approaches rely on learning rates, which control how they react to changes in the data stream, but can be hard to tune in online settings. Leveraging advancements in learning-rate-free methods, we develop a learning-rate-free G-OCP algorithm with strong group-coverage guarantees that hold under weaker assumptions than those required in prior work. Empirical results show that our method provides group coverage, produces interval lengths competitive with those of standard methods, and reacts more effectively to changes in the data than fixed-learning-rate methods.

items.title: Rank and computation of the pathlifting Jacobian of a DAG ReLU network
items.summary: This paper provides a self-contained proof of the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian of a DAG ReLU network by performing an induction on the network's number of hidden nodes. In fact, the induction is elementary, and the key recipe is to consider the skeleton matrix of the network, a sparse matrix encoding the network paths, and transform the representation of one of its hidden neurons into an output node. The proof relies on intermediate propositions which link the pathlifting, its Jacobian, the network parameters, and its skeleton matrix, which, on top of permitting to conclude on the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian, also provide a way to compute it without backpropagation and whose computation cost is super efficient in practice compare to usual backpropagation. The paper is provided with a Python module that implements the different propositions of the paper for feed forward networks and is used to experimentally quantifies the computational gain of computing the pathlifting Jacobian with the proposed theory.

items.title: Dealing with Logs and Zeros in Regression Models
items.summary: Log regression is widely used to express effects in percentage terms, but zeros, heterogeneity and retransformation pose distinct difficulties. We unify the interpretation, identification and estimation of proportional effects through weighted individual percentage changes. We connect these parameters to pseudo-maximum likelihood estimation, characterize finite-sample differences between consistent estimators, and establish relationships with log regression. We develop a new shifted-log transformation that yields unit-invariant proportional-effect parameters and use it to construct iterated ordinary least squares (IOLS), an algorithm that estimates power-mean models through repeated OLS regressions. We prove global numerical convergence, consistency and asymptotic normality, and extend the approach to endogenous regressors. Furthermore, we develop fixed-effect cancellation and bias-correction methods that address incidental-parameter bias in common panel settings under general working variances, extending beyond the familiar Poisson-PML case. Finally, simulations document numerical reliability, competitive speed and finite-sample performance, while an application to economic development illustrates their empirical relevance.

items.title: Nonlinear Joint State and Noise Estimation under Packet Dropouts and Additive Measurement Corruption
items.summary: This paper investigates joint state and noise covariance estimation for nonlinear systems subject to dual reliability impairments: random packet dropouts and additive measurement corruption. This scenario poses challenging nonconjugate inference, as clean and corrupted measurements share an unknown baseline covariance $\boldsymbol{R}_k$ with fixed known corruption covariance $\boldsymbol{E}_k$. Packet reception is observable, whereas the authenticity of received measurements remains latent and must be inferred. To resolve this intractable estimation problem, we cast joint posterior inference as a variational optimization problem and develop a conjugate variational inference adaptive Kalman filter with dual reliability (CVIAKF-DR). The proposed method retains analytical updates for the prediction covariance and two reliability probabilities, while adopting CVI to estimate the state and baseline measurement covariance. The covariance update combines the analytical contribution from clean measurements with Monte Carlo gradient estimates for corrupted measurements. Numerical results on a re-entry tracking benchmark demonstrate the superior accuracy of the proposed method in both state and noise covariance estimation. Remarkably, even built upon the linear Kalman filtering (KF) framework that is originally designed for linear systems, our method achieves more accurate estimation performance than dedicated nonlinear filtering algorithms based on the cubature Kalman filter (CKF).

items.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
items.summary: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

items.title: Schur multipliers, vanishing minors and Gaussian conditional independence
items.summary: Conditional independence in a Gaussian vector is the vanishing of almost-principal minors of its covariance matrix $Σ$. A sensitivity analysis replaces $Σ$ by the Schur product $Δ\circΣ$, where the symmetric multiplier $Δ$ differs from one exactly at the changed positions. Such a change generally destroys some conditional independences, and we determine which minors stay zero. A vanishing minor is preserved for every matrix exactly when the corresponding block of $Δ$ has rank one. When variances or covariances change, each almost-principal minor of $Δ\circΣ$ is a polynomial in the amounts added, with minors of $Σ$ as coefficients, and a conditional independence survives every such change exactly when they vanish. In an undirected graphical model, changing variances joins the neighbours of the perturbed vertices, while changing covariances leaves a structure read from the graph by a separation rule, possibly not graphical. Both extend to ancestral graphs, directed acyclic graphs included, and identify the entries that can vary freely. For the other entries, blocks of rank one along a junction tree characterize the multipliers that preserve a decomposable model. A sensitivity analysis can therefore rest on the conditional independence structure after the change, as illustrated on examination marks of 88 students.

items.title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands
items.summary: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.

items.title: A General Theory of Nonparametric Response-Adaptive Randomization
items.summary: Response-Adaptive Randomization (RAR) assigns incoming patients to treatments with probabilities that depend on previously observed responses. While most existing RAR procedures rely on finite-dimensional summaries of treatment performance (such as rates, means, or model parameters), we develop a nonparametric (NP) distribution-based framework in which the treatment outcome distributions are learned sequentially and adaptation is driven by their functionals. The framework naturally accommodates multiple treatments and is particularly suited to endpoints for which average effects may conceal relevant differences across the outcome distribution. We introduce an ethical NP-RAR rule driven by a pre-specified distributional score and a nonparametric extension of the multi-arm efficient randomized adaptive design (NP-ERADE) able to approach generic distribution-dependent targets selected according to ethical or inferential optimality criteria. We establish strong consistency and joint functional central limit theorems for the empirical treatment distributions, together with asymptotic normality of functional scores, estimated targets and allocation proportions. We further show that the NP-ERADE allocation proportions attain the semiparametric efficiency bound for the target. We develop post-trial inference for score contrasts and distributional features, including crossing locations, and investigate finite-sample properties, robustness and inferential performance via simulations.

items.title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
items.summary: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

items.title: Anytime Valid Conformal Prediction on Streaming Time Series
items.summary: Sequential prediction on streaming time series is essential for continuous monitoring and risk control in applications such as finance, energy, and healthcare systems, where prediction intervals must remain valid at arbitrary stopping times and adapt to potential distributional shifts. Conventional conformal prediction provides model-agnostic uncertainty quantification but relies on exchangeability, which is violated under distributional shifts. Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI) relaxes this assumption by updating the miscoverage level in response to the realized prediction errors, but it only guarantees that the realized average miscoverage rate along a single trajectory approaches the target level in the long run. Risk-sensitive monitoring instead requires controlling the true miscoverage rate, i.e., the conditional probability that a prediction set misses, which measures the reliability of the set itself rather than the misses that happened to be realized. We show that, without assumptions on the distributional shifts, it is impossible to have such control for every single prediction set at arbitrary stopping times. We therefore target the true running and rolling average miscoverage rates. Our methods combine ACI with anytime valid confidence sequences. With high probability, the true running average miscoverage rate stays below the target level uniformly over time, and so does the true rolling average for any window rule. The efficiency loss for the rolling average vanishes for windows that grow sufficiently fast, but not for fixed windows.

items.title: Renewable Estimation for Generalized Nonparametric Regression with Dynamic Spline Bases and Likelihood Pullback
items.summary: Streaming datasets require statistical models to be updated as new observations arrive, often without repeated access to the full history. In generalized nonparametric regression, a fixed spline space may limit approximation accuracy when the initial representation is insufficient. However, when the basis is expanded, the historical summaries represented in the previous spline space must be re-expressed in the enlarged spline space, which requires a suitable mechanism. We propose a renewable penalized-likelihood algorithm for canonical exponential-family nonparametric regression that combines nested cubic-spline refinement with a Gram-metric pullback of the retained historical likelihood quadratic under the streaming setting. The algorithm incorporates incoming-batch likelihood contributions and updates historical score and curvature summaries at the actual fitted center. The Gram-metric pullback preserves the retained historical quadratic over the embedded previous space. Under explicit regularity and algorithmic conditions, we establish L2-consistency at rate O_p(N^{-2/5}) for a fixed target in H^2[0,1]. We further establish that the energy-norm discrepancy between the renewable estimator and a matched offline estimator is of smaller order, where the offline method is fitted based on the full data and using the same realized terminal spline space and penalty. Simulations demonstrate the benefits of dynamic bases when the initial spline representation is restrictive, with additional gains from historical summary pullback. Additional experiments assess computational cost and storage of the proposed method relative to the offline method. Applications to real datasets also illustrate the proposed method.

items.title: Causally-interpretable meta-analysis using aggregate data
items.summary: Evidence syntheses and meta-analyses are used to inform clinical practice guidelines and health economic evaluations. However, heterogeneity of treatment effects poses a significant challenge. Conventional meta-analysis addresses heterogeneity through random-effect assumptions, which are not supported by design and lead to estimates that may not apply to any real-world population. Causally-interpretable meta-analysis (CIMA) offers a rigorous framework for specification, identification, and estimation of causal effects when combining information from multiple randomized trials. Initial development of CIMA focused on using individual data from randomized trials, but such data are often unavailable in practice. Here, we propose a new version of CIMA that only requires aggregate data from trials, addressing the limitations of traditional meta-analysis methods while relying only on aggregate data. The method leverages the trials' reported estimates of marginal and one-at-a-time subgroup treatment effects and descriptive statistics for baseline covariates to build moment equations for identifying and estimating a parametric conditional average treatment effect (CATE) function. The average treatment effect in a new target population is obtained by marginalizing the CATE function over the individual covariate data that defines the target population. The method can also be used to obtain causally-interpretable indirect treatment comparisons in the target population. We establish the asymptotic properties of the method, assess its finite-sample performance in simulation studies, and illustrate the application of the method by re-analyzing a published meta-analysis for SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with heart failure.

items.title: Optimal Importance Sampling Densities for Estimating Several Expectations at Once
items.summary: Simulation studies often estimate several quantities from a single sample, and the best importance sampling density depends on how the errors on these quantities are combined. We characterise the optimal auxiliary density for a general error criterion. We show that it is the nominal density reweighted by a weighted length of the vector of estimated functions, where the weights are set by the error criterion, or by the curvature of the loss when the criterion comes from a loss on the errors. We also provide a lower bound on the best achievable error. The optimal density is explicit for smooth losses, including the usual losses on covariance matrices. We also derive allocation laws for the cells of a histogram and characterise the minimax density for the probabilities of several events. When there is no closed form, we show how to compute the optimal density numerically.

items.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
items.summary: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.

items.title: A conic optimization framework for shape-constrained functional regression analysis
items.summary: Standard regression methods do not always guarantee that the estimated model reflects prior knowledge about how predictors relate to the response, which motivates constrained regression. When the effects to be estimated are smooth nonlinear functions, a natural family of constraints is that of shape constraints, such as sign, monotonicity, or curvature, which encode qualitative properties that these functions are often expected to satisfy. While shape-constrained estimation of smooth functions is well established in classical regression with scalar covariates and response, its extension to functional regression, where the coefficients are themselves functions, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose the functional shape-constrained conic P-spline estimator (FunSCOPE), a unified framework for shape-constrained functional linear regression that covers scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and function-on-function models, and in which any combination of the shapes above can be imposed on the functional regression coefficient. Building on a P-spline approach, the desired shapes are expressed as conditions on the scalar regression coefficients, which leads to an estimation problem formulated as a conic optimization problem. For univariate coefficients, as in scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and a particular case of the function-on-function regression, the concurrent case, these conditions are both necessary and sufficient, in contrast to existing approaches, which provide only sufficient conditions; for bivariate coefficients, as in general function-on-function models, they are neither necessary nor sufficient. Numerical experiments show that FunSCOPE outperforms competing methods in terms of estimation error and computational time.

items.title: Pairwise Target Rotation for Factor Models
items.summary: Factor analysis is used to characterize latent variables by examining relationships among manifest variables. In exploratory factor analysis (EFA), various factor models are considered to uncover the latent structure. Now, the success of EFA lies with the model's interpretability, as the objective is to build a factor model that is not only supported by data, but is also meaningful. Achieving such, however, is challenging, as gauging interpretability is difficult and subjective, owing to rotational indeterminacy. Thus, we propose a new index that measures the interpretability of a factor model. The index does this by evaluating the agreement between a priori information, such as semantic information from items, and the loadings. We also introduce pairwise target rotation, a rotation method that maximizes interpretability based on the index. In general, this method allows for an intuitive yet flexible way of incorporating a priori information, such as semantics, in factor rotations, which can help in performing EFA more effectively. Based on simulations, the index correctly indicates better fit when noise levels are lower and the new rotation outperforms classical orthogonal rotations across diverse conditions in terms of recovering the latent structure. Finally, we applied the method to empirical datasets, providing evidence linking item semantics and latent constructs, consistent with recent findings.

items.title: Training-Time Batch Normalization Reshapes Local Partition Geometry in Piecewise-Affine Networks
items.summary: The effect of batch normalization (BN) on the function realized during training is less understood than its effect on optimization. We study training-time BN in continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) networks through the affine regions they induce in local $\ell_\infty$ windows around the data. Conditioned on a mini-batch, every switching hyperplane of a BN layer with learned parameters and a general CPA activation is a translate of a hyperplane through the batch centroid, at an offset given by a standardized quantity times the batch spread, independent of the raw bias. We prove an exact formula, valid under general position, for the number of regions in a window in terms of window cuts and interior intersections. For a BN layer it gives a lower bound on the local count in terms of the standardized offsets; the bound depends on the batch only through its spread and not on the biases or the batch location. Without BN the best such bound is $1$: for any weights and batch, some biases leave the window as a single region. We prove that the formula holds in deeper layers, inside parent affine regions of any rank. By the exact formula, BN increases the expected local count whenever it increases the expected numbers of window cuts and of interior intersections, which we examine empirically. Offset distributions of networks trained on synthetic data, MNIST, CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet show higher window-cut rates under BN, and exact enumeration in two dimensions attributes most of the additional BN regions to interior intersections.

items.title: Unraveling time-varying causal effects of multiple exposures: integrating Functional Data Analysis with Multivariable Mendelian Randomization
items.summary: Mendelian Randomization is a widely used instrumental variable method for assessing causal effects of lifelong exposures on health outcomes. Many exposures, however, have causal effects that vary across the life course and often influence outcomes jointly with other exposures or indirectly through mediating pathways. Existing approaches to multivariable Mendelian Randomization assume constant effects over time and therefore fail to capture these dynamic relationships. We introduce Multivariable Functional Mendelian Randomization (MV-FMR), a new framework that extends functional Mendelian Randomization to simultaneously model multiple time-varying exposures. The method combines functional principal component analysis with a data-driven cross-validation strategy for basis selection and accounts for overlapping instruments and mediation effects. Through extensive simulations, we assessed MV-FMR's ability to recover time-varying causal effects under a range of data-generating scenarios and compared the performance of joint versus separate exposure effect estimation strategies. Across scenarios involving nonlinear effects, horizontal pleiotropy, mediation, and sparse data, MV-FMR consistently recovered the true causal functions and outperformed univariable approaches. To demonstrate its practical value, we applied MV-FMR to UK Biobank data to investigate the time-varying causal effects of systolic blood pressure and body mass index on coronary artery disease. MV-FMR provides a flexible and interpretable framework for disentangling complex time-dependent causal processes and offers new opportunities for identifying life-course critical periods and actionable drivers relevant to disease prevention.

items.title: Do Coding Agents Deceive Us? Detecting and Preventing Cheating via Capped Evaluation with Randomized Tests
items.summary: A growing failure mode in agent evaluation and training is that models can achieve high evaluation scores (e.g., test pass rates) by exploiting shortcuts instead of solving the intended task, making these scores deceptive. This makes evaluation scores unreliable as measures of true task-solving ability. We propose CapCode, a framework for constructing coding datasets with randomized tests whose best achievable non-cheating score is deliberately capped below 100%. This capped-score design gives evaluation scores a clearer interpretation: scores substantially above the cap are implausible and therefore provide evidence of cheating. To prevent cheating, we propose CapReward, a reward design based on the CapCode principle to discourage optimization beyond the cap. Experiments across multiple datasets show that CapCode detects cheating while preserving performance ranking of models, and CapReward reduces cheating behavior, yielding models that better follow the intended task specification.

items.title: Kähler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
items.summary: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a Kähler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We descend according to a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via ill-curvature-conditioned, or lack thereof, landscapes. We focus on Calabi-Yau metrics specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential, so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture. In non-compact settings, we can write the metric determinant with respect to a background in terms of a function, pluriharmonic or real. Using Yau's Liouville theorem, we get a small eigenvalue blow-up effect under nontrivial background interaction, geometric invariance of the endomorphism constant, and almost low rank assumptions. In an empirical setting, a Ricci-flat metric will not form, but large eigenvalues can be a local condition and hold empirically on open sets even in generalized Kähler cases due to lower bounds on the Ricci potential. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist via geometric modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

items.title: Bayesian variable selection via collapsed importance-weighted variational inference over discrete model spaces
items.summary: Bayesian variable selection under spike-and-slab priors provides interpretable posterior inclusion probabilities for individual predictors, but exploring large discrete model spaces using conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can be computationally challenging. We develop a collapsed importance-weighted variational framework for Gaussian linear regression. The framework analytically integrates out the remaining model parameters and directly approximates the posterior over binary inclusion indicators using a factorised Bernoulli distribution. To improve posterior inclusion probability estimation while retaining the computational simplicity of the factorised variational family, we replace the conventional evidence lower bound with a tighter variational Rényi importance-weighted lower bound. We establish a finite-sample upper bound on posterior inclusion probability approximation errors and show that, under suitable conditions, the optimised variational inclusion probabilities converge to their exact posterior counterparts as the number of importance samples increases and the Rényi parameter decreases appropriately. We further establish that analytical marginalisation tightens the variational objective and the corresponding inclusion probability error bound, while reducing importance-weight variance and improving the asymptotic efficiency of importance-sampling post-processing. To address the challenges of estimating gradients with respect to the variational parameters when the inclusion indicators are discrete, we leverage recent advances in variance-reduced score-function estimators, together with an annealing strategy to stabilise optimisation. Simulation experiments and empirical applications demonstrate improvements in posterior inclusion probability estimation relative to standard variational inference and two existing variational approaches.

items.title: Enhancing Mixed Oil Length Prediction through Graph Representation Learning
items.summary: During the pipeline transportation of refined oil products, the inevitable formation of mixed oil segments poses considerable economic challenges to pipeline networks. Therefore, it is important to accurately predict the length of these mixed oil segments. Although previous methods have achieved relatively accurate predictions by integrating machine and deep learning algorithms, they ignore the statistical dependencies that remain among real-world mixed oil samples, which degrades model accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a novel Sample Dependencies Incorporated Graph Representation Learning (SDI-GRL) model. By representing samples and pipeline features as nodes of a graph, SDI-GRL connects dependent samples through their shared features, allowing message passing to propagate information across related samples. This graph-based framework allows our model to capture the statistical dependencies among samples absent in prior works. A case study on a mixed oil dataset demonstrates that our SDI-GRL model surpasses the strongest existing approach, reducing both the RMSE and the MAE by more than 10%.

items.title: Dynamic Regret for Non-Stationary Linear Bandits via Misspecification Reductions
items.summary: Many online decision-making problems involve both round-specific feasible actions and drifting reward models: eligible ad impressions, feasible prices, and available treatments can change over time, while user preferences, demand curves, and patient responses may evolve. Motivated by these applications, we study non-stationary linear bandits with round-specific feasible decision sets. Our key contribution is a blockwise reduction that connects parameter drift in non-stationary linear bandits to model misspecification in contextual linear bandits while preserving the round-specific decision benchmark. This connection allows us to leverage misspecification-adaptive learning to obtain dynamic-regret guarantees for general time-varying decision sets. For a known path-length budget $P_T$, we establish these guarantees for general compact, adaptive non-anticipating decision sets under an oblivious parameter path, and for $K$-armed contextual linear bandits under an oblivious environment. For general time-varying decision sets, our bounds improve the dependence on $T$ and $P_T$ from the $\widetilde O(T^{3/4}P_T^{1/4})$ guarantees available for existing LinUCB-based approaches to $\widetilde O(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3})$, matching the non-stationary lower-bound dependence up to logarithmic factors.

items.title: Semiparametric regression with stagewise empirical risk minimization
items.summary: Maintaining both interpretability and accuracy remains a fundamental challenge in regression analysis. This paper addresses these two objectives through a semiparametric approach that combines a parametric crude guess with its nonparametric adjustment. In particular, the nonparametric adjustment is implemented via a machine learning technique called ``stagewise empirical risk minimization algorithm.'' Once a set (dictionary) of functions (words) is prepared, this algorithm constructs a convex combination of words selected iteratively from the dictionary. This selection is based on the empirical risk derived from the Bregman divergence, which enables the proposed estimators to be applied in broad settings, including generalized linear models. This paper examines these proposed semiparametric estimators theoretically and numerically. In the theoretical study, we derive a non-asymptotic error bound for the estimators constructed from a general data-dependent dictionary. Among the concrete dictionaries proposed in this paper, some can be utilized to correct variable selection in LASSO-based parametric regression, which is investigated in the numerical study. Moreover, simulation studies investigate practical performance of the proposed estimators, while real data applications further confirm their predictive performance. These studies indicate that the proposed semiparametric estimators can address the above challenge in several settings.

items.title: Two-Stage Staffing with Random Arrival Rate: A Simulation Optimization Approach
items.summary: In service systems, the arrival rate in the same time period and day of the week exhibits randomness, yet can be more accurately estimated or forecast right before that period, which motivates a two-stage staffing scheme with advance base staffing and pre-shift surge staffing. Existing approaches usually impose strong assumptions on the arrival process and service systems' operational logic and other further approximations (i.e., stylized models) to derive explicit staffing policies. This paper proposes a simulation optimization approach (SOA) for more general arrival processes and service systems by effectively addressing some intertwined challenges. By recasting the original formulation into computationally tractable structures and designing an efficient coordinate-search algorithm, it constructs a two-stage staffing lookup table offline, which allows managers to make real-time surge staffing decisions without any further simulation. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed SOA has significantly better staffing performance and substantially broader applicability compared to existing approaches. Even under the stylized models, the cost savings delivered by our SOA compared with existing approaches range from the low tens to several tens of percent, depending on different problem parameters; the advantage further amplifies when the actual problem deviates from the stylized models. In a nurse-staffing case study grounded in real-world data, the proposed SOA delivers approximately 8% to 13% cost savings over a state-of-the-art benchmark.

items.title: Alternative prior specifications and extension to hybrid-controlled trials in Bayesian designs using external data
items.summary: Bayesian methods incorporating external data are attractive for clinical trials with limited patient availability, but controlling the type I error rate remains challenging. Psioda and Ibrahim (2019) proposed a simulation-based framework using external data, which evaluates the Bayesian type I error and power as rejection probabilities averaged over sampling priors. However, when the external data show a large treatment effect, the null sampling prior can degenerate and the Bayesian type I error rate approaches the frequentist rate. Moreover, the robust mixture prior used as the analysis prior has a second component as informative as the external data, potentially biasing estimates, and the framework does not accommodate hybrid-controlled trials. We propose an alternative sampling prior specification, assess estimation bias under the analysis prior, and extend the framework to hybrid-controlled trials. In simulations, the existing specification required sample sizes comparable to or larger than those of frequentist designs, whereas the proposed specification reduced the required sample size but allowed the frequentist type I error rate to exceed the nominal level. A weakly informative second component also reduced estimation bias under prior-data conflict. A pediatric cutaneous lupus erythematosus case study illustrates the method.

items.title: Nonsense rank correlations between independent random walks
items.summary: Yule's nonsense correlation persists for Spearman's rho and Kendall's tau between independent random walks. Neither coefficient concentrates at zero as the sample size grows. For centred random walks with finite increment variances, we derive a universal joint limit expressed through Brownian occupation functionals. Integral formulas give limiting variances of approximately 0.222 and 0.108, respectively, below the Pearson value of 0.241. Rank correlations thus reduce the limiting dispersion on their respective coefficient scales. We prove that both marginal limits have symmetric densities and represent them exactly as limits of polynomial densities determined by Gaussian moment integrals. Spearman's conventional t test and Kendall's normal approximation are asymptotically invalid, with rejection probabilities tending to one under process independence.

items.title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
items.summary: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

items.title: Tree-aggregated compositional regression under measurement error
items.summary: Compositional data arise in many applications, including microbiome studies, where taxonomic or phylogenetic trees describe relationships among taxa. These trees allow taxa with a common regression coefficient to be modeled as a group. An association may be specific to an individual genus or shared across a broader taxonomic group. Measurement error can make an association shared across a group appear specific to smaller groups, even when coefficient signs are preserved. We develop Tree-Aggregated Regression with Correction for Observation Error, or TARCO, to estimate latent coefficients and identify groups along the tree. We establish finite-sample conditions for exact recovery of the true subtree groups and derive bounds on prediction and coefficient estimation errors. The guarantees extend to settings where the measurement error covariance is estimated from auxiliary replicates. Simulations show improvements in prediction and coefficient estimation over tree aggregation without measurement error correction, and illustrate how the choice of tree penalty affects group recovery. In a gut microbiome analysis, TARCO identifies shared associations with body mass index and shows how correction changes their relative strengths across taxonomic groups.

items.title: False Discovery Rate Control in Ordered Sequential Testing: Rejection-Count and Fallback Procedures
items.summary: We study false discovery rate (FDR) control for a fixed family of hypotheses tested sequentially in a prespecified order. Each decision uses only the current and preceding $p$-values, is not subsequently revised, and permits continued testing after non-rejections. We distinguish generalized fixed-sequence procedures based on preceding rejection counts from fallback-type procedures that additionally use recursively transferred testing levels. For rejection-count procedures, we study a position-dependent calibration under independence and a linear rule calibrated through null marginal distribution functions under positive left-tail dependence under the null. We clarify their connections to existing fixed-sequence and online FDR methods. The fallback construction combines the total number of preceding discoveries with level transfer along consecutive rejections, allowing thresholds to reflect the arrangement of earlier outcomes. We establish its FDR control under history-based positive regression dependence and, with a position-specific correction, under arbitrary dependence. For all four constructions, the guarantees extend to every deterministic testing time within the planned horizon. Gaussian simulations assess the effects of signal placement, dependence, and allocation weights. They demonstrate power gains over selected benchmarks while identifying the conservativeness of the arbitrary-dependence correction.

items.title: Faster Algorithms for Structured Linear and Kernel Support Vector Machines
items.summary: Many machine learning problems are quadratic programs, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs). A general quadratic program has input size $Θ(n^2)$, and assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), no $O(n^{2-o(1)})$ time algorithm exists when the objective matrix is positive semidefinite (Backurs, Indyk, and Schmidt, NeurIPS'17). SVMs, however, are given by $n$ data points of dimension $d$, often much smaller than $n$, and have only $O(1)$ equality constraints. In this work, we design the first nearly-linear time algorithm for solving quadratic programs whenever a low-rank factorization of the quadratic objective matrix is given, the number of linear constraints is small, the coefficients of the objective and some optimal solution are bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(n)$, and some feasible point has all entries between $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. For linear SVM on $d$-dimensional data, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $\widetilde O(nd^{(ω+1)/2}\log(n/ε))$ when $(d+1)^{ω-1}\le n$ and the data points have norms at most $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and margin at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, where $ω<2.258$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Its output satisfies the equality constraint only approximately. For Gaussian kernel SVM, when $d=O(\log n)$, the squared dataset radius is $o(\log n/\log\log n)$ and the dual variables lie in a box $[0,R]^n$ with $R\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $n^{1+o(1)}$ for any accuracy $ε\ge 1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$. We also prove that, assuming SETH, when the squared dataset radius is $Ω(\log^2 n)$, $Ω(n^{2-o(1)})$ time is required on some inputs to reach error $\exp(-Θ(\log^2 n))$ for the program without the bias term. This improves upon the prior best lower bound in both the dimension $d$ and the squared dataset radius.

items.title: Semiparametric Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation in Linear Models with Unspecified Error Distributions
items.summary: Causal mediation analysis distinguishes pathways through which a treatment affects an outcome. In linear models, ordinary least squares may leave information in the error distribution unused. We develop a semiparametric framework for joint inference in linear mediation models with treatment-mediator interaction and unspecified error distributions. A stacked estimating system integrates regression-error scores and propagates uncertainty from both regressions and the baseline-covariate distribution through natural-effect decompositions. Under the stated model and regularity conditions, we characterize the natural-effect influence functions and establish an OLS-relative asymptotic variance and local-power ordering. We further develop density-score estimation and joint inference for residual-correlation sensitivity analysis of unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding. Reduced-form regressions and joint uncertainty propagation for their coefficients, residual variances and cross-covariances yield pointwise sensitivity curves and variance-explained contours under explicit working assumptions. Simulations show reduced root mean squared error across several non-Gaussian settings and markedly higher power for a weak indirect effect under asymmetric-mixture errors. The power advantage over ordinary least squares and interaction-adapted Huber comparators persists after independent null calibration. Evaluations also examine interval coverage, numerical success, full sensitivity curves and variance misspecification. An analysis of the randomized JOBS II behavioral intervention illustrates how natural-effect estimates, uncertainty and confounding sensitivity can be interpreted together. Complete estimating equations, a deterministic multi-start algorithm and reproducible numerical output accompany the analysis.

items.title: Anomaly detection using surprisals
items.summary: Anomaly detection methods are widely used but often rely on ad hoc rules or strong assumptions, and they often focus on tail events, missing "inlier" anomalies that occur in low-density gaps between modes. We propose a unified framework that defines an anomaly as an observation with unusually low probability under a (possibly mis-specified) model. For each observation we compute its surprisal (the negative log generalized density) and define an anomaly score as the probability of a surprisal at least as large as that observed. This reduces anomaly detection for complex univariate or multivariate data to estimating the upper tail of a univariate surprisal distribution. We develop two model-robust approximations to these tail probabilities: an empirical approximation based on the observed surprisal distribution and a GPD approximation that fits a Generalized Pareto Distribution above a high threshold. For the empirical approximation we give conditions under which tail ordering is preserved and derive finite-sample confidence guarantees via the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality. For the GPD approximation we establish broad tail conditions ensuring classical extreme-value behavior. Simulations and applications to French mortality, Test-cricket and Old Faithful geyser data show the approach remains effective under substantial model mis-specification.

items.title: On the Structure of Risk Contribution: A Leave-One-Out Decomposition into Inherent and Correlation Risk
items.summary: Risk Contribution (RC) is a widely used risk attribution metric that assigns each position a share of portfolio volatility, with contributions that sum to total portfolio volatility. This paper proposes a leave-one-out decomposition of RC into two interpretable components at the position level: an inherent term (position's own scaled variance) and a correlation term (covariance with the other holdings). Unlike the X-sigma-rho framework, which uses the position's correlation with the full portfolio, ICD uses covariance with the other holdings, yielding qualitatively different diagnostic signals when a position is large relative to the portfolio. The contribution is the interpretive framing and an exact identity linking the components to incremental volatility (iVol), which allows the discrete condition under which a position reduces portfolio volatility to be stated in closed form. That condition differs from the marginal condition and the two can disagree for over-hedged or levered positions. The decomposition also inherits RC's strict additivity. Empirical illustrations on three multi-asset portfolios show the components shift differently across regimes, distinguishing stand-alone volatility spikes from correlation breakdown, and demonstrate value for risk reporting, stress testing, and attribution.

items.title: Decorrelation Before Variable Selection: Left and Right Transforms and Their Trade-Off
items.summary: Decorrelation has two forms. A left transform keeps coefficients and changes noise; a right transform keeps noise and changes coefficients. Cholesky whitening alone keeps noise variables inactive when true ones come first; decorrelation preserving coefficients and noise loses information.

items.title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
items.summary: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.

items.title: Balancing Weights for Causal Mediation Analysis
items.summary: Causal mediation analysis decomposes the average treatment effect into components that operate through intermediate variables and a component that does not. This paper studies weighting estimation of generalized mediation functionals, whose contrasts include natural direct and indirect effects, for any fixed finite number of causally ordered mediators. Inverse propensity score weights are vulnerable to (a) weight instability, because they are products of estimated probability ratios, and (b) finite-sample covariate and mediator imbalance, which can bias the estimator. We instead propose sequential balancing weights, which address (a) by minimizing weight dispersion and (b) by imposing exact balance. Stage one balances covariates between a treatment group and the full sample. Each later stage adds the next mediator and balances a treatment group against the preceding weighted group. A finite-sample bias decomposition of the augmented weighting estimator determines these variables and targets. When exact balance cannot be attained in a small sample, the procedure relaxes the balancing conditions by tolerances selected without using the outcome. Under the stated assumptions, the estimated weights converge at every stage to their population inverse-probability counterparts, with errors from preceding stages entering additively. We also establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency of the augmented weighting estimator, together with conditions for consistent variance estimation. In the main simulation design with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights outperform the compared methods in bias, root mean squared error, and coverage. In a small media-framing experiment with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights reduce the imbalance left by propensity-score weighting.

items.title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
items.summary: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

items.title: Beyond Global Divergences: A Local-Mass Perspective on Bayesian Inference
items.summary: Global objectives, such as KL divergence and ELBO, are widely used in Bayesian inference for measuring distributional discrepancy. This paper studies distributional ``local-mass behaviours'' that are not directly captured by such global objectives. We introduce and use two mathematical tools: (1) Mass Index for recording the polynomial and logarithmic decay scales of local mass, and (2) regularised extended KL (RE-KL), a set-localised divergence that can be formulated in the presence of singular components. Mass Indices help characterise how Bayesian updating changes local mass: (1) power-log likelihood factors shift it explicitly, and (2) parameter-dependent supports, or their smooth softenings, may change the local scale through the amount of mass that remains near the parameter value. Using local RE-KL, we prove absolute, relative, and directional inequalities for comparing local small-ball masses under the two KL directions. Together, these results provide a local theoretical account of local mass behaviour. Experiments provide controlled illustrations of the local behaviour, and show that the directional comparison remains visible in the variational posteriors of Bayesian neural networks up to ResNet-50 on ImageNet. Code is available at https://github.com/Forsythia0604/Local-Mass-Framework.

items.title: Latent Annealed Posterior Sampling with a Variance-Preserving Local Gaussian Approximation for Sparsely Observed Random Fields
items.summary: Posterior inference for random fields from sparse observations presents two major challenges: accurately characterizing complex spatial uncertainty and controlling conditional sampling costs as spatial resolution increases. We propose latent annealed posterior sampling (LAPS). LAPS first maps the random field into a lower dimensional latent space, while a Branch--Trunk coordinate decoder enables field evaluation at arbitrary spatial locations. Flow matching then learns the latent prior distribution. Based on this learned prior, LAPS performs posterior sampling through multilevel annealing. At each level, prior flow transport generates a reference state, which is combined with Gaussian noise using variance-preserving coefficients to construct a local Gaussian approximation of the conditional prior. This approximation is then combined with the observation likelihood to define a local posterior, from which latent posterior samples are generated using preconditioned MALA. Numerical experiments show that LAPS accurately approximates posterior distributions, preserves distinct posterior modes, and decouples posterior conditioning from output resolution. Across two Gaussian benchmarks, LAPS closely matches exact posterior references, with sliced Wasserstein distances $1.8\%$ and $2.4\%$ higher than those obtained from independent exact posterior samples. In the bimodal posterior benchmark, LAPS reduces the sliced Wasserstein distance from $0.2693$ to $0.1499$ and consistently recovers both modes across all test scenarios. For the two dimensional Navier--Stokes random field, LAPS substantially improves marginal posterior calibration while maintaining nearly constant evaluation time as the output grid is refined from $64^2$ to $192^2$. These results demonstrate that LAPS offers a favorable tradeoff among posterior accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and computational efficiency.

items.title: Spectral divide-and-conquer MCMC for long stationary time series
items.summary: Bayesian inference via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods can be prohibitively slow for long time series. Distributed Bayesian inference across multiple cores or machines is non-trivial since simple data splits in time perform badly under temporal dependence. We show that a systematic partitioning of the periodogram observations in the frequency domain gives a fast and accurate posterior approximation for stationary series that can also be used when the computations exceed the memory capacity of a single computational node. Our method uses the asymptotic independence of periodogram observations in the Whittle likelihood to develop a distributed fast Fourier transform combined with embarrassingly parallel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms in modern cluster-computing frameworks. We establish that the error of the spectral divide-and-conquer MCMC posterior approximation relative to the exact time-domain posterior converges to zero in probability in a shrinking neighbourhood of the full-data Whittle posterior mode. The proposed method is shown to be competitive with the current state-of-the-art distributed MCMC for time series when dependence is weak, and substantially more accurate in a highly persistent setting. The methodology is used to perform a rolling forecast evaluation of one-second market liquidity costs from histories of up to 24 million observations.

items.title: Safe Policy Learning under Regression Discontinuity Designs with Multiple Cutoffs
items.summary: We study policy learning under the regression discontinuity (RD) design, where deterministic treatment assignment requires extrapolation to identify improved treatment cutoffs. We develop a robust optimization approach that leverages the multiple cutoffs common in RD settings to minimize worst-case welfare loss relative to the status quo policy. Under the maintained assumptions, the resulting cutoffs guarantee overall welfare at least as high as that under the existing policy. We also establish oracle-gap bounds for the learned policy. Finally, we illustrate the proposed methodology through simulation studies and apply it to data from an educational assistance program in Colombia.

items.title: RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number
items.summary: We train a reinforcement learning agent to simplify hard unknot diagrams and pair it with a learned crossing selector to search for short unknotting sequences. Three examples found by the agent lead to an infinite family of prime two-bridge knots of unknotting number three whose connected sums with the figure-eight knot also have unknotting number three, and fifteen new unknotting upper bounds were found on the set of prime knots up to 13 crossings.

items.title: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
items.summary: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence.
