Results confirm this: despite their reasoning capacity, judged correctness remains consistently lower under less-structured presentations of the same evidence - most sharply for quantitative cross-company reasoning and 3-hop branch motifs - indicating that reasoning alone does not fully offset how evidence is structured; KG-linked presentation also uses fewer input tokens by design. We release the benchmark, provenance annotations, model outputs, evaluation records, and supporting technical documentation.

items.title: AIDA: An AI Outage Registry with Evidence from On-Chain MEV
items.summary: Generative AI coding tools have lowered the cost of writing trading software, but no systematic dataset records when these services fail. We introduce the AI Incident and Disruption Archive (AIDA), a multi-vendor registry of 5,868 deduplicated outage incidents across 30 providers from 2025 to 2026, with foundation-model incidents verified against primary status-page or postmortem URLs. Pairing AIDA with 5,041,034 verified maximal extractable value (MEV) transactions by 8,516 Ethereum addresses, their contract creations, and a 22-month Base Layer-2 panel of 1,099,593,191 swaps and 29,120 private executors, we establish two findings. First, entry into MEV expanded where code and public state suffice, as active arbitrage addresses quadrupled from late 2024 to late 2026 and liquidators grew by a third, while sandwich attackers, who need private order flow and builder access, declined. Execution nonetheless remained concentrated, with the top fifty addresses executing two thirds of verified trades. Second, AI outages stall new trading code while deployed bots keep trading. On Ethereum, addresses releasing a private executor fall to 0.67 on the day of an eight-hour disruption (0.68 for executor creations during OpenAI outage hours) and to 0.66 at lag two before rebounding on day three; on Base, operator top-level creations fall to 0.76 during OpenAI hours and executor-deploying operators to 0.88 at lag two. Non-trading creations, automated factory clones, and live arbitrage and sandwich execution across both chains remain unchanged. Cheaper code thus lowers the barrier to building MEV contracts, while private order flow, latency and capital still determine who wins execution.

items.title: Dynamic Strategy Selection
items.summary: We consider the problem of dynamically selecting among competing strategies using observable predictors. To mitigate estimation noise and excessive switching, we regularise the estimated policy with a switching cost, which may exceed actual transaction costs when these are too small to provide sufficient regularisation. Since switching costs make current choices affect future decisions, we formulate the problem using dynamic programming. The optimal policy is estimated using a reinforcement learning algorithm based on iterated regressions, making the procedure simple to implement. We apply the method to monthly rotation among momentum, value, profitability, and defensive U.S. equity factors over a sample of about 60 years. Using a parsimonious set of state variables, the estimated policy outperforms both the myopic dynamic policy and the best fixed factor in hindsight in out-of-sample evaluation. Under weak conditions, we show theoretically that the decision rule estimated from empirical data is asymptotically consistent for the unknown optimal decision rule. Simulation results illustrate the finite-sample relevance of these asymptotic results.

items.title: Hard to Fool: A Bounded LLM Research Loop for Quantitative Finance, and What Two Dozen Campaigns Found
items.summary: Agentic research loops that let a language model propose a change, run a fixed experiment and keep whatever improves the metric work well in machine learning. In trading research the same loop is a machine for producing false discoveries: a backtest that "improves the metric" is, by default, overfit, look-ahead, a multiple-comparisons artifact, cost-free, or market drift wearing a strategy. We describe Autonomous Quant Researcher, an open-source loop built on the opposite premise: the model proposes, and only trusted code decides. Proposals are strict declarative JSON over a fixed vocabulary, so there is no model-written code to sandbox. Evaluation runs on immutable chronological stores split into discovery, validation and a final holdout that can be opened exactly once, after a durable receipt is written. Acceptance is a conjunction of absolute gates (positive edge and net P&L after costs, a positive weekly-cluster bootstrap lower bound, survival at elevated costs, per-year stability and sample floors), never a single score. Duplicates are refused before they spend a trial, and every formulation, refusal, crash and result is kept in a hash-chained, append-only ledger. We report every campaign run to date, across 0DTE options priced from traded option bars, overnight SPX verticals, daily ETF rules, technical-analysis premises, Kalshi crypto binaries, earnings options, off-exchange volume and a pre-registered alternative-data campaign. Most hypotheses fail, and we report them. Two results survive their pre-registered bars. The clearest example of the loop working is a failure: a language-model survivor that passed discovery and validation with Sharpe ratios near 3 and fell to 0.26 on its single holdout use. The value of such a loop lies less in what it finds than in how hard it is to make it report something that is not there.

items.title: Constrained defined-contribution pension management: A reparameterized neural network approach
items.summary: This paper studies constrained defined contribution (DC) pension management under a two-factor financial market model. The pension participant is allowed to invest in cash, two nominal bonds, an inflation-linked bond, and a stock index. Moreover, they can also purchase term life insurance to manage pre-retirement death risk. Unlike traditional literature, we consider a pension member restricted to a general non-empty, closed, and convex trading constraint set that includes no short-selling, no borrowing, and portfolio-mix constraints as special cases. Such restrictions reflect common limits on pension-account trading. To solve the problem, we construct a family of unconstrained artificial markets, in which the original trading constraints are satisfied by adjusting the drift terms of the risky assets. Using a duality transformation, we derive the Lagrangian dual problem and propose a reparameterized neural network method to compute lower and upper bounds on the primal value function. We calibrate our model with U.S. data using a Kalman filter method, and find that our method produces a smaller duality gap than the benchmark methods. We also compare the constrained results with the unconstrained explicit solution and find that trading constraints substantially change wealth accumulation, portfolio strategies, and insurance demand. This highlights that unconstrained solutions may provide misleading guidance for pension management in practice.

items.title: Geometric Observables for Financial Regime Detection
items.summary: We extract four geometric observables -- Berry Phase Rate, Spectral Entropy, Reduced State Purity, and Hamiltonian Sensitivity -- from a learned spectral embedding of equity-index returns and evaluate them as regime-shift detectors against 46 classical and machine-learning baselines on 17 historical crises spanning 2000-2024. Under walk-forward nested hyperparameter selection on nine labelled windows, the Berry Phase Rate achieves an unbiased out-of-sample median Cohen's $d = 0.72$ (95% percentile-bootstrap CI $[0.34, 1.18]$, 10,000 resamples) and produces approximately 67% fewer false alarms per year than a label-supervised Random Forest (1.2 vs. 3.6 per year). Reduced State Purity attains the highest in-sample separability of any method ($d = 0.83$), tied closely by the Absorption Ratio ($d = 0.80$); geometric and classical channels are largely uncorrelated (mean $|ρ| \approx 0.22$), suggesting they capture distinct risk signals. Score construction is unsupervised; hyperparameter selection is the only supervised step.

items.title: A general technique for explicit quantile representations
items.summary: This work proves existence of contours independent of probability level for exact quantile integrals of strictly positive real-analytic densities. Explicit constructions cover five broad distribution families and yield a finite-interval representation of Black-Scholes implied volatility using forward functions.

items.title: Market-Based Probability of Stock Returns
items.summary: This paper describes the dependence of market-based statistical moments of returns on statistical moments and correlations of the current and past trade values. We use Markowitz's definition of value weighted return of a portfolio as the definition of market-based average return of trades during the averaging period. Then we derive the dependence of market-based volatility and higher statistical moments of returns on statistical moments, volatilities, and correlations of the current and past trade values. We derive the approximations of the characteristic function and the probability of returns by a finite number q of market-based statistical moments. To forecast market-based average and volatility of returns at horizon T, one should predict the first two statistical moments and correlation of current and past trade values at the same horizon. We discuss the economic reasons that limit the number of predicted statistical moments of returns by the first two. That limits the accuracy of the forecasts of probability of returns by the accuracy of the Gaussian approximations. To improve the reliability of large macroeconomic and market models like BlackRock's Aladdin, JP Morgan, and the U.S. Fed., the developers should use market-based statistical moments of returns.

items.title: Price-Volume Correlations Are Always Zero
items.summary: We argue that the use of the empirical time series of values, volumes, and prices of consecutive trades made during the averaging interval to calculate the price-volume correlation in a way that follows the definition of correlation always gives zero correlation. We show that the usual expression for the empirical calculation of the correlation misleads the researchers and doesn't fulfill the definition of price-volume correlation. The mistake has its origin in the dependence of volume weighted average price on the mean values and volumes of trades during the averaging interval but not on time series of prices only. The true sense of the declared positive or negative results of the empirical calculations of price-volume correlations made by numerous researchers in reality is determined by the difference between the volume weighted average price and its limiting expression of average price, which is correct only when all volumes of consecutive trades are constant, and multiplication of this difference by the mean trade volume. To empirically determine the statistical dependence between time series of prices and trade volumes, one should calculate the correlations between prices and squares of trade volumes or correlations between squares of prices and squares of volumes. We derive the expressions for empirical calculations of these correlations.

items.title: Valuation Model of Chinese Convertible Bonds Based on Monte Carlo Simulation
items.summary: We tackle the problem of pricing Chinese convertible bonds(CCBs) using Monte Carlo simulation and dynamic programming. At each exercise time, we use the state variables of the underlying stock to regress the continuation value, and apply standard backward induction to get the coefficients from the current time to time zero. This process ultimately determines the CCB price. We then apply this pricing method in simulations and evaluate an underpriced strategy: taking long positions in the 10 most undervalued CCBs and rebalancing daily. The results show that this strategy significantly outperforms the benchmark double-low strategy. In practice, CCB issuers often use a downward adjustment clause to prevent financial distress when a put provision is triggered. Therefore, we model the downward adjustment clause as a probabilistic event that triggers the put provision, thereby integrating it with the put provision in a straightforward manner.

items.title: Exponential Seniority Weighting Chain-Ladder Reserving
items.summary: We develop a tractable state-space version of the chain-ladder model. The state-space dynamics acts on the accident year axis which, in contrast to the classical chain-ladder model, makes accident years dependent. This state-space version yields an exponential seniority weighting in the chain-ladder factor estimation, and it admits an analytical likelihood representation that enables us to compute the seniority weighted chain-ladder reserves and their prediction uncertainty: the one-year uncertainty is available in closed form and the total uncertainty requires a Monte Carlo simulation from the fully tractable likelihood representation.

items.title: A Financial Brain Scan of the LLM
items.summary: We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to "brain scan" large language models, mapping internal activations to interpretable concepts and enabling targeted "steering" of specific features. We show that prompting models to adopt specific preferences activates many unintended concepts, complicating causal inference. In contrast, SAEs permit smooth, more isolated steering of target concepts. Furthermore, our scans reveal a stark disconnect between the model's internal feature contributions and its self-generated explanations, showing that these explanations are unreliable guides to its reasoning. Finally, SAEs provide a lightweight intervention for existing models, producing interpretable embeddings and allowing researchers to attenuate specific economic biases.

items.title: Valuation Reveals Uncertainty
items.summary: This paper studies the recovery of uncertainty from dynamic sublinear valuation rules. Robust valuation assigns each payoff its worst-case expected value over a family of plausible models, thereby inducing a dynamic sublinear valuation rule. While valuation rules are observable in practice, the underlying uncertainty structure remains latent. Under suitable conditions, we show that an uncertainty structure can be recovered from an observed valuation rule and provide an explicit recovery procedure. The construction characterizes the joint uncertainty in the discount factor and the law of the state process.

items.title: Mitigating Return Drag and Regime Whipsaws in Sector Rotation: An Asymmetric Downside-Aware Nested Clustered Optimization Framework
items.summary: Hierarchical clustering and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) mitigate the mathematical ill-conditioning of classical Markowitz covariance matrices. However, two structural vulnerabilities persist in equity markets: (1) symmetric variance penalizes upside and downside return dispersion identically, inducing acute return drag against soaring momentum sectors; and (2) unconstrained Hidden Markov Models (HMM) exhibit hyper-active regime switching (whipsaw instability), incurring excessive turnover and transaction drag. We propose Asymmetric Downside-Risk Nested Clustered Optimization with Sticky Regime Dynamics (Asym-Sticky-NCO) for tactical sector rotation across all 11 S&P 500 GICS sectors. The framework substitutes symmetric covariance with the Bawa-Lindenberg downside semi-covariance matrix across both hierarchical tree clustering and two-stage allocation. Furthermore, we introduce a Sticky Gaussian HMM incorporating a diagonal self-transition persistence prior (\k{appa}) and confidence-adaptive boundaries (δ) to enforce macroeconomic persistence. Strictly non-anticipative walk-forward backtesting across 65 out-of-sample months (August 2020 to December 2025) demonstrates that the architecture elevates CAGR from 10.65% (Plain NCO) to 13.41% (+276 bps/year), delivers a 97.74% total return versus 72.99%, suppresses maximum drawdown to 14.22% (versus 23.93% for the S&P 500), and achieves a Calmar ratio of 0.94 (+38.2% over S&P 500; +84.3% over Baseline Regime-NCO). Crucially, sticky dynamics cut regime whipsaws by 75.0% (from 16 to 4 switches) and reduce monthly turnover from 60.78% to 30.48%, addressing core limitations of machine learning asset allocation.

items.title: Beyond Anonymous Order Flow: Wallet Identity as a Feature for Short-Horizon Return Prediction
items.summary: Conventional public order-book data summarize trading without identifying the accounts behind it. Hyperliquid's Level-4 record also exposes persistent pseudonymous wallet addresses. We reconstruct full-depth books from consensus-ordered messages and evaluate wallet identity as a feature for short-horizon return prediction. The July 1-27, 2026 record covers 17.1 billion messages, 14.3 million aggressive orders by 147,113 wallets, and $84.3 billion in taker notional across ten markets. In the three model markets, notional-weighted ten-second markout rankings persist across adjacent ten-day windows (Spearman rho = 0.52); covariate-adjusted validation markouts reach 3.11 basis points in the top ventile. On a 100-millisecond grid, eleven features describing previously scored top-decile wallets raise one-second out-of-sample R2 from 10.88% to 12.

items.title: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity
items.summary: This article advocates the development of a decentralized exchange protocol for Ethereum based on Walrasian equilibrium. Building on previous work (arXiv:2111.02719, arXiv:2210.04929), it develops a mathematical framework that incorporates liquidity from independent automated market makers (AMMs). Trade orders are represented by continuous monotonic pairwise supply functions and external AMMs are represented by concave swap functions. Under a connectivity condition, we establish the existence of a common clearing-price vector and external swaps that jointly fulfill the prescribed orders while leaving a nonnegative surplus of every token. External AMMs execute ordinary swaps according to their own pricing rules, including swap fees. For the selected clearing-price vector, the prescribed external swaps maximize the value of the batch surplus. We also establish structural properties of equilibrium, including invariance of individual net trades across equilibria, and formulate equilibrium computation as a convex optimization problem. We then outline Walraswap, an exchange protocol for Ethereum with off-chain batch construction and on-chain settlement. Its proposed governance and solver accountability mechanisms aim to encourage public order disclosure and discourage censorship. The protocol design explores how the mathematical construction could support decentralized trading with reduced opportunities for maximal extractable value.

items.title: Safe Portfolio Learning from Untrusted Predictions: Signed Trust, Abstention, and Cross-Universe Polarity Failure
items.summary: Portfolio use of machine predictions must often proceed while the predictions' economic direction, reliability, and timing remain untrusted, and while feedback from overlapping multi-period positions arrives with delay. A controller chooses among Safe, Follow, and Reverse portfolio actions, so signal orientation is learned rather than assumed. A share-adaptive master updates action probabilities from matured Safe-relative rewards, an evidence gate can abstain by transferring unsupported directional probability to Safe, a delayed collateral budget reserves worst-case loss capacity before exposure is funded, and a protected split account caps the capital adaptive decisions may touch. The architecture carries a dual certificate, tracking regret against switching action sequences under delay and one-sided intervention, together with a pathwise collateral safety bound that holds when predictions fail. On a 24-stock development universe a conservative prediction-assisted overlay stays near equal-weight performance at a fraction of the turnover. On a frozen 82-stock holdout, the pre-specified Reverse orientation fails to outperform Equal Weight; a separately labeled post-holdout diagnostic shows that permanently flipping the sign to Follow also does not recover a return edge. Under the post-holdout controller, protected wealth remains within 15.9 basis points of the Safe benchmark throughout. The contribution is safe adaptive use of untrusted predictions, not demonstrated alpha.

items.title: Does the Market Anticipate? Can it? Should it?
items.summary: A nuance to 'no arbitrage' is studied: it can be suboptimal to act upon an arbitrage immediately; in such cases optimised trading can suppress the anticipation of predictable risk-outcomes, creating an apparent Status Quo Bias. This is shown for asset-pricing under model- or event-risk. Unlike standard treatments, we allow pre-horizon revelations of risk-outcomes; the associated technical challenges are addressed through results from the weak viability and (in)side-information literature. The conflict between 'anticipation', 'no arbitrage' and 'information efficiency', and the competition between the 'signal-to-noise of data' and the 'inference-free risk-premium drift', are exposed.

items.title: Stablecoin Integration and Stress Transmission Through Crypto-Asset Service Providers: Evidence from Austria
items.summary: Stablecoins are increasingly entangled with traditional finance, making their response to stress a financial stability concern. However, blockchain pseudonymity and the lack of geographic identifiers force existing work to rely on indirect proxies to infer and locate market participants. In this paper, we exploit a regulatory registry that directly identifies the on-chain addresses of every crypto-asset service provider (CASP) registered in Austria at the end of 2024, reconstructing their Bitcoin, Ether, USDT, and USDC activity through May 2025. Austrian CASPs intermediate roughly $30 billion in cumulative external transfers, while transfers among them are negligible. Combining two transaction-level signals, interaction with CASP cold wallets and on-chain transaction frequency, we classify CASP counterparty activity as retail-like or institutionally mediated. Around stress events, the two groups exhibit distinct flow responses that are obscured in aggregate data. After the FTX bankruptcy, we observe retail-like withdrawals and institutional deposits across assets. After Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failure, retail-like USDC deposits and institutionally mediated withdrawals are consistent with USDC's asymmetric redemption access. Registry-based, transaction-level measurements thus offer a reproducible basis for cross-jurisdictional monitoring of how cryptoasset markets transmit risk.

items.title: A mathematical study of the excess growth rate
items.summary: The excess growth rate, defined as the gap in Jensen's inequality for the logarithm, is a fundamental functional in portfolio theory. In this paper, we present a mathematical study motivated by information theory. We begin by establishing its properties and showing that it has rich connections with information-theoretic concepts such as the Helmholtz free energy, L. Campbell's measure of average code length and large deviations. Our main results consist of three axiomatic characterization theorems of the excess growth rate, in terms of (i) the relative entropy, (ii) the gap in Jensen's inequality, and (iii) the logarithmic divergence that generalizes the Bregman divergence. Furthermore, we study maximization of the excess growth rate and compare it with Kelly's growth optimal portfolio. Our results not only provide theoretical justifications of the significance of the excess growth rate, but also establish new connections between information theory and quantitative finance.

items.title: CosmosAlpha: Multi-Relational Graph Search with Pareto-Guided Exploration for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining
items.summary: Discovering predictive alpha factors from noisy financial data is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantitative finance. LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized. Consequently, information remains localized along parent--child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at https://github.com/wzhmtldswz/CosmosAlpha

items.title: How market volatility responds to a preceding price trend: a lag-resolved measurement in cryptocurrencies and equities
items.summary: We quantify the response of market volatility to a preceding price trend as a function of lag at minute resolution. The asymmetry of the response is investigated. The sample consists of trades in three of the largest cryptocurrencies on a single exchange and in three large US stocks and the S&P 500 exchange-traded fund between 2020 and 2026. For the cryptocurrencies the asymmetry is positive, matching the sign of the leverage effect. It follows the trend: it is greatest at the first measurable lag, 20 minutes, and weak at negative lags, where the trend follows the volatility. At those lags a scan over window lengths resolves a small component of opposite sign that has not yet been disentangled from what the statistic itself generates. For Bitcoin and Ether the asymmetry decays to one half by a lag of roughly an hour and a half. Decomposition under time reversal divides the asymmetry into a T-even part and a T-odd part. Only the latter carries an arrow of time. For Bitcoin and Ether the T-odd part is detected. At the first lag it is between 0.4 and 0.9 of the T-even part at windows of 10 and 20 minutes. At 20 minutes this is the ratio produced by a purely one-sided response in this statistic: at that window the response is consistent with being wholly one-sided in time. None of the equities exhibits a detectable T-odd part at 20 minutes in the straight-line fit over 2.5 trend scales. This fit is the shared instrument of comparison. The fund's return-variance correlation displays an arrow of time; the cryptocurrencies' asymmetry is independent of the shapes of the fits, and Bitcoin's and Ether's of their ranges. On simulated and shuffled data without coupling, the analysis yields zero with errors of the correct size. It also recovers the time scale of a one-sided response embedded in a simulated market.

items.title: Partially Active Automated Market Makers
items.summary: We introduce a new class of automated market maker (AMM), the \emph{partially active automated market maker} (PA-AMM). PA-AMM divides its reserves into two parts, the active and the passive parts, and uses only the active part for trading. At the top of every block, such a division is done again to keep the active reserves always being \(λ\)-portion of total reserves, where \(λ\in (0, 1]\) is an activeness parameter. We show that this simple mechanism reduces adverse selection costs, measured by loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR), and thereby improves the wealth of liquidity providers (LPs) relative to plain constant-function market makers (CFMMs). As a trade-off, the asset weights within a PA-AMM pool may deviate from their target weights implied by its invariant curve. Motivated by the optimal index-tracking problem literature, we also propose and solve an optimization problem that balances such deviation and the reduction of LVR.

items.title: FinTech Adoption, Bank Profitability, and Stability: The Mediating Role of Operational Cost Efficiency in Bangladesh's Commercial Banking Sector
items.summary: While financial technology (FinTech) is seen as a contributor to bank performance, the empirical evidence of digitization's ability to translate into improved profit and stability outcomes and efficiency gains, within emerging systems dominated by banks is not conclusive. The direct impact of a composite FinTech Adoption Index (FTI) on the profitability (ROE) and stability (ln(Z-score)) of Bangladesh's commercial banks is explored in this study along with whether operational cost efficiency (CIR) acts as a mediator. The study is conducted using a balanced panel of 30 commercial banks between 2015 and 2024, supplemented by an entropy-weighted index of FinTech as a robustness check, using a two-step System GMM to address dynamic persistence and endogeneity issues. The adoption of FinTech presents no significant relationship with profitability, stability or cost efficiency, while cost efficiency does not significantly transmit the effect of FinTech to either outcome. The alternative measure suggests that adoption is not only significantly negatively related to profitability, but is also associated with a significantly improved (not worse) cost-to-income ratio, which indicates the sensitivity to measurement rather than any one consistent effect on performance. These findings qualify the expected performance benefits of FinTech and have implications for investment sequencing and regulation of digital transformation in emerging banking markets.

items.title: Aggregate Calibration Can Mask Stress-State Undercoverage: Bounded-Memory Forecast Intervals under Recurrent Financial Stress
items.summary: Sequential forecast intervals are often evaluated by aggregate coverage even when calibration memory is bounded. This can be misleading when economically important states recur after long absences: a recent-only buffer may satisfy its overall coverage target while no longer containing errors from earlier episodes of the returning state. We study this problem in next-day financial range forecasting, holding the forecasting model, conformity score, adaptive update, and memory budget constant while varying the historical residual information available at each query. Recent-only first-in, first-out (FIFO) calibration is near nominal in aggregate but undercovers substantially during high-volatility states in both an exchange-traded fund development panel and a fixed stock panel. An unbounded state-history reference yields a lower observed stress-period interval score; Rare replay yields lower high-VIX interval scores than the matched Recent-n and Hybrid-n controls in both panels, and the state-structured versus recent-only contrast is largest near stress re-entry. Bounded calibration memory is therefore part of the forecasting information design, and aggregate calibration alone can conceal state-specific reliability failures.

items.title: Selection-Aware Certification of Client-Constrained Fraud Rule Portfolios Under Synthetic Distribution Shift
items.summary: Selecting fraud-rule portfolios to satisfy a precision or recall floor can overfit the data used for selection. We study finite-family certification for bounded OR portfolios, comparing point-estimate selection, a fixed safety margin, and one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower bounds with Bonferroni adjustment. In a factorial follow-up with 6,400 datasets from two author-designed synthetic generators, full-validation certification reduced the held-out floor-violation rate by 29.1 percentage points on average versus full-validation point selection, while reducing deployment by 31.7 points. Compared with a fixed 0.05 margin, certification reduced violations by 22.2 points and deployment by 29.4 points; results varied across conditions. Using the full rather than half validation sample increased deployment by 17.1 points on average, without a uniform reduction in shifted-test violations. In a separate 400-dataset no-shift sweep, certification deployment rose from 61.3% to 90.2% as validation size increased from 1,500 to 15,000; no violations occurred among 2,887 deployed portfolios tested on 100,000-row holdouts. A temporal case study on the public synthetic Bank Account Fraud Base dataset used recall at a 5% false-positive-rate cap; the selected candidate pool captured less than 1% of test fraud, showing limited coverage in this setup. Together, these experiments characterize how finite-family certification changes the reliability-deployment tradeoff for bounded OR portfolios under specified synthetic conditions. The evidence covers the evaluated generators and one public synthetic BAF case study; it does not estimate performance on real transaction populations or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift. The authors revised and rewrote this abstract after receiving a draft from OpenAI Codex.

items.title: Multidimensional Views Behind Target-Price Revisions: An LLM-Based Representation of Analyst Outlooks
items.summary: A target price compresses an analyst's multidimensional views into a single number. We propose an LLM-based text representation that extracts these views from research reports as question-based outlook scores with supporting evidence. The questions organize reported views on earnings, valuation, industry conditions, and other investment dimensions into a compact representation of analyst sentiment. In walk-forward evaluation, the scores improve prediction of subsequent target-price revisions beyond current-revision momentum and sector differences. They outperform financial dictionary and FinBERT sentiment measures. These findings suggest that structured questions can capture information about subsequent analyst actions that is not fully reflected in the current numerical revision. By linking each dimension to an explicit investment question and supporting report evidence, the approach makes the extracted outlooks available for inspection and interpretation. It offers a way to complement target-price signals with a multidimensional view of the judgments expressed in analyst narratives.

items.title: Decomposing Rank Reversals under Temporal Nonstationarity: Alignment, Aggressiveness, and Instability
items.summary: Under temporal nonstationarity, model performance rankings reverse across training horizons due to heterogeneous sensitivities to memory. While existing literature addresses adaptive lookbacks, effective model complexity, and empirical forecast evaluation in isolation, no unified framework explains the structural mechanics driving these rank reversals. We bridge this gap by deriving a model-agnostic decomposition of out-of-sample $R^2$ into target alignment, miscalibrated aggressiveness, and predictive instability. Within this framework, we mathematically characterize complexity phase boundaries, establish closed-form optimal-memory equations for ridge regression under local drift, and extend these guarantees to complex model architectures via surrogate bounds. We validate these theoretical dynamics by benchmarking 14 linear, tree-based, and neural architectures across large-scale financial panels. In doing so, our framework demonstrates that empirical model rank reversals are driven by predictable surges in miscalibrated aggressiveness, providing a rigorous mechanistic diagnosis of generalization under temporal shift.

items.title: PanelGP: A Probabilistic Factor Model for Asset-Return Panels
items.summary: We develop PanelGP, a conditional factor model for large panels of stock returns in which firm characteristics determine the factor loadings and economic conditions determine the expected factors. Both relations are estimated nonparametrically with Gaussian-process priors. The kernel choice nests instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) as well as smooth nonlinear maps. Asset-specific loading innovations and common factor innovations separate idiosyncratic from systematic risk, so one estimated model forecasts both expected returns and their covariance matrix. Estimation uses sparse variational inference with a joint posterior over loadings and factors. Because each predicted return is bilinear in a Gaussian state, the predictive covariance matrix and the cumulants of any portfolio have closed forms. In simulations, the estimator recovers the nonlinear maps and the variance parameters. For S&P 500 constituents over 1995-2024, nonlinear loadings rank stocks better than affine loadings and improve the Gaussian log score. Relative to IPCA, the resulting portfolios have higher Sharpe ratios, also net of trading costs, and the minimum-variance portfolio has lower volatility. The predicted variances rank stocks and months by risk but are too compressed.

items.title: Robust distortion riskmetrics over Bregman--Wasserstein balls and their intersections
items.summary: We study the worst-case values of distortion riskmetrics over Bregman--Wasserstein balls around a reference distribution. Unlike the squared $2$-Wasserstein distance, Bregman--Wasserstein divergences can penalize upward and downward deviations differently. Our main result applies to generalized distortion functions $g:[0,1]\to\R$ of bounded variation, with $g(0)=0$ and suitable endpoint regularity, which need not be monotone, normalized, or upper semicontinuous. For strictly convex generators satisfying a two-sided $p$-growth condition, we obtain a one-dimensional dual representation of the worst-case value. When a positive Lagrange multiplier makes the divergence constraint binding, we identify a unique quantile function through a least concave majorant and characterize when it attains the supremum. For absolutely continuous generalized distortion functions, we characterize the solution through an isotonic projection; we also study more general generators and shape constraints, including unimodality. Finally, we extend the analysis to intersections of Bregman--Wasserstein balls, describing models acceptable to several parties involved in decision making, and illustrate the results numerically.

items.title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024-2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model's signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t = 1.7) on the blinded January-July 2026 test. The commercial models' readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.

items.title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting
items.summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.

items.title: Generating Financial Time Series by Matching Random Convolutional Features
items.summary: Generating realistic financial time series is challenging as training data is often limited to a single historical path. With such scarce data, overfitting is hard to avoid, especially under adversarial training where a trained discriminator can memorize the training samples. To mitigate this, recent approaches train generators to minimize the discrepancy between untrained feature representations of real and generated time series. In these works, the feature maps are based on path signatures, which can fail to capture relevant time series properties at tractable truncation depths. In this work, we instead train generators by matching random convolutional features of real and generated time series. Existing random convolutional feature maps, such as Rocket and Hydra, have been shown to provide informative representations of real-world time series, but cannot supervise generative models because they are non-differentiable. We introduce SOCK (SOft Competing Kernels), a fully differentiable random convolutional feature map, suited to train generative time series models. We show that generators trained by matching random SOCK features outperform signature and diffusion baselines on most evaluation metrics across a wide range of small-sample financial datasets. We further demonstrate SOCK's expressiveness on two-sample hypothesis testing and time series classification tasks, where SOCK matches or outperforms existing unsupervised feature maps.

items.title: Model Risk Analysis for Entropic Hedging Strategies
items.summary: Market incompleteness causes residual profit and loss after hedging that is accounted for with valuation adjustments and bid-offer spreads acting as model risk buffers for the derivative price. Entropic risk optimisation is a general framework for modelling these adjustments. When the prices are quadratic Gaussian, the coupled equations for price and hedge ratios are solved exactly, with a decomposition of the entropic risk into convexity, dimensionality, funding and strategy contributions that are attributed in the explanation of realised P&L. The results are applicable when the underlying prices follow Gaussian processes, such as fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. The article concludes with analysis of the continuous hedging limit for these processes, and a discussion of their application in data-driven regressions.

items.title: Symbol-based residual certification of reduced and neural surrogates for tempered-fractional CGMY pricing
items.summary: We certify reduced and neural approximations of European-put price trajectories under the Carr--Geman--Madan--Yor model by residual bounds for the spline Galerkin discretisation of the tempered-fractional pricing equation. The Galerkin matrices are Toeplitz sections of an explicit periodised Fourier symbol; summing the alias series to a stated tail makes the assembled system exact to $10^{-8}$. A Lévy--Khintchine argument gives the parameter-explicit bound $λ_{\min}(S_I)\ge r\,m_{\min}$ for the symmetric part, valid for $Y\in(0,2)\setminus\{1\}$, replacing numerical spectral estimates. A banded comparison norm built from the mass and stiffness symbols yields a rigorous certificate at $O(N)$ cost with explicit effectivity, and empirical interpolation of the symbol makes the operator affine in about 36 terms with a rigorous error transfer, so a reduced model is certified at a cost independent of $N$; a three-stage rule escalates to the full-order bounds only when needed. At the resolution that prices the whole parameter box to one cent ($N=1024$), the full-order certificate costs 6% of a direct solve, and the certified POD--Galerkin model of rank 80 costs 3% of it and settles 99.8% of $10^4$ queries without touching the full space. No false accept occurs on any query with a reference solution (150 inside the parameter box, 264 outside), and outside the box the certificate accepts 193 of the 210 queries on which the reduced model is still within one cent. The neural reduced models trained here miss the one-cent tolerance by a factor of at least 46; the certificate detects this at every query in a few milliseconds and explains it as a trade-off between temporal smoothness and coefficient accuracy. A residual certificate for the American put is proved as an outlook.

items.title: Penalize the Common Trade: A Collision-Aware Layer for Learned Portfolios
items.summary: Different learning systems can make nearly the same trade when they share data, objectives, or representations. The market then sees decision concentration even if the models look diverse. We call exposure to this shared direction a signal collision. A linear-impact game shows the basic externality: each allocator chooses too much common exposure because it does not bear the full price effect imposed on others. An overlap-dependent toll recovers the social choice, and a feedback model gives the exact gain at which return-responsive allocation becomes unstable. We also state the restrictive spectral conditions under which a leading eigenportfolio can reveal the collision direction. These results motivate a simple post-model layer: subtract a penalty for loading on the recent common return mode before forming the portfolio. In a frozen panel of ten liquid cross-asset ETFs, 760 completed weeks from January 2012 through July 2026, and exact self-financing costs of 10 basis points per dollar traded, this layer changes maximum drawdown from 23.6% to 14.1%, volatility from 12.6% to 10.7%, and excess-return Sharpe from 0.664 to 0.667. A volatility-matched momentum diagnostic still draws down 19.9%. Paired stationary-bootstrap uncertainty is wide: the 95% interval for drawdown improvement is $[-3.3,18.4]$ percentage points and includes zero. The result establishes a reproducible risk-control association and specifies the holdings-and-flow validation needed to attribute the common direction to AI crowding. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.

items.title: Specification LASSO and a Flexible Characteristics-Based Asset Pricing Model
items.summary: This paper studies a partially linear semiparametric additive model that allows for interactions among variables in high-dimensional settings. We propose the Specification LASSO (S-LASSO), a two-step method that integrates LASSO and Adaptive Group LASSO to simultaneously perform variable selection and model specification. Theoretically, we establish that S-LASSO possesses oracle properties in terms of selection consistency and asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that S-LASSO outperforms existing alternatives across a variety of scenarios. Empirically, we apply S-LASSO to a characteristics-based asset pricing model, exploring the linear and nonlinear effects of asset-specific characteristics on cross-sectional returns, as well as their interactions with firm size.

items.title: Can We Stop the Backtest Yet? Anytime-Valid Promotion Tests for Adaptive Financial Research Agents
items.summary: Financial research agents can generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the resulting selection process. Candidates appear at data-dependent times, weak rules are abandoned, and promising ones are watched until they cross a reporting threshold. We introduce PROMOTE, a protocol that assigns every candidate predictable testing wealth at birth and accumulates a cost-aware e-process only from subsequent returns. If lifetime allocations sum to at most one, a weighted Ville argument bounds the probability of ever promoting a rule whose declared bounded net score has always had nonpositive conditional mean. The result permits dependent candidates, adaptive births, and indefinite monitoring. We audit the implementation in two settings. A retrospective pseudo-out-of-sample replay contains 24 panel--rule hypotheses, 3,000 shared-sign null paths, injected alternatives, and public ETF and industry data. Repeated unadjusted tests produce a family crossing in 94.5% of null paths, versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; at a 15-bp aligned ETF-component perturbation, PROMOTE has 70.1% target power and median crossing session 2,327. A separate exact mean-zero experiment lets an agent select candidate identities and birth times from past scores; the funded gate has 1.77% false-family crossings across 3,000 programs. The market replay produces zero promotions after costs. The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null; it is not a certificate that an earlier edge remains profitable at deployment. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.

items.title: EventGPT: Next-Event Pretraining on Banking Customer Histories
items.summary: A model pretrained to predict a customer's next event can estimate the probability of future events without training on their labels and provide a reusable representation for supervised downstream banking tasks. We pretrain EventGPT, a hierarchical causal transformer, by next-token maximum likelihood estimation on the public Multimodal Banking Dataset (MBD-mini: 100,224 clients, 38.8 million transactions and 66.3 million geolocation pings). Keeping one state per event, EventGPT trains in about two hours on one L4 GPU at windows up to 8,192 tokens. From its next-event distribution, with no labels, EventGPT scores five targets of the form "the client makes a transaction of a given kind for the first time next month" at ROC-AUC 0.79 to 0.92. Gradient boosting on 114 engineered features needs 10,000 to 300,000 labeled client-months to match it on four targets and stays below it on the fifth. For product prediction, frozen EventGPT embeddings score below the engineered features (mean ROC-AUC 0.787 against 0.808 over five test folds), and a rank-averaged ensemble of EventGPT, profile fields and token counts with the engineered features adds 0.014 to 0.017, of which 0.007 to 0.016 is EventGPT's own. The code and pretrained weights are released.

items.title: The Inference-Compute Frontier for Limit Order Book Prediction
items.summary: We identify an empirical inference-compute frontier for limit order book prediction on FI-2010. A power law fitted to low- and mid-compute models extrapolates to an excluded MLPLOB-style mixer family whose work is $56$--$2{,}515$ times the largest budget in the corresponding fit. Across nine folds and five horizons, pooled $R^2$ is $0.934$ on the realized target frontier, with 59\% lower RMSE than constant endpoint extrapolation, and $0.731$ on all excluded operating points. Measured latency gives a weaker relationship and reorders model families. We therefore design FastBiNLOB to pack computation into dense temporal and feature mixing. H120 exceeds the published state-of-the-art macro-F1 on two of four horizons in every one of five seeds. Under our CPU/MPS protocol, H96 reduces median latency by 23.6\% relative to the W128 MLPLOB reference, and H120 by 60.2\% relative to a TLOB-inspired dual-axis attention reference.

items.title: Adapting Altman's bankruptcy prediction model to the compositional data methodology
items.summary: Using standard financial ratios as variables in statistical analyses has been related to several serious problems, such as extreme outliers, asymmetry, non-normality, and nonlinearity. The compositional-data methodology has been successfully applied to solve these problems and has always yielded substantially different results when compared to standard financial ratios. An under-researched area is the use of financial log-ratios computed with the compositional-data methodology to predict bankruptcy or the related terms of business default, insolvency or failure. Another under-researched area is the use of machine learning methods in combination with compositional log-ratios. The present article adapts the classical Altman bankruptcy prediction model and some of its extensions to the compositional methodology with pairwise log-ratios and three common statistical and machine learning tools: logistic regression models, k-nearest neighbours, and random forests, and compares the results with standard financial ratios. Data from the sector in the Spanish economy with the largest number of bankrupt firms according to the first two digits of the NACE code (46XX "wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles") were obtained from the Iberian Balance sheet Analysis System. The sample size (31,131 firms, of which 97 were bankrupt) was divided into a training and a validation dataset. The training dataset was downsampled to one healthy firm to each bankrupt firm. No outliers were removed. Focusing on predictive performance, the results show that compositional methods are better than standard ratios in terms of sensitivity (recall), with mixed results regarding specificity, compositional random forests and compositional logistic regression behaving the best.

items.title: Finite-horizon Optimal Consumption and Investment with Costly Income Adjustment
items.summary: We study optimal consumption and investment for an investor who receives labor income until a fixed retirement date, can raise the income rate irreversibly at a constant price per unit of income flow, and cannot borrow against future income. A pathwise argument shows that no income is purchased during a final period before retirement whose length depends only on the interest rate and the price. Before this period the dual problem has two free boundaries: a lower one generated by the borrowing constraint and an upper one, at which income is purchased, that escapes to infinity as the final period begins. The analysis of this problem is our main mathematical contribution. During the final period it is a single obstacle problem, which we solve, together with the regularity of its free boundary, by established methods. Before that period a partial hodograph transformation straightens both free boundaries and turns the problem into a quasilinear parabolic equation with oblique boundary conditions on a fixed interval. Comparison principles, explicit barriers and regularity theory for quasilinear equations then give existence, uniqueness and smoothness. Transforming back and gluing the two constructions yields global regularity: both free boundaries are infinitely differentiable and the value function is a classical solution at every positive wealth level. A dual budget process verifies optimality. We also derive coupled Volterra integral equations for the free boundaries, prove exponential convergence to the perpetual problem under a scalar condition, and find numerically a purchase threshold that is U-shaped in the time to retirement.

items.title: Interpretable Allocation and Model-Predictive Rebalancing of Equity Portfolios, Tested on Real and Synthetic Markets
items.summary: A live equity portfolio poses three problems: which stocks to hold, when to trade, and whether the strategy holds up beyond the observed market. We built one system for all three and tested it on 373 US equities, calibrated on 2014-2024 and traded from January 2025 to September 2026. A selection rule chose stocks by score, by a bandit, or at random, and one of seven weighting rules, four consumer-theory utilities, and three standard portfolios, set share counts under limits on budget, single-stock weight, portfolio volatility, and turnover, with each stock's preference weight a bounded score of its trend, market beta, and the market's recent direction. A model-predictive controller forecasts portfolio value with a multi-asset geometric Brownian motion and re-planned at its horizon, when the value left its forecast band, or at a drawdown stop. To probe deeper declines than the real window held, we also ran the system on simulated markets from per-asset hidden Markov generators with jumps, linked by market and sector factors. On real prices, the stocks chosen mattered more to terminal wealth than the weighting rule, and the early re-plans shrank the worst drawdown in most rule combinations against a fixed calendar without consistently raising wealth. In the deepest simulated declines, every combination, random picks included, ended above simulated SPY and the equal-weight universe in the median, even without early re-plans, so the margin came from shared parts of the system, not from stock selection or re-plan timing. A market hedge that tightened a beta cap as the market weakened cost wealth on real prices but paid off in the most sustained simulated declines, and the generator's persistent trends favored score-based selection more than the real market did, which suggests a synthetic test judges stock selection fairly only if its generator does not build in that persistence.

items.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
items.summary: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.

items.title: TensorLOB: Structure-Preserving Tensor Learning for Limit Order Book Forecasting
items.summary: The limit order book (LOB) records outstanding buy and sell orders across multiple price levels. Its state evolves over time across market side, price level, and order attribute, naturally forming a multiway structure. However, existing LOB models typically flatten these dimensions into a matrix model, thus obscuring the existing structural relationships. Starting from first principles and the market-microstructure intuition of the LOB, we design TensorLOB to operate entirely in the tensor domain. TensorLOB uses mode-wise tensor contractions for feature extraction and directly contracts the learned representation with low-rank class-weight tensors for prediction, retaining the distinct roles of time, side, level, and attribute modes. Experiments on the FI-2010 benchmark show that TensorLOB achieves the highest accuracy, recall, and F1 score across all four evaluated horizons. This proof of concept highlights the potential of high-dimensional modelling of multi-way latent information intrinsic to financial markets, which has so far been largely overlooked.

items.title: Optimal Annuitization, Consumption, and Investment with Costly Capital Injections
items.summary: We study a joint optimal decision of portfolio, consumption, and annuitization for a pension-plan manager who balances retirement consumption benefits against the cost of maintaining the solvency of pension account. The pension sponsor provides costly capital injection to prevent negative wealth. Annuity purchases are irreversible, and injected funds remain in the liquid account and earn interest. Using the Legendre transform, we derive a semi-explicit solution to the associated free-boundary problem and verify the optimality of the resulting strategies. We identify an endogenous annuity-income threshold separating injection-active and injection-inactive regions and characterize six policy regimes arising from the interplay between capital injections and consumption constraints. Compared with the no-injection benchmark, capital injections delay annuitization, alter the structure of the annuitization boundary, and permit positive holdings in risky assets even at zero liquid wealth. Numerical results further reveal that cheaper annuities may increase the expected capital contributions required from the pension sponsor.

items.title: Dynamic star-shaped risk measures and $g$-expectations
items.summary: Motivated by static monetary and star-shaped risk measures, this paper investigates representation theorems within a dynamic framework. We show that dynamic monetary risk measures can be represented as the lower envelope of a family of dynamic convex risk measures, and normalized dynamic star-shaped risk measures can be represented as that of a family of normalized dynamic convex risk measures. Furthermore, we establish the intrinsic link between dynamic monetary risk measures and dynamic star-shaped risk measures. Moreover, we examine the associated sensitivity and time consistency issues for such risk measures. Finally, we characterize star-shapedness of risk measures induced by bounded quadratic BSDE solutions and illustrate normalized time-consistent examples through $g$-expectations.

items.title: Beyond Binary Detection: Type-Aware Hallucination Analysis and Hierarchical Detection in Financial Question Answering
items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions over financial filings, where an unfaithful answer can mislead investment, compliance, or client decisions. Hallucination detectors are a common safeguard, but they are usually evaluated with a single binary score that reveals neither which kinds of errors analysesed nor why. This paper studies hallucination detection on PHANTOM, a long-context benchmark built from SEC filings, at the level of hallucination type. We first analyze 15,443 paired hallucinated and faithful answers without any detector and find that hallucinated answers are more than twice as long as faithful ones, and that lexical grounding separates the two classes only because faithful answers are bimodal. We then generate hallucinations in nine financially motivated categories, confirm each with a separate verification pass, and diagnose an LLM-based detector on 4,086 usable examples. Generation success varies from 66.3% to 100% across categories. The detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category; these misses are unrelated to input length but rise with how far an answer departs from the correct one. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype, raising binary accuracy to 95.6% and subtype accuracy to 56.1%. The results show that type-level evaluation exposes detector weaknesses that aggregate metrics conceal.

items.title: Asymptotics for a continuous-time risk model with multivariate strongly regularly varying claims and stochastic investment returns
items.summary: In this paper we study the finite-time asymptotic behavior of the entrance probability of the discounted aggregate claims into an extreme region in a multidimensional risk model. Our non-standard risk model is not restricted to the Levy-Renewal framework, that represents a usual assumption for the stochastic returns and the counting process of the claim vectors, respectively. For the modeling of the distribution of claim vectors, we introduce the notion of set-based multivariate (strongly) regularly varying distributions. For the new set-based classes we provide certain closure properties and some examples to show the difference from the usual definitions of multivariate regularly varying distributions. This set-based framework provides a broad and flexible framework to the actuarial applications, and facilitates the modeling of dependence among the claim vectors that arrive at different time epochs. The two main results of the paper establish a unified asymptotic expression, that demonstrates the presence of multivariate linear single big jump principle. Despite of the assumptions the asymptotic expression remains explicit. In the first main result we suppose that the common distribution of the claim vectors belongs to the class of set-based multivariate regularly varying distributions, and the stochastic returns satisfy a general moment condition. In the second main result, we restrict the claim vectors in the class of setbased multivariate strongly regularly varying distributions, relaxing the moment condition on the stochastic returns. Finally, we conduct a numerical study to illustrate the accuracy of the proposed asymptotic approximation and investigate its sensitivity to the main model parameters.

items.title: Reduction of the integro-differential equation to an ordinary differential equation in ruin models with investment in a risky asset
items.summary: We study ruin models with the surplus invested in a risky asset and Erlang-distributed claims: non-life insurance, annuity payments and the mixed model. Assuming that the integro-differential equation for the survival probability has a classical twice continuously differentiable solution, we prove that this solution satisfies a linear ordinary differential equation. We construct explicit annihilating operators and write the coefficients of the reduced equation in closed form through binomial coefficients (for the mixed model with equal shape parameters). A converse criterion is obtained: a bounded solution of the reduced equation satisfies the integro-differential equation if and only if the residual vanishes at zero initial capital together with its derivatives of order below that of the annihilator. The exponent of the power branch at infinity is determined by the parameters of the risky asset alone and does not depend on the shape parameter. For the mixed model we classify the fundamental set of solutions: the exponentially growing modes are excluded by boundedness. The connection coefficient of the power branch is nonzero by a known power-law lower bound for the ruin probability, and in the annuity model by the reduced equation and the boundary condition at zero. Hence the ruin probability has power-law asymptotics with a positive constant for all shape parameters and all positive exponents, and a complete asymptotic expansion up to a multiplicative constant in all three models. For non-life insurance with Erlang claims of order two the expansion coefficients are computed by an explicit recurrence.

items.title: The Laplace transform of the time of ruin in the Cramér--Lundberg model with Erlang $E_2(μ)$ claims: spectrum, exact moments and matrix reduction
items.summary: We study the Laplace transform of the time of ruin in the classical Cramér--Lundberg model with claims having an Erlang distribution of shape parameter 2. We derive an integro-differential equation with two boundary conditions. For every positive discount rate, we show that its characteristic polynomial has one negative root and two distinct positive roots. Boundedness excludes the growing exponential term and yields a representation of the transform as a sum of two decaying exponentials. We construct a finite-dimensional matrix reduction of the convolution chain. For a model parameter set, we obtain exact expressions for the ruin probability, the mean time of ruin, and higher moments, including the third moment at zero initial surplus. We prove analyticity in the discount rate and justify the resulting moment series. We consider the analytic continuation of the representation to negative discount rates separately. For Erlang claims with an arbitrary positive integer shape parameter, we establish a closed linear system and the asymptotics of the root continuing the zero root at zero discount.

items.title: Long-term yields of short-rate models as Feynman-Kac ground states: a variational quantum eigensolver with single-setting energy estimation on two NISQ platforms
items.summary: We show that the long-term yield of a short-rate model is the ground-state energy of a Schrodinger operator obtained from the Feynman-Kac bond-pricing equation, so that it can be computed by a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We treat the Vasicek, Cox-Ingersoll-Ross and Black-Karasinski models; the last has no closed form. Calibrated monthly to the U.S. Treasury curve from 1985 to 2026, the long-term yield follows the 30-year yield with an in-sample correlation of 0.98. The Hamiltonian is stoquastic, so its ground state is positive and the energy can be estimated from computational-basis samples with a single measurement setting. On ibm_cleveland, gate noise appears mainly as bit flips of the high-order qubits. A bit-flip deconvolution with a tail set fixed by a WKB criterion, combined with readout mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation, gives four-qubit estimates within 33-125 bp of the grid ground-state energies for all three models, and within 23-67 bp for Treasury-calibrated parameters. On IonQ Forte Enterprise the same analysis reduces the error in the same proportions. On the same circuits, a Pauli-measurement VQE deviates by 791-1,129 bp, so the single-setting estimator gives about ten times smaller errors with one setting instead of nine. An on-device VQE converges from 4,939 bp to 130 bp.

items.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
items.summary: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $β/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $Θ((s/β)^2\log(1/δ))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

items.title: Sublinear Markov Semigroups Beyond Uniqueness
items.summary: To what extent does a local operator on smooth test functions determine a sub-Markov semigroup and its underlying structure of laws? Many existing approaches work with Feller semigroups on the space \(C_b\) of bounded continuous functions and rely on uniqueness, often established through a comparison principle for the associated evolution equation. However, even when the local operator is linear, uniqueness may fail and a \(C_b\)-Feller restriction may exclude the associated canonical semigroup. We discover that the space \(\operatorname{USC}_b\) of bounded upper semicontinuous functions offers a natural setting for this study. Within this framework, a complete description of the relationships among sublinear local operators, sublinear sub-Markov semigroups, and their underlying structures of laws is achieved without assuming uniqueness. Under suitable regularity and Lyapunov conditions, we construct the greatest semigroup compatible with a prescribed sublinear local operator and obtain a stochastic representation in terms of a Markov process under sublinear expectations. We characterize all sublinear sub-Markov semigroups dominated by this greatest semigroup in two ways: through a one-to-one correspondence with stable subfamilies of its representing laws, and through an order relation between their infinitesimal generators and the prescribed local operator. We further characterize the greatest semigroup via the greatest viscosity subsolution of the associated Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation. These results clarify what information about global stochastic evolution can be recovered from local infinitesimal descriptions and what freedom remains in the absence of uniqueness. The resulting characterizations are new even when the local operator is linear.

items.title: Agentic AI in Automated Markets
items.summary: Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs). We study how heterogeneous agent behavior shapes stress, risk-adjusted performance, liquidity, and volatility in these types of markets. Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower. Each archetype is defined by its reward function within a common, asset-agnostic exposure-control environment, and each is trained with a value-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) and with REINFORCE using a learned baseline. A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) motivates the hypotheses. Herd-followers produce the most frequent but shortest stress episodes, manipulators the fewest but most persistent, and rational agents the most stable rolling Sharpe ratios despite higher return volatility. SHAP attributions tie these patterns to drawdown and cross-asset signals, short-term volatility and position state, and momentum, respectively. The results motivate behavior-specific regulation rather than uniform limits on volatility or turnover.

items.title: HARN: Hierarchical Associative Resonance Network for Event-Driven Multi-Timeframe Forecasting
items.summary: Live financial forecasting must synchronize asynchronous bar completions across timeframes without using stale or unavailable information. We introduce HARN (Hierarchical Associative Resonance Network), an event-driven architecture that anchors each event to the finest configured timeframe and maintains persistent states and matrix-valued associative memories across temporal levels. Its timestamp-masked transition updates a level only when its completed-bar timestamp matches the current anchor, preserving inactive representations. HARN integrates causal multi-scale encoding, residual-driven gated associative writes, all-to-all cross-level resonance, and ordered bottom-up evidence aggregation to produce forecasts at each temporal level. Predictions are expressed as basis-point changes and reconstructed on the price scale for evaluation. We evaluate HARN on four assets spanning equities, foreign exchange, and gold (AAPL, EURUSD, USDCHF, and XAUUSD), using chronological 70/15/15 splits, 32-bar lookbacks, one-step horizons, and three random seeds. HARN obtains lower anchor-timeframe test mean absolute errors (MAEs) than the evaluated single-timeframe PatchTST and TimeXer baselines on all four assets. HARN's MAEs are 0.508, 0.000306, 0.000263, and 2.552, respectively; PatchTST records 2.074, 0.000759, 0.000638, and 9.563, while TimeXer records 2.882, 0.010838, 0.014144, and 15.297. These descriptive comparisons do not isolate architectural effects from differences in inputs, target formulations, or training procedures. Single-run component ablations on AAPL and EURUSD show small, non-monotonic differences. The results demonstrate HARN's feasibility for asynchronous multi-timeframe forecasting, while motivating controlled comparisons and broader ablations to establish its relative advantages and component contributions.

items.title: Efficient Monte Carlo Valuation of Corporate Bonds in Financial Networks
items.summary: Valuing corporate bonds in systemic economies is challenging due to intricate webs of inter-institutional exposures. When a bank defaults, cascading losses propagate through the network, with payments determined by a system of fixed-point equations lacking closed-form solutions. Standard Monte Carlo methods cannot capture rare yet critical default events, while existing rare-event simulation techniques fail to account for higher-order network effects and scale poorly with network size.
