We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.

items.title: Digital Twin Enabled Talkative Power Conversion
items.summary: Talkative Power Conversion (TPC) is a paradigm in which communication is integrated directly into switched-mode power electronic converters (PECs) by modulating their inherent switching ripple. TPC enables simultaneous power transfer and information exchange without dedicated transmitter-side communication hardware, and avoids additional wiring. This paper combines, for the first time, the Digital Twin (DT) concept with the TPC paradigm. By establishing interaction between one or several physical power converters and their virtual counterpart(s), the DT framework enables enhanced modeling, prediction, and optimization of individual or networked PECs. We distinguish three coupling architectures--embedded DT, remote DT, and networked DT--and demonstrate the added value of combining DT and TPC concepts when the DT and PEC are not co-located. The proposed framework is based on state-space modeling in conjunction with Kalman filtering and facilitates joint treatment of data transmission, parameter estimation, and system operation, thereby improving robustness, adaptability, and power efficiency. The presented approach highlights the potential of DT-enhanced TPC as a key enabler for future cyber-physical energy systems with tightly integrated power and communication functionalities.

items.title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
items.summary: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation. In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

items.title: Hands-On Beyond Classrooms: Elevating Control Engineering Education with Take-Home Labs
items.summary: This study shows how take-home laboratories can be integrated into control engineering education to strengthen hands-on learning in both introductory and advanced courses. The work provides evidence that a compact experimental platform can support conceptual understanding, student engagement, and course performance in a broadly applicable way. Control engineering courses often rely heavily on theory and simulation, which may limit students' ability to connect abstract concepts with practical implementation. Low-cost take-home laboratories offer a scalable alternative that can help bridge this gap across different educational settings. The curricular change, consisting of the introduction of take-home laboratory kits into the semester projects, was intended to improve students' motivation, deepen their understanding of core control principles, and enhance their performance in coursework and final assessment. Students used the kits for modeling, identification, and control design tasks, while learning outcomes were evaluated through questionnaires, midterm test scores, and final exam grades. Student feedback indicated strong acceptance of the new format and improved understanding of the subject matter. Statistical analysis showed a significant difference between cohorts before and after the curricular change, with modest but measurable effect sizes. The results suggest that take-home laboratories can support both motivation and academic performance, while also improving students' appreciation of the practical relevance of control engineering.

items.title: Learning to Clear Peer-to-Peer Energy Markets
items.summary: Peer-to-peer energy markets are a promising paradigm for integrating distributed energy resources. A large body of work models their clearing as distributed optimization or generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems which let prosumers coordinate trades and local resources without a central operator. Yet, the computational and communication burden of distributed optimization and GNE-seeking algorithms poses a major challenge to deployment at scale. We propose a learning-to-optimize framework for decentralized markets that uses historical data to accelerate clearing algorithms without additional communication. To enforce convergence by design, we train summable augmentations to a baseline algorithm, using graph neural networks to learn permutation-equivariant updates for markets of varying size and topology. We instantiate the framework for computing a variational GNE in the market model of Le Cadre et al. (2020) with a distributed Douglas-Rachford algorithm, but the idea extends to other models and base algorithms. Numerical experiments show improved convergence and illustrate the robustness of our method to out-of-distribution instances.

items.title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System
items.summary: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.

items.title: A Hybrid Systems Approach to Parameterizing the PERC1 Model for Data Centers Using Synchrophasor Measurements
items.summary: The Power Electronic Reconnecting and Ceasing (PERC1) load model represents the timed ceasing and reconnection of large power-electronic loads, including data centers. Voltage thresholds and timers govern its response, with a ramp on reconnection, making it a hybrid dynamical system. This paper formulates PERC1 as a hybrid automaton and uses that structure to identify its parameters from synchrophasor records of grid disturbances. We propose a four-stage identification procedure: mode-sequence identification, estimation of logic parameters from event-time constraints, and joint Gauss-Newton refinement using hybrid trajectory sensitivities and saltation matrices. The resulting salted Fisher information is then used to analyze parameter identifiability. Two structural results are established. The detection and actuation delays are identifiable only through their sum unless a second dip interrupts the reconnection ramp, and a single disturbance leaves one unidentifiable direction in each threshold-delay pair, which two disturbances with different voltage slopes resolve. A case study using synthetic 60 frames/s synchrophasor records demonstrates recovery of the ceasing and reconnection dynamics and identifies poorly observable parameters.

items.title: Towards Microphone-Invariant Speech Representations for Transformer-Based Voice Disorder Detection
items.summary: Automatic voice disorder detection from speech offers strong potential for early diagnosis and continuous disease monitoring. While models based on pre-trained transformers have improved detection performance, their robustness to microphone variation remains underexplored, particularly for consumer-grade devices. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first study of microphone mismatch in transformer-based binary voice disorder detection across 20 smartphone microphones. While most mismatched microphone conditions cause moderate performance degradation, the worst-case condition reduces unweighted average recall by up to 12.53 percentage points. To address this, we introduce a Barlow Twins-inspired module to learn microphone-invariant representations. Our approach reduces the performance gap between matched and mismatched conditions by up to 62%, while maintaining comparable matched-condition performance. Qualitative analysis of the embedding space demonstrates more compact, distinct speaker clusters across microphones. Importantly, results indicate generalisation to unseen microphones across manufacturers, smartphone generations, and release periods, without requiring any inference-time adaptation.

items.title: Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
items.summary: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.

items.title: LZn : Robust LoRa Frame Synchronization Under Frame Collisions and Ultra-Low SNR Conditions
items.summary: LoRa has become a widely adopted wireless modulation scheme in LPWANs due to its low cost, long range, and minimal transmission power. However, collisions between frames of the same spreading factor -- common in dense LoRa deployments -- prevent conventional LoRa receivers from detecting and correctly decoding frames. Recent work has introduced methods to improve recovery, yet their detection stage degrades sharply under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and high collision rates. In this work, we introduce LZn, a synchronization scheme driven by a minimum-based spectral intersection across consecutive symbols. While preamble search incurs a modest overhead, LZn reduces the cost of fine synchronization by two to three orders of magnitude compared to existing collision-tolerant receivers. Our method enables robust frame synchronization even under multiple packet overlaps or extremely low SNR conditions. We evaluate LZn on simulations and three independent, real-world LoRa datasets. LZn improves detection sensitivity by up to 10 dB and increases detection probability by up to 1.54x. In real-world datasets, LZn improves decoding by 3.46x in the most challenging single-user scenario and up to 1.22x in collision scenarios compared to the second best collision-tolerant scheme (TnB). These results demonstrate that LZn substantially improves the frame recovery of LoRa receivers, while remaining compatible with real-time requirements.

items.title: Robust Data-Driven Output-Feedback Reference Governor with Quantified Model Uncertainty
items.summary: This paper constructs a data-driven reference governor (DDRG) from input--output data and supplied deterministic disturbance bounds. A data-consistent model set quantifies the uncertainty remaining in each prediction direction. With exact output measurements, the DDRG propagates output-history uncertainty while retaining exact applied-reference histories and converts the resulting tubes into constraint margins. Under a common contraction condition in a selected history norm, explicit terminal feasibility inequalities certify infinite-horizon continuation under a held reference and yield a closed invariant admissible set. A scalar update selects the largest certified step toward the requested reference, with recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction from certified initialization. A separate bounded-measurement-noise extension derives the errors-in-variables model set and the additional physical-output margin through a measured-history certificate. On the coupled benchmark, longer nested records reduce one-step prediction disagreement at the probe regressor, and propagation accounts for most of the gap between the tube and true-model envelopes at the reported constraint row and prediction step.

items.title: A Disease-Centric Vision-Language Foundation Model for Precision Oncology in Kidney Cancer
items.summary: The non-invasive assessment of renal masses remains a critical challenge in urologic oncology, where diagnostic uncertainty frequently causes overtreatment. Here, we develop RenalCLIP, a vision-language foundation model for precision oncology in kidney cancer. Utilizing 27,866 computed tomography scans from 8,809 patients across diverse multi-center cohorts, we employ a two-stage pre-training strategy to align domain-specific visual and textual representations. RenalCLIP achieves enhanced performance and generalizability across ten core clinical tasks, spanning anatomical assessment, diagnostic classification, and survival prediction, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art general-purpose foundation models. Furthermore, RenalCLIP demonstrates strong data efficiency in diagnostic classification, achieving peak baseline performance using only 20% of the training data. The model also exhibits robust zero-shot diagnostic capabilities, effective image-text retrieval, and high-quality medical report generation. Our findings establish RenalCLIP as a powerful, generalizable tool to enhance diagnostic precision, refine prognostic stratification, and personalize the management of renal masses.

items.title: Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback
items.summary: In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

items.title: A Novel Reinforcement Learning Based Framework for Scalable MIMO Interference Alignment
items.summary: Interference alignment (IA) is a widely recognized approach for mitigating inter-cell interference in multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) networks. Despite its effectiveness, practical deployment remains constrained by two major challenges, i.e., the need for global channel state information (CSI) at each transmitter and the complexity of deriving closed-form solutions for intricate MIMO systems. This work aims to maximize network throughput by effectively mitigating interference using an IA-inspired learning algorithm that addresses its aforementioned challenges. First, we propose a predictive, transformer-based IA framework that estimates CSI to reduce signaling overhead in small-scale MIMO systems. Next, we formulate the IA problem as a multi-objective optimization problem based on subspace coordination and develop two reinforcement learning-based algorithms to enhance the scalability of IA in large-scale MIMO systems. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly outperform conventional baselines with up to 30% average user throughput gains over the best performing baseline.

items.title: Online Neural Network Training via Closed-Loop Model-Free Tracking Control: An Empirical Study
items.summary: Training artificial neural networks predominantly relies on offline, gradient-based backpropagation algorithms. In contrast, biological circuits process and retain information through decentralized, continuous-time adaptation. In this work, we explore an online, gradient-free learning methodology by formulating the tuning of synaptic weights as a closed-loop trajectory tracking problem driven by model-free control principles. Rather than performing global optimization across static parameters, decentralized controllers adjust synaptic interactions in real-time using solely local input-output tracking errors. We present an exploratory benchmark neural architecture, whose purpose is to assess the dynamic resilience of the proposed approach, particularly in tracking target outputs and adapting to abrupt non-stationarities and structural perturbations (such as topological changes or dynamic dropout) without requiring offline retraining. This empirical preliminary study provides a proof-of-concept for control-theoretic learning paradigms and outlines the foundation for scalable, dynamically evolving connectome frameworks.

items.title: AHEADance: Anticipatory Humanoid Dance from Streaming Audio
items.summary: A humanoid that dances to streamed music must commit each motion chunk before it has heard the music that chunk accompanies, and must continue from motion it has already committed. We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker. ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music model's forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and weighted by reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song's beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model's own committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real dance. Three music evaluators, each validated on real G1 dance, test synchronization, song and style. On a physical Unitree G1, it dances while the music plays and comes to rest when it stops, without a fall. Project page: https://ihcr.github.io/AHEADance

items.title: Second-Order Physics-Informed Learning of Road Traffic State using Probe Vehicles
items.summary: We propose a Physics-Informed Learning framework for reconstructing traffic density and velocity state from sparse trajectory data. The proposed framework relies on the simple idea that a second-order model captures non-steady-state behaviors as minor modifications to first-order solutions. Therefore, the approach implements a tailored second-order correction to the density and the speed of a first-order estimate. This framework is evaluated in a ring-road scenario with real and simulated data. Results show that the implemented framework improves state estimation by achieving lower error and variance than previously investigated frameworks. These results hold for scenarios with heterogeneous driver behaviors (real data) and with different driver behavior models (simulated data), consistent across different penetration rates.

items.title: A High-Resolution TOA Estimation Algorithm Based on Compressed Sensing for Coherent Multi-Band Signals
items.summary: High-resolution time-of-arrival (ToA) estimation is crucial for accurate ranging and localization in future wireless networks. While multi-band operation can synthesize a large virtual bandwidth by probing several separated subbands, the resulting non-contiguous frequency layout induces pronounced sidelobes and dense local maxima in the delay response, making reliable ToA estimation challenging. This paper studies coherent multi-band ToA estimation from a single multi-band channel state information (CSI) snapshot. We derive a multiband least-squares formulation and analyze its point-spread function (PSF) and Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) to characterize the effects of the subband layout on delay accuracy and sidelobe ambiguity. Building on this analysis, we propose a low complexity two-stage particle swarm optimization estimator and incorporate it into orthogonal matching pursuit with a RELAX-type cyclic refinement procedure for multipath delay estimation, mitigating basis mismatch and improving robustness to the dense local maxima induced by non-contiguous multi-band layouts. Numerical results are consistent with the PSF and CRB analyses and show that the proposed framework approaches the CRB in the single-path setting and achieves accurate multipath delay estimation with low computational complexity. Real channel measurements further validate the predicted impact of different subband layouts on delay-estimation performance.

items.title: Finite-Step Algorithms for Input-Constrained Control Barrier Function-Based Safety Filters
items.summary: Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters commonly rely on quadratic programs (QPs) to modify nominal control inputs while satisfying safety constraints. For safety-critical applications, however, the solution must be computed reliably under actuator limitations and with predictable computational effort. General-purpose QP solvers typically rely on numerical convergence criteria, which do not directly provide finite bounds on algorithmic steps or distinguish solver failure from mathematical infeasibility. This paper considers CBF-QPs with a single affine safety constraint, componentwise input bounds, and diagonal quadratic weights. Exploiting the established scalar dual structure of continuous quadratic knapsack problems, we obtain a necessary and sufficient pointwise feasibility condition and an exact breakpoint-based solution procedure. The algorithm requires at most 2n positive breakpoint events for n inputs, reducing to at most n events when the nominal input is admissible. In the latter case, an exact saturation--redistribution algorithm computes the optimal solution in at most n passes. We further describe how the structured solution can be combined with verified floating-point constraint evaluation to distinguish certified feasible commands, certified infeasibility, and unresolved numerical cases. The resulting framework provides an exact and computationally predictable solution procedure for a practically relevant class of input-constrained CBF safety filters.

items.title: Observing Earth's ionospheric irregularities from the Moon
items.summary: Radio signals that propagate through the Earth's ionosphere carry information about possible irregular plasma structures. Such irregularities manifest themselves as amplitude signatures that depend on the propagation and observation geometry [1, 2]. Conventional ground and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) measurements sample these effects close to Earth. Here we present a systematic characterization of terrestrial ionospheric irregularities using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) amplitude observations from the lunar surface, at distances of approximately 356,000-398,000 km from Earth's surface [3]. Using nearly 93 h of 1-Hz lunar-surface observations of GPS L1/L5 and Galileo E1/E5a collected by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), we reconstruct the propagation and scanning geometry to characterize the spatiotemporal signatures of amplitude and phase fluctuations. At lunar distance, the Fresnel scale approaches its finite-source limit, extending the observations to a propagation regime beyond conventional near-Earth configurations. Detrended receiver-reported carrier-to-noise density ratios ($δC/N_0$) reveal pronounced polar amplitude fluctuations at both frequency bands, also visible in the original measurements. Within the regions and local times sampled, large fluctuations occur in about 30% of valid one-minute polar windows, compared with less than 5% in either the equatorial or mid-latitude band. These findings support using the lunar surface as a vantage point for studying Earth's polar ionospheric irregularities and testing how propagation and scanning relative to the magnetic field shape their amplitude signatures. Future lunar observations could extend this approach to long-term monitoring of Earth's ionospheric irregularities

items.title: Beyond the Pseudo-Inverse: GIM Precoding for Per-Antenna Power Minimisation in MU-MIMO
items.summary: We study linear precoder design for multi-user MIMO downlink under per-antenna power constraints (PAPC), which arise naturally when each antenna port has its own power amplifier. While the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse is the unique optimal generalized inverse for zero-forcing precoding under a total power constraint [1], we prove this optimality does not extend to the MMSE/RZF case under PAPC. Any precoder in the Generalized Inverse Matrix (GIM) family shares the same effective channel and per-user SINRs as the pseudo-inverse baseline, while its null-space component reshapes the per-antenna power profile. This separation principle enables minimising peak per-antenna power at fixed SINR targets with zero SINR penalty. We characterise the convex peak-power problem over this family and its active-set optimality, establish MRT and ZF asymptotic limits, and provide a convergent first-order subgradient algorithm. Simulations with 8-64 antennas confirm gains of 1.9-3.7 dB over pseudo-inverse RZF, with GIM-MMSE eliminating essentially all PAPC violations up to 20% per-antenna budget imbalance. The framework applies directly to fully-digital massive MIMO. Cell-free and hybrid analog-digital arrays are promising extensions.

items.title: Non-Myopic Safety Filtering with Learned Intervention Cost-to-Go
items.summary: Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters minimize instantaneous deviation from a nominal control command, but a sequence of pointwise-minimal interventions need not minimize cumulative intervention effort. This paper proposes a discrete-time non-myopic safety filter using a learned approximation of the optimal intervention cost-to-go over CBF-admissible policies. The approximation enters through a relaxed Bellman-residual constraint, while the original barrier condition remains hard. Feasibility is equivalent to that of the conventional CBF filter, and forward invariance remains independent of approximation accuracy under the stated assumptions. We derive a trajectory-wise performance certificate that requires neither the optimal value function nor an approximation-error bound. Under additional approximation and horizon assumptions, a suboptimality bound contains an explicit endpoint approximation-error term together with accumulated tolerance and relaxation terms. Numerical results for a collision-avoidance problem show an approximately 50% reduction in mean cumulative intervention effort relative to conventional CBF filtering over 100 initial conditions not used during training or parameter selection. The improvement is consistent across three independently trained networks, while maintaining the prescribed safety constraints and requiring less online computation than the tested predictive filter.

items.title: A Modified Rao-Blackwellised Particle Filter Based on Updated Process Noise Covariance for Chemical Reaction Networks
items.summary: It is necessary to characterize chemical reaction networks (CRNs) accurately to facilitate engineering of both synthetic and naturally occurring biological systems. Estimation of multiple unknown parameters and states in CRNs requires first, an identifiability analysis, and then adoption of a suitable estimation technique. In this paper, we took an example of a reduced order gene expression system, performed parameter sensitivity analysis for multiple unknown parameters, and used a modified Rao-Blackwellised particle filter (RBPF) to estimate parameters and states. The proposed framework estimates parameters using a particle filter and states using an extended Kalman filter (EKF) with process noise covariance updated recursively based on chemical Langevin equation (CLE). We compared the accuracy of parameter estimation, error in state estimation, and whiteness of the innovation sequence for the proposed filter with fixed choices of noise covariance. We found that the RBPF with updated noise covariance finds a balance between these three criteria, demonstrating its suitability for joint state and parameter estimation for stochastic CRNs.

items.title: Learning Morse Lyapunov functions through invertible neural networks
items.summary: Towards data-driven stability certificates of dynamical systems, we are witnessing renewed interest in studying and exploiting the structure of Lyapunov functions. Especially Lyapunov functions that are locally quadratic (i.e., Morse) gained popularity ever since it was understood that they can be written as the norm squared of a diffeomorphism. This topological representation alludes to parametrizations using invertible neural networks. In this note we discuss when and how such functions can be learned. In particular, using neural ODEs (NODEs), we characterize Sobolev approximation of these diffeomorphisms on compact sets and show how this naturally relates to stability. We also connect our results to PLNets and supply numerical experiments for illustration.

items.title: Risk-Aware Handover Management Approach for Non-Terrestrial Networks with the NTN-Connect Simulator
items.summary: The continuous movement of low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites in non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) leads to frequent handovers, requiring joint optimization of visibility duration, transmit power, and user quality-of-service (QoS). This work address this issue by proposing a risk-aware handover management framework that minimizes transmit power and maximizes admitted users under per-satellite power budgets and user-rate chance constraints, while a preference score term penalizes short duration associations. We decompose the resulting mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) into an inner power allocation subproblem and an outer generalized assignment association subproblem. The inner subproblem reformulates the chance constraint into its deterministic counterpart using the value-at-risk (VaR) closed-form. The obtained transmit power allocation is then used in the association subproblem, which is solved optimally using an off-the-shelf solver. Finally, we employ the polynomial-complexity Hungarian algorithm to solve the relaxed assignment problem and enforce the per-satellite power budget using a knapsack algorithm. Simulations, using the proposed NTN-Connect simulator, on the OneWeb and Starlink constellations show that the proposed low-complexity solution achieves near-optimal performance and better performance compared to the risk-aware maximum stay (RA-MST) and risk-aware maximum received signal received power (RA-MRSRP) baselines. On the Starlink constellation, it increases the inter-handover interval (IHI) from $0.37$ to $1.47$~min, reducing the handover rate by $75\%$. At a maximum-IHI operating point, it reduces the total transmit power by 1.1 dBW (22\%) while increasing the admission rate from 97.4\% to 99.3\%.

items.title: Locally homogeneous PID gain-scheduling for motion control systems
items.summary: A method for upgrading linear PID controller to a locally homogeneous PID regulator is developed. The homogeneous PID shares the gains with linear PID while the tuning of local homogeneity degrees could allow better regulation quality comparing with the linear algorithm. The homogeneous algorithm is obtained by means of the scaling the gains of the linear controller dependently of the current value of the output and its derivative. The linear algorithm can be recovered from the homogeneous one by assigning zero homogeneity degree. The tuning scheme for the homogeneous controller is suggested and illustrated experimentally in comparison with a standard PID control, which is robustly designed by the loop-shaping around the critical frequency range. The experiments are accomplished on a linear-motion stage system with voice-coil-motor and noisy contactless output measurements.

items.title: Learning and Verifying Stabilizing Controllers with Structured Neural Control Lyapunov Functions
items.summary: This work investigates the joint learning of neural controllers and control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) for nonlinear discrete-time systems. We exploit the structural properties of Input Convex Neural Networks and Polyak-Łojasiewicz Networks to guarantee positive definiteness of CLF candidates by construction, reducing the conditions requiring formal verification. We develop a mixed-integer programming framework to formally verify the remaining stability conditions and introduce an iterative region of attraction (ROA) expansion procedure to enlarge the certified ROA without retraining. Experiments on an inverted pendulum and a path-tracking system demonstrate the advantages of structured neural CLFs, particularly PLNets, and illustrate how their structural bounds influence the geometry of the certified regions. Our code is available at: https://github.com/JLedesMart/Structured-Neural-Control-Lyapunov-Functions.

items.title: A Rollout-Based Approach to Real-Time Topology and Dispatch Control in the AI4RealNet L2RPN Benchmark
items.summary: Operating transmission networks under uncertain outages requires coordinating discrete network topology actions with continuous adjustments to generation and storage, while respecting operational constraints and real-time computational limits. We present a rollout-based controller that combines discrete and continuous decisions under the uncertain contingency policy of the L2RPN AI4RealNet 2026 challenge. Power-flow approximations and convex optimization identify the most promising actions, followed by short-horizon simulations to predict their effect on congestion, renewable curtailment, and redispatching costs. A further policy exploits the benchmark's specific attack protocol: keeping selected lines disconnected prevents some adversarial outages from being initiated. On the benchmark's $118$-bus network, the controller completed $189$ of $208$ final-test scenarios (score $64.39$) and achieved the second-best ratio of score to computation time among the five top-ranked entries, behind one that scored lower. Our results show that combining structured optimization with simulation-based action selection is effective even without a learned decision rule, and fast enough for real-time control. Code and reproduction material: https://github.com/DavidKrame/RAD_agent__AI4RealNet_competition.

items.title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis
items.summary: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

items.title: Layer-wise Linear Probing of an Encoder-free Audio-capable Language Model
items.summary: Encoder-free audio-capable multimodal language models pro- vide a unique setting for studying how speech representations emerge inside a language-model decoder. In Gemma-4-12B, short waveform frames are projected directly into the shared embedding space, and all subsequent contextual processing is performed by the decoder layers. We use this architecture to examine where acoustic, phonetic, segmental, and paralinguis- tic information becomes linearly accessible across depth. Us- ing the TIMIT corpus, we extract all 49 representations from the frozen model, including the embedding output and the out- puts of its 48 decoder layers. We train linear probes for log- F0, log-energy, voicing, phone identity, word-onset structure, speaker identity, recorded speaker gender, and dialect-region labels. The results show a broad progression in linear acces- sibility. Acoustic properties are most strongly decodable in the early layers, paralinguistic attributes are most accessible in the early-to-middle layers, and phone identity and boundary- sensitive information reach their highest performance around layer 11. Several properties remain strongly decodable across broad near-peak regions rather than at a single uniquely optimal layer. In deeper layers, phone identity and closed-set speaker identity decline sharply, while voicing, log-F0, and gender re- main more accessible. These findings provide an initial map of how speech information develops when the decoder is the first contextual stage to process audio.

items.title: An Algebraic Approach to Continuously Updating GMM: Estimation and Inference
items.summary: The continuously updating GMM estimator (CUE) minimizes a nonconvex objective. We give an algebraic solution in linear instrumental variables models with a fixed joint variance estimate that allows for heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, or clustering. With one endogenous regressor and a positive definite variance estimate, the objective is a ratio of polynomials. Its global minimum is obtained by comparing the objective at no more than 4k-2 real stationary points and at infinity, with k instruments. The roots can be computed as eigenvalues of a companion matrix. We extend the results to singular variance estimates and characterize the multivariate minimum using finitely many stationary objective values. These results provide methods for computing CUE, overidentification statistics, and likelihood ratio-based tests. Simulations show that local optimization can lead to substantially different estimates and test decisions. The algebraic results are exact, although their numerical implementation requires care in computing polynomial coefficients and roots.

items.title: On the equilibrium lattice of supermodular games
items.summary: This paper shows how the meet and join of any pair of equilibria in a super- modular game can be constructed. The method relies on two one-directional best-response processes that I call contagion up and contagion down. Starting from any action profile, applying this pair of processes in opposite orders produces two equilibria that define its equilibrium envelope. The endpoints of the envelope are precisely the least and greatest equilibria reachable through arbitrary asynchronous best-response dynamics, and can only move closer together as players revise their actions. These and other results show how appending one-directional adjustment processes to the familiar equilibrium lattice structure allows us to explore the relationships between equilibria further.

items.title: Fooling Yourself: how narratives shape beliefs
items.summary: Narratives often combine diagnostic evidence with truthful but nondiagnostic details. In a two-state experiment with known signal likelihoods, we test whether such details distort belief updating. Although Bayes' rule prescribes no revision, nondiagnostic signals induce revisions consistent with considering both states equally likely. Such revisions are most frequent when nondiagnostic signals appear as clues in a story, less frequent in an abstract urn problem, and virtually absent when the same story replaces these clues with explicit no-information messages. Simulations show that these revisions reduce belief accuracy and delay decisions, an effect communicators could exploit without lying.

items.title: Platform Recommendation and Competition in Search Markets
items.summary: Recommendation rules affect both sellers' incentives and the alternatives consumers expect to find. We develop a framework for evaluating these rules with heterogeneous sellers, endogenous pricing and advertising, and costly consumer search. For a broad class of separable recommendation scores, we establish conditions under which a unique market equilibrium exists. Three applications illustrate the use of the framework. A stronger reward for low prices does not necessarily lower equilibrium prices and benefit consumers when products are sufficiently differentiated in qualities. Quality guidance can lower the price of each product and benefit consumers while raising the average transaction price. With heterogeneous match distributions, a reward for the best initial inspection can help consumers with advertising fixed and harm them when advertising adjusts. A two-type design extension shows that no finite optimum over implementable outcomes uses positive weights on both quality and low prices, even when the platform values consumer surplus.

items.title: Recommendation Quality and the Concentration of Consumption: Experimental Evidence from Netflix
items.summary: We study an experiment with 8.5 million users on Netflix's recommender system to measure how improvements in recommendation technology affect the set of products that get consumed. Improvements increase total consumption and users' reliance on recommendations while diffusing recommendations and consumption away from the most popular titles ("superstars") toward a larger number of moderately popular titles ("middle-tail"), with minimal effects on the most niche titles ("long-tail"). Our results challenge the notion that recommender systems polarize consumption -- raising the consumption shares of the head and tail at the expense of the middle -- and suggest that the returns to investing in middle-tail products grow as algorithms improve and platforms scale.

items.title: A nonparametric test for diurnal variation in spot correlation processes
items.summary: The association between log-price increments of exchange-traded equities, as measured by their spot correlation estimated from high-frequency data, exhibits a pronounced upward-sloping and almost piecewise linear relationship at the intraday horizon. There is notably lower-on average less positive-correlation in the morning than in the afternoon. We develop a nonparametric testing procedure to detect such variation in a correlation process. The test statistic has a known distribution under the null hypothesis, whereas it diverges under the alternative. We run a Monte Carlo simulation to discover the finite sample properties of the test statistic, which are close to the large sample predictions, even for small sample sizes and realistic levels of diurnal variation. In an application, we implement the test on a high-frequency dataset covering the stock market over an extended period. The test leads to rejection of the null most of the time. This suggests diurnal variation in the correlation process is a nontrivial effect in practice. We show how conditioning information about macroeconomic news and corporate earnings announcements affect the intraday correlation curve.

items.title: The "Rough" HAR Model
items.summary: This paper proposes discrete-time approximations to rough continuous-time models of realized variance (RV). The leading rough models can be viewed as autoregressive processes driven by fractional Gaussian noise. We show that the Wold representation of this noise concentrates its dependence at the first lag when the Hurst parameter is below one half. Augmenting the autoregressive (AR) and heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) models with a first-order moving-average (MA(1)) component therefore approximates the roughness, and the MA coefficient maps almost linearly into the Hurst parameter. We refer to these extensions as the "rough" AR and "rough" HAR models. Estimating them on the log RV of ten ETFs, we find negative MA coefficients for every asset, and the implied Hurst parameters align closely with the estimates from the continuous-time models. In the HAR literature, the negative MA(1) component is a significant feature that has been largely overlooked. In out-of-sample comparisons, the "rough" models outperform their classical counterparts for nearly every asset and horizon, with the largest gains at short horizons, and their accuracy is comparable to that of the rough continuous-time models but much easier to estimate by standard off-the-shelf software.

items.title: Counterexamples to EFX for Submodular and Subadditive Valuations
items.summary: The existence of EFX allocations is a fundamental question in fair division. In this paper, we construct a three-agent, eight-good instance with monotone subadditive valuations such that no allocation satisfies $α$-EFX for any $α> \frac{1}{\sqrt[6]{2}} \approx 0.89$. We also provide a closely related three-agent, eight-good instance with submodular (in fact weighted coverage) valuations for which no EFX allocation exists. A key feature of our construction is its symmetry: the agents' valuations are identical up to a relabeling of the goods. Thus, EFX can fail even when agents differ only in how the goods are labeled. This symmetry makes the counterexamples compact and human-verifiable, yielding simple combinatorial obstructions to the existence of EFX.

items.title: Exploiting Common Volatility Dynamics in High-Dimensional Portfolio Selection
items.summary: We study how commonalities in monthly realized stock volatilities can be exploited for high-dimensional covariance forecasting and portfolio selection. We compare latent factor models with ARMA models that pool dynamic parameters within pre-specified groups of stocks. We show that pooled ARMA models admit an exact dynamic factor representation with group-specific dynamics and stock-specific loadings. The implied static factor representation involves group-specific factors that need not be pervasive. Combining volatility forecasts with realized dynamic conditional correlations and nonlinear shrinkage, we evaluate out-of-sample minimum variance portfolios of S&P 500 constituents. Pooling-based approaches consistently outperform the alternatives across portfolio constraints and model specifications.

items.title: Match Rate Is Not Match Quality
items.summary: Third-party identity-resolution vendors commonly emphasize match rate, the share of submitted records they can link to identifiers for advertising activation, as their core metric of quality. Yet a high match rate does not necessarily mean that those matched identifiers belong to the submitted records (i.e., the intended targets). In this paper we explore match quality as an alternative metric to match rate, utilizing a unique data set to evaluate match quality. We are able to compare two demographics, age and gender, from a submitted record (voter files) to the same demographics in self-reported surveys matched to mobile advertising identifiers linked together by two leading identity-resolution vendors. The data and matching was from 2019-20. There is substantial ambiguity in match quality of the returned records. First, both vendors' activation files contain multiple device identifiers per match. Second, match quality among audited pairs (Vendor A) and for explicitly labeled individual-level matches (Vendor B) is only 21.8% and 23.6%, respectively. Utilizing a mixture model that assumes that correct links always agree on these two demographics and incorrect links agree 10% of the time, these rates imply conditional identity-level precisions of approximately 15% and 13%, respectively. This paper utilizes identity-resolution products that are several years old, but the question we address remains fundamental: match rate alone cannot establish whether advertisers are reaching the people they intended. Evaluating identity resolution requires independent evidence of match quality alongside match rate.

items.title: Influence Functions: A Unified Differentiation-Based Framework
items.summary: This paper introduces a direct differentiation-based framework that unifies the derivation of influence functions across parametric, nonparametric, and semiparametric models. We show that the Riesz representer of the functional derivative is obtained by orthogonally projecting the identification function onto the subspace of mean-zero functions, so the influence function is a linear transformation of the moment function. This approach extends seamlessly to infinite-dimensional parameters and reveals a common algebraic form across both finite- and infinite-dimensional cases. It demonstrates that the slower nonparametric convergence rate arises from approximating the infeasible Dirac delta function. The same framework further applies to semiparametric multi-step plug-in estimation, where it automatically yields locally robust moment functions. Crucially, by employing distributional derivatives, the method accommodates non-smooth moment conditions without imposing classical differentiability.

items.title: Feasible Search Behavior
items.summary: Consider a situation wherein a decision maker sequentially searches for the best alternative among heterogeneous options with an arbitrary search order. The agent partially learns the value of an option when inspecting it. The information structure jointly determines the ex-ante and ex-post value of investigating each option, thereby shaping the entire learning path. We characterize the set of all search behaviors compatible with some information structure, which forms a polytope. A single information structure rationalizes all these search behaviors, which minimizes the agent's welfare among all information structures. Under certain symmetry assumption over primitives, we also examine the set of all feasible pairs of search and choice behaviors, with and without option sellers' price competition, and prove the same results. Our study not only provides a simple framework for analyzing how information shapes ordered learning paths, but also offers sharp insights into information design and identification problems in such environments.

items.title: Allocating Common-Value Goods
items.summary: We study a simple problem of allocating common-value goods. The designer seeks to allocate the goods to as many unit-demand agents as possible without monetary transfers, while agents, who possess partial private information about the goods, are willing to receive them only when the goods are of high value. Mechanisms screen each agent's private information using the information of other agents, and in doing so shape what agents learn from other agents about the value of the goods. The optimal mechanism can be summarized by two parameters: one adjusts the allocation probability, while the other governs the amount of learning induced by allocation. Although the designer prefers to allocate the goods, the optimal mechanism excludes some agents and, as a result, may withhold allocation even when all agents would be willing to receive them. The optimal mechanism has the same structure even when payments are available, but it does not exclude any agent and involves strictly positive payments that are not increasing in allocation probability.

items.title: Embedding Foundation Model Predictions in Discrete-Choice Models with Structural Guarantees
items.summary: Tabular foundation models achieve strong accuracy on choice prediction tasks, but their predictions often violate the economic logic those tasks require: raising a price can increase predicted demand, implied estimates of willingness to pay are frequently negative or implausible, and unavailable alternatives receive nonzero probability. We propose TabFM-Logit, an adapter that takes a foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature and embeds them inside a multinomial logit's utility. In Stage 1, we fit the multinomial logit's structural coefficients by maximum likelihood with sign constraints. In Stage 2, we freeze those coefficients and fit a small neural correction operating on the foundation model's predictions. We prove that this composition exactly preserves the multinomial logit's marginal rate of substitution, so the analytically computable value of time becomes a mathematical guarantee rather than an empirical accident, and that training the two stages jointly breaks identifiability of the structural coefficients. Counterfactual derivatives and response signs are therefore the multinomial logit's by construction, and the foundation model contributes accuracy on observed choices. On respondents and households unseen in training, the adapter gains 5.7-6.8 percentage points (pp) of test accuracy on Swissmetro, 1.5 pp on LPMC, and 3.3-3.6 pp on IoT-Wearables over the multinomial logit (4.2 pp on average), stays within 1.0 pp of the raw foundation model, maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and keeps the multinomial logit's values of time exactly. The gain is largest where the multinomial logit is weakest and smallest where it is already strong. In every case it comes with the multinomial logit's guarantees, which the raw foundation models lack.

items.title: A Tail-Geometric Approach to Kotlarski's Lemma with Order Statistics
items.summary: We develop a tail-geometric approach to nonparametric identification in repeated-measurement models based on large within-unit gaps. Differencing eliminates the common latent component, while conditioning on a large gap pushes the idiosyncratic errors into opposite tails. Under a regular thinner-than-Gaussian tail condition, an idiosyncratic component concentrates around a deterministic, gap-dependent location. Consequently, the corresponding observed measurement, after recentering, reveals the distribution of the common latent component up to location. The idiosyncratic distribution can then be recovered through deconvolution. This principle applies both to the classical two-measurement Kotlarski model and to settings where only order statistics are observed. Applications include auctions and wage-offer models, whether all offers are observed or only the top-ranked ones are available.

items.title: Difference-in-Differences Estimators for Treatments Continuously Distributed at Every Period
items.summary: When studying the effects of taxes, tariffs, or prices using panel data, the treatment is often continuously distributed in every period. We develop difference-in-differences (DID) estimators for such settings. We partition units into switchers, whose treatment changes between consecutive periods, and stayers, whose treatment remains constant. Under a parallel-trends assumption, we show that the slopes of switchers' potential outcomes with respect to the treatment are nonparametrically identified by DID comparisons between switchers and stayers sharing the same baseline treatment level. Conditioning on the baseline treatment is key, as it ensures that the underlying parallel-trends assumption accommodates time-varying treatment effects. We then study two weighted averages of these slopes, discuss their respective advantages, and propose for each a doubly robust, semiparametrically efficient, and $\sqrt{n}$-consistent estimator. Finally, we extend our framework to instrumental variables and illustrate it by estimating the effects of gasoline taxes on prices and fuel consumption.

items.title: AI Behavioral Science: A Framework and Agenda
items.summary: We discuss the challenges and opportunities present in the rapidly emerging area of ``AI Behavioral Science.'' We frame it via three themes. First, as AI becomes ubiquitous and is increasingly proprietary and opaque, it becomes vital to develop models of AI and methods for assessing AI behavior. We outline how tools developed to assess people's behaviors by social scientists can be used to model, assess and infer AI's behaviors biases, tendencies, and heuristics. Second, we also discuss how AI can change the ways in which we learn about human behavior. Beyond its computational power, AI offers new techniques for simulating, inferring, predicting, and analyzing human behaviors. Third, as humans and AI are interacting in increasingly complex and intertwined systems, we need to analyze and model human-AI interactions including how human and AI behaviors depend on interactions at the individual level, how interacting systems of humans and AI behave, and ultimately how AI's integration into society affects economic and political outcomes. We discuss current research, questions, agendas, and goals in each of these three themes and how they depend upon each other.

items.title: Plausibly Exogenous Instruments in Probit Models: Sensitivity Bounds for Average Partial and Interaction Effects
items.summary: Sensitivity analysis for imperfect instruments usually targets a linear two-stage least squares coefficient, yet many applications have binary outcomes and probability-scale targets. We extend the plausibly exogenous framework to the control-function probit, targeting average partial and interaction effects. We derive the generated-regressor variance, union and local-to-zero intervals, and their asymptotic coverage under stated model and calibration conditions. A violation stated on the wrong latent scale can miscalibrate the interval by a factor set by the endogeneity correlation. Applications to Catholic schooling, sibling sex composition and Confucian clans compare probit and linear analyses. Stata and R implementations accompany the analysis.

items.title: Long-Term Quantile Treatment Effects with Combined Experimental and Observational Data
items.summary: This paper studies the identification, estimation, and inference of long-term quantile treatment effects (LTQTEs) when short-term experimental data are supplemented with long-term observational data. Under a latent unconfoundedness framework, we establish identification of the LTQTE curve and derive the corresponding efficient influence functions. Building on these influence functions, we propose a semiparametrically efficient estimation procedure and develop a multiplier bootstrap method for uniform inference on the LTQTE curve, yielding valid simultaneous confidence bands over a continuum of quantile indices.

items.title: Weighted Proportional Toll Sharing on General Highway Networks
items.summary: We extend the Segments Equal Sharing (SES) method of \citet{wu2024} from line highways to general highway networks, including networks with cycles. The input is an exogenously specified profile of route flows. We introduce the Weighted Proportional Sharing (WPS) method, which distributes each route's mileage revenue in proportion to weighted segment lengths and its fixed-surcharge revenue in proportion to positive segment surcharges. Route SES is recovered under homogeneous weights within each revenue component. We show that WPS is the sum of two weighted Shapley allocations and that the underlying route games extend the dividend and Shapley representation of linear SES. Two axiomatic characterizations identify WPS. The first uses additivity and proportional treatment of segments used on every positive-revenue route. The second combines sub-highway efficiency and weighted average balanced contributions under a route cancellation rule. We also extend Segments Proportional Sharing to general networks, identify it with the $τ$ value of the corresponding route game, and characterize it axiomatically. For Segments Compensated Sharing we characterize a weighted average tree allocation by consistency across rooted branch settlements and averaging under a specified root lottery. A cyclic example shows that different route splits can change the allocation even when origin--destination volumes and aggregate toll revenue are held fixed.

items.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
items.summary: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.

items.title: Does the AI Reviewer Alleviate or Aggravate the Maintenance Burden? Evidence from GitHub Copilot Reviewer
items.summary: This study examines how AI-based code reviewers reshape contribution behavior and maintenance dynamics in open-source software (OSS) communities. AI reviewers provide scalable, fast, and standardized evaluations. They reshape contributions as well as maintainers' workload. Leveraging the introduction of GitHub Copilot Reviewer on GitHub as a natural experiment in 2025, we investigate how AI review affects maintainers' workload and review efficiency as well as contribution behavior. We find that repository maintainers initially face a sharp increase in PR submissions and a higher review workload after the adoption of the AI reviewer. Over time, human contributions decline while the increase in bot-generated PRs is sustained. Interestingly, survival analysis reveals that AI reviewers increase review efficiency for human PR contributions, whereas bot PRs take longer to review and merge. Our findings suggest that while AI reviewers increase review efficiency, they aggravate the maintenance burden by encouraging more code contributions via humans and bots.

items.title: Difference-in-differences for mediation analysis using double machine learning
items.summary: We propose a difference-in-differences (DiD) framework with mediation for possibly multivalued discrete or continuous treatments and mediators, aimed at identifying the direct effect of the treatment on the outcome (net of effects operating through the mediator), the indirect effect via the mediator, and the joint effects of treatment and mediator, consistent with the framework of dynamic treatment effects. Identification relies on a conditional parallel trends assumption imposed on the mean potential outcome across treatment and mediator states, or (depending on the causal parameter) additionally on the mean potential outcomes and potential mediator distributions across treatment states. We propose ATET estimators for repeated cross sections and panel data within the double/debiased machine learning framework, which allows for data-driven control of covariates, and we establish their asymptotic normality under standard regularity conditions. We investigate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods in a simulation study and illustrate our approach in an empirical application to the US National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, estimating the direct effect of health care coverage on general health as well as the indirect effect operating through routine checkups.

items.title: Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling
items.summary: We establish the asymptotic theory of the exact maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for discretely observed multivariate ergodic diffusions under high-frequency, long-span sampling, solving an open problem posed by \citet{YCW2019} and \citet{Li2013}. The drift may grow linearly, and the volatility is bounded away from zero and either bounded or proportional to $1+|x|$. When the sampling interval decays polynomially, the exact MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, with rates $\sqrt{nΔ_n}$ for drift and $\sqrt n$ for diffusion parameters. Under an additional condition on ergodic averages, and when the time span $nΔ_n$ also grows polynomially, its moments converge as well. The proof never analyzes the exact likelihood directly: it shows that a closed-form density expansion of sufficiently high order is uniformly accurate in relative terms at every observed transition, so that the two log-likelihoods differ by $o_P(1)$ uniformly in the parameter. The same argument yields accuracy conditions under which an approximate likelihood is asymptotically equivalent to the exact one; in particular, the approximate MLE of Yang, Chen and Wan converges to the true parameter. For the delta-expansion estimator of fixed order $K\ge1$, we derive the leading bias explicitly. It shows that $nΔ_n^{K+1}\to0$ cannot be weakened when the bias constant is nonzero, and that the bias falls on the drift parameters for even $K$ and on the diffusion parameters for odd $K$. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the predicted biases.

items.title: Just After Minimum Wage Hikes: Short-Run Labor-Demand Response and Reallocation
items.summary: How labor markets adjust immediately after minimum wage hikes remains an open, policy-relevant question. This paper studies short-run minimum-wage effects in Japan's spot labor market using Timee data and a wage-bin difference-in-differences design. We find a normalized net employment-share change of $-0.010$, with similar estimates for vacancies and total working hours. Weekly and daily estimates show that these effects emerge immediately after implementation and then stabilize. Effects are more negative where the minimum-wage bite is higher and in restaurant work. Net share effects are negative for midnight shifts and postings offering transportation reimbursement. Gender-targeted and beginner-targeted postings show no significant net change. Decomposing vacancies by employers' posting histories, we find that incumbent employers cut postings below the new floor while employers that did not post before the revision post just above it. Cross-employer reallocation, a multi-year process in standard labor markets, thus begins immediately in spot gig work.

items.title: Nested logit: model structure and normalisation
items.summary: Nested logit remains a widely used model, especially in applied work. However, there remains substantial confusion surrounding the existence of different versions of the model, different normalisations for the same version, and different software implementations. This paper argues that the labels in common use, RU1 and RU2, and the name non-normalised nested logit (NNNL) itself, have contributed to the confusion. The model is written in two forms: one in which utilities are divided by the structural parameter of the nest that contains them, which is consistent with utility maximisation by construction, and one without that division, known as NNNL. The difference between these forms is not one of normalisation. Normalising at the top or at the bottom gives the same model, and NNNL is itself normalised. What distinguishes the forms is whether the division is performed. In short, normalisation changes the units, whereas division changes the model. The undivided form coincides with the utility-consistent one only under specific conditions, and otherwise is consistent with utility maximisation only under utilities other than those specified, in which generic coefficients become nest-specific. The paper highlights that RU1 has been used for three different specifications, compares how widely used software packages normalise and report their parameters, and illustrates the consequences with calculated examples. The recommendation is that models be described by what they do, rather than by these labels.

items.title: Simple Communication
items.summary: We study simple communication in a multidimensional cheap talk model with aligned preferences. An expert communicates with a decision-maker using a score, i.e., an aggregator of a multidimensional state into a one-dimensional message. Even though the expert and the decision-maker share the same payoffs, equilibrium payoffs are lower than those achievable under commitment to a score. Under quadratic-loss utility, any equilibrium score must be linear in the state or a coarsening of a linear score. Finally, for normally distributed states, we characterize the equilibrium linear scores and show they include the ex-ante best and worst linear scores.

items.title: Clicks, Carbon, and Risk: Climate Attention, Persistent Financial Risk, and Real-Sector Activity
items.summary: Do shifts in public climate concern alter persistent financial risk and subsequently matter for real activity? We combine daily U.S. sectoral equity returns with a monthly Climate Concern Index (CCI) constructed from internet search intensity and decomposed into adverse and transition-oriented components. GARCH-MIDAS estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity: adverse climate concern raises persistent volatility in carbon-intensive Energy activities, while transition-oriented attention tends to reduce persistent volatility in regulated Utilities, with important differences across sub-sectors. We then construct a persistent-risk differential between Energy and Utilities and examine its predictive content for sectoral real activity using local projections. Innovations associated with adverse climate concern precede declines in Oil and Gas industrial production and employment over the following quarters, while comparable Utilities responses are limited. The production result is preserved when the financial predictor is reconstructed using the more closely matched Oil, Gas, Coal equity sub-sector and remains economically similar across several robustness checks. Overall, the findings establish a link between climate concern, persistent sectoral financial risk, and subsequent real-sector activity.

items.title: Moral Inversion: Expressive Payoffs and the Reliability of Consensus
items.summary: Moral inversion is a public consensus on an account that falsely reverses responsibility for a harm. We study how expressive payoffs affect its emergence in a sequential social-learning model. A larger payoff makes an account more attractive to endorse, but also makes each endorsement of that account weaker evidence in its favor. We show that under a single-peakedness condition on private beliefs a larger payoff both increases the probability of an incorrect consensus on the favored account and reduces its reliability. Without this condition, both comparisons can reverse, and the informativeness of the public record can strictly improve in the Blackwell order. Finally, we show that a sufficiently large increase in the expressive payoff nevertheless restores the benchmark comparative statics.

items.title: Who Pays for Product Returns? Advertising and Return Policies
items.summary: An online marketplace decides how consumers, firms, and the platform share the cost of product returns. We study this decision when the platform earns commissions and sells prominent placement. Consumers inspect, try, and return products; firms bid for the first position and then set prices. Earlier display attracts more trials but can retain a smaller fraction of them. For small positive losses, assigning return costs to consumers raises the value of prominence relative to reimbursing firms by the same amount. Advertising therefore shifts the platform's preferred division of a given return bill toward consumers. We characterize the joint allocation for small positive return losses and give a cost condition under which the platform pays nothing. In markets with frequent returns, the platform can instead share the bill with consumers: a higher commission makes it pay more to encourage shopping and retained sales. Results at finite losses show that advertising can change the optimal policy from firm-paid free returns to full consumer payment, reducing both commissions and consumer surplus. This advertising-induced policy change can lower or raise total welfare, depending on whether savings from fewer trials and returns offset the loss from reduced. participation.

items.title: AI Adoption in S&P 500 Firms
items.summary: The adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) by large enterprises is an important potential source of aggregate productivity improvement and labor market impact. We study AI adoption of S&P 500 firms over the period 2016 to 2025, estimating adoption at the enterprise level. While generative AI tools are useful for personal and professional applications, our focus is on the deep integration of AI in the business processes of large enterprises which are bellwethers for firm adoption more broadly. We develop a novel measure to assess deep AI adoption (and distinguish it from AI hype) that is based on SEC 10-K filings, where laws and regulations ``prohibit companies from making materially false or misleading statements." In 2025, 11% of S&P 500 enterprises had AI deeply integrated into their business processes, and a further 10% were using AI in the production of goods and delivery of services. AI adoption has more than quadrupled from 5% in 2022 with slowly accelerating adoption among non-technology firms but very aggressive adoption in the technology sector which accounts for two-thirds of deeply integrated enterprise adoption. Firm profitability shows a "J-curve" as firms move from no adoption to deep adoption, but we observe no differences in capex or productivity. Among technology firms, but not others, AI adoption is higher for firms with more employees and higher values of Tobin's q.

items.title: Estimation and Model Selection in Factor Models with Long Memory
items.summary: Panels in economics, finance and climate science are often driven by common components that differ in memory, such as common trends, cycles, or joint shocks. We study approximate factor models whose common factors are fractionally integrated with heterogeneous and unknown memory and develop the asymptotic theory of principal components for the panel in levels. Our theory builds on the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix being ordered by memory asymptotically: a nonstationary factor group with memory $d>1/2$ generates eigenvalues of order $NT^{2d-1}$, whereas stationary factors generate eigenvalues of order $N$. Principal components estimate the factors consistently up to rotation, while adjacent factor groups are separated at a rate given by their memory gap. The information criteria of Bai and Ng remain consistent for the total number of factors, with their penalties acting as thresholds on eigenvalues that are asymptotically ordered by factor memory. When the nonstationary factors lose their variance advantage, estimation in levels remains consistent, whereas after differencing the factors can become undetectable. A Monte Carlo study shows that factor-number selection in levels tolerates more idiosyncratic noise than selection after first differencing. For monthly temperatures at $308$ European weather stations, our methods select two factors. The first is a persistent common warming factor.
