The estimated common component implies that 2021-2025 was $2.15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ warmer than 1960-1990, with the strongest warming in Eastern Europe. After first differencing, the criterion selects one factor, and loses regional heterogeneity as compared to the model in levels.

items.title: The Online LSTM Prediction Models and The Term Structure of Predictions
items.summary: We examine and illustrate the properties of the Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) prediction models applied online to stationary inputs. We discuss the effects of: a) the network architecture that defines the admissible prediction functions, b) the objective function used to measure the prediction accuracy, and c) the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm. We also study the prediction optimality, the term structure of predictions, the filtered memory dynamics. We also introduce a set of diagnostic tools for memory-based prediction models that focus on the estimated dynamics of the hidden states.

items.title: Convex Order and Moment Persuasion
items.summary: We study Bayesian persuasion with multidimensional states when the sender's payoff depends on the distribution of posterior means. The choice of information policy in such an environment reduces to an optimization over distributions of posterior means dominated by the prior in convex order. We study extreme points of this feasible set using results on irreducible-component structure from martingale transport theory. When the prior assigns zero mass to the union of the relative boundaries of the non-singleton components, then on each such component the distribution of posterior means is dominated by the prior in convex order. In such cases, extreme points must satisfy affine independence of the conditional posterior-mean support in almost every component. Without boundary negligibility, local affine independence remains necessary but is not sufficient. Unlike in the one-dimensional case, in environments with multidimensional states, extreme points can have uncountably many lower-dimensional components that are not singletons.

items.title: Settling the Time and Structural Complexity of Bertrand Networks
items.summary: In the seminal Bertrand network game introduced by Babaioff et al. (2013), each seller posts a single price to captive buyers and to the markets it shares with neighboring sellers, where sellers cannot price discriminate across the markets. Although the existence of equilibria and polynomial-time algorithms to compute them in trees (Babaioff et al. (2013)) have been known, it has been a major open problem whether there exist efficient algorithms to compute them for general graphs. In this paper, we resolve this open question negatively by proving that computing any constant-error approximate Nash equilibrium in a Bertrand network is $\PPAD$-complete. This hardness holds even on sparse bipartite graphs of maximum degree five with constant integer market weights. Complementing our hardness result, we design an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS) when both the maximum degree and the number of sellers with captive buyers are bounded. Beyond time complexity, since exact equilibria require randomizing prices over continuous intervals, another fundamental question left open by Babaioff et al. (2013) is whether an exact equilibrium can always be represented with a finite number of price intervals, \ie whether its structural complexity is finite. We resolve this question affirmatively by proving that every achievable equilibrium revenue profile can be realized by an equilibrium with structural complexity $O(2^n)$, which leads to an exact algorithm running in doubly exponential time. We further show that this bound is tight: there exist instances for which the unique equilibrium realizing target revenue profiles has structural complexity $Ω(2^n)$.

items.title: Reserve Systems in Dynamic Settings: Account Design and Inherited Rights
items.summary: Research on reserve systems mainly considers static settings, formulating and studying choice rules for a given allocation problem. Dynamic settings are different in that the problem is not given. Over time, more positions become available, and each time the institution must build the current problem from its past. We distinguish the ledger, which stores information about earlier allocations, the account, which transforms these data into the current problem, and the choice rule, which selects an outcome for that problem. The same choice rule can implement very different policies under different accounts. If each new batch is assigned while holding earlier recipients and their categories fixed, then as batches shrink, over-and-above, the most generous reserve policy we study, can select nearly the same recipients as minimum guarantee, the most conservative one. Cumulative implementation uses a different account, which reconsiders the categories of earlier recipients, and prevents this compression. We characterize it by resource-release invariance. With arrivals or changes in priorities, the ordinary choice rule might reject an earlier recipient whose appointment has to be honored. We introduce and characterize retain, reassign, and boost (RRB) choice rules, under which every incumbent retains her appointment and can have her category changed. Combining RRB with individual-proposing deferred acceptance gives a strategy-proof mechanism under which each incumbent keeps her appointment or receives one she prefers. Applications include waiting lists in school and university admissions, public recruitment, and court-ordered corrections.

items.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

items.title: The Economics of AI Foundation Models: Openness, Competition, and Governance
items.summary: Foundation model developers choose how open to make their models. Greater openness lowers downstream adaptation costs but can also make competing models easier to use. In a two-period model, an incumbent chooses its license fee and openness, a deployer adapts the model for users, and an entrant offers a competing model. Usage builds model-specific experience that lowers the deployer's future adaptation cost, creating a data flywheel that favors continued use of the incumbent. We identify conditions under which optimal openness falls and then rises as learning strengthens. The incumbent moves from full openness and a high fee to restricting openness for retention, then to a low fee that builds enough usage and experience to retain the deployer despite greater openness. A full-openness mandate can induce the incumbent to abandon this low-fee strategy. The higher fee can reduce first-period adaptation despite greater openness. An openness trap arises when this welfare loss exceeds the second-period gain from easier adaptation of the entrant's model. The trap can disappear when experience transfers across models. Full integration eliminates the fee between the incumbent and deployer but commits deployment to the incumbent, potentially forgoing a rival that is cheaper to adapt. Integration raises their joint profit, consumer surplus, and welfare when learning is sufficiently strong, but can lower them when learning is weak. A small usage subsidy can benefit both developers, the deployer, and consumers. It can instead induce a fee increase larger than the subsidy and reduced openness, raising the deployer's net payment per use and adaptation costs. The resulting reduction in adaptation lowers welfare even before subsidy expenditure is deducted. These findings connect AI policy to developers' pricing and openness responses and the portability of deployment experience.

items.title: Irrational Random Utility Models
items.summary: The Random Utility Model (RUM) is the leading model to represent the aggregate choices of a heterogeneous population of preference maximizers. We show that if (and only if) preferences are sufficiently uncorrelated, RUM choices can also be generated by a population of decision makers who do not maximize any preference. In proving this result, we also characterize the general class of choices generated by such irrational populations, with applications beyond the RUM framework. We discuss the relevance of our results for the falsifiability of the rational interpretation of RUMs, the inference of individual rationality from aggregate choices, and the nature of welfare judgments.

items.title: Tax Salience: How Requiring Transparency Affects the Price of Equality
items.summary: Less-salient taxes can ease the classic trade-off between equality and efficiency by making people respond less to taxation. But deliberately obscuring taxes may be viewed as dishonest. This creates a three-way trade-off between equality, efficiency, and honesty. We analyze this trade-off in a simple setting with a linear income tax. We define and characterize the morally efficient frontier, trading off utilitarian welfare against honesty or transparency. Complete honesty is Pareto inefficient but not morally inefficient. More generally, increasing honesty reduces utilitarian welfare. When utilitarian welfare is decomposed into equality and efficiency, the cost of honesty falls most robustly on equality: Higher salience always reduces equality, while the effect on efficiency is ambiguous. This asymmetry arises because salience increases the price of equality, which is the efficiency cost of a marginal increase in equality. Our approach could be applied to other settings in which utilitarian and procedural or deontological values conflict.

items.title: Optimal Network Design under Node Failures
items.summary: Networks are frequently constructed before it is determined which nodes will persist. We address the design problem in scenarios where nodes fail independently, links are costly and must be established in advance, and the benefits to surviving nodes diminish with distance. Examples include supplier, interbank, and infrastructure networks. Among all possible networks, the complete, star, and empty configurations are each welfare-optimal within specific ranges of link costs. However, with four or more nodes, failures introduce a range of costs in which every optimal network contains more links than the star but fewer than the complete network. At the lower end of this range, we show that the optimal networks are exactly those obtained by removing a matching from the complete network. We develop an exact algorithm for complete multipartite networks. It finds an optimal network by dynamic programming in a number of operations that grows with the fourth power of the number of nodes, although the class itself grows superpolynomially. For networks with up to six nodes, restricting the design to this class results in no loss under explicit conditions. We also characterize pairwise-stable networks within this class and establish their existence for every level of link cost. Finally, we quantify the cost of misjudging failure risk. Overestimating node survival leads to overbuilding and can yield lower welfare than building nothing, whereas underestimating it never does. Under uncertain failure risk, design should therefore favor conservative reliability estimates.

items.title: Ranking Statistical Experiments via the Linear Convex Order and the Lorenz Zonoid: Economic Applications
items.summary: This paper introduces a novel ranking of statistical experiments, the linear-Blackwell (LB) order, which can equivalently be characterized by (i) the dispersion of the induced posterior and likelihood ratios in the sense of the linear convex order, (ii) the size of the Lorenz zonoid (the set of statewise expectation profiles), or (iii) the variability of the posterior mean. We show that the LB order provides a necessary and sufficient criterion for comparing experiments uniformly across decision problems with quasi-concave payoffs and principal-agent problems with separable payoffs.

items.title: The Geoengineering Put: Ecological Debt, Termination Risk, and Asset Prices
items.summary: Solar geoengineering offers an inexpensive and fast-acting way to lower global temperatures without removing carbon from the atmosphere. As warming intensifies, climate-vulnerable countries face growing incentives to deploy geoengineering unilaterally. The economic and financial consequences of this prospect remain largely overlooked. We develop a general equilibrium macro-finance framework in which geoengineering acts as a put option on climate damages, funded by the "ecological debt" of masked warming. If deployment stops, temperatures snap back in a catastrophic termination shock. Anticipation of geoengineering raises current brown firm valuations and lowers the optimal carbon tax, helping explain two puzzles in the existing literature: high brown-firm valuations and low carbon taxes. As ecological debt grows, however, termination risk transforms brown firms into toxic assets. Geoengineering also reshapes green innovation: it buys time for a breakthrough, but can weaken innovation incentives by lowering energy and carbon prices. Termination risk partly restores research incentives and directs them toward carbon removal, which can retire ecological debt. Our calibrations show that the geoengineering put can raise welfare across a range of parameter assumptions. Our framework clarifies how this conclusion depends on uncertain parameters and where further research is most needed.

items.title: Never too LATE: Exploiting restrictions for inference on the Local Average Treatment Effect
items.summary: Under the exclusion restriction, independence, and monotonicity assumptions, Imbens and Angrist (1994) show that the Wald estimand is equal to the local average treatment effect (LATE). However, these assumptions entail additional restrictions, which we exploit for inference on the LATE. Specifically, we propose a conditional likelihood ratio test that we show controls asymptotic size uniformly over a large class of data-generating processes. The test has very low computational cost: it requires no simulation and involves solving at most four quadratic programming problems. Monte Carlo simulations show that our test can offer substantial power gains over the Wald and Anderson-Rubin tests, including when the instrument is weak.

items.title: Sharp High-Dimensional Gaussian Approximations over Rectangles without Covariance Restrictions
items.summary: We study how well a sum of $n$ independent random vectors with $p$ coordinates can be approximated by a Gaussian vector with the same mean and covariance. We measure the error over rectangles, so the bounds apply to maxima and simultaneous confidence regions. The coordinates may be arbitrarily dependent, even exactly linearly dependent, and the bounds do not deteriorate as the covariance matrix becomes singular. After standardizing the coordinate variances, bounded or sub-exponential coordinates give the $n^{-1/2}$ sample-size rate up to logarithmic factors, with the size or tail bounds held fixed. The main upper bounds retain the Gaussian expected maximum, improving the rates when the coordinates are strongly dependent. Fourth-moment refinements give further improvements when large observations contribute little to individual coordinate variances. If we instead impose a fixed moment bound of order $q>4$ on the largest absolute coordinate, together with a coordinate fourth-moment bound, the rate becomes $n^{-1/2+1/q}$ up to logarithmic factors. At $q=4$, the slower $n^{-1/4}$ rate is unavoidable, confirming our earlier conjecture. We also allow the bounds on observation size to grow with $n$. Lower-bound examples show that the dependence on sample size, observation size, and Gaussian width is sharp up to logarithmic factors in the regimes studied, and in several regimes the upper and lower bounds match including the logarithmic terms.

items.title: Pricing Expertise with Information Spillovers
items.summary: Why do experts charge value-based fees for some services and flat fees for others? For example, an analyst charges the same fee for a stock report whether the client invests a thousand dollars or a million, while an investment bank charges a higher fee for a fairness opinion on a large merger than on a small one. We consider the problem of an expert who sells expertise to a client whose private type determines his project and how much he has at stake. Because project states are correlated, cheaper expertise about a related project can substitute for expertise about his own. We develop a Markov model of information spillovers and provide an explicit characterization of the optimal menu. With perfect spillovers, as with a stock report, a common flat fee for full information is optimal. With sufficiently weak spillovers, as with a fairness opinion, each client receives full information at a value-based fee equal to his willingness to pay. Between these extremes, low types can receive distorted expertise at their full willingness to pay, while middle and high types receive full information. Middle types pay a common base fee plus a project-specific fee that rises with what is at stake, and high types pay a value-based fee equal to their willingness to pay. Because higher types lose more by buying expertise about another project, the project-specific fee can rise faster than willingness to pay, so client surplus can peak among middle types and fall to zero at the top.

items.title: A Game of Throngs: How Spotlight Tourism Reshapes Local Economies
items.summary: In July 2017, San Juan de Gaztelugatxe, a modest chapel in the Basque Country, appeared as "Dragonstone" in Game of Thrones, transforming a locally known site with limited tourism activity into a global tourist destination overnight. We exploit this exogenous spotlight shock to estimate its causal effects on the local economy using a novel administrative dataset and a Synthetic Control approach. We find an abrupt increase in tourism activity, far exceeding the effects documented in the literature. Despite this surge, employment gains in tourism-related sectors were largely offset by losses elsewhere, resulting in no net effect on total employment. We also document signs of housing-market overheating, with increases in both property transactions and prices. We find no evidence that the shock displaced the local population. Instead, it led to a roughly twofold increase in arrivals from abroad. Taken together, these findings suggest that a substantial increase in tourism activity does not necessarily translate into broad-based local economic gains. Instead, tourism-led growth may entail significant sectoral reallocation and housing-market pressures, underscoring the importance of looking beyond tourism activity alone when assessing its wider economic effects.

items.title: How an Economy Shrinks in Space: Concavity-on-Jobs and Upward Consolidation under Demographic Decline
items.summary: When a country's population declines, the aggregate economy appears to contract on the intensive margin: industrial diversity intact, every industry a little smaller. At the regional level, contraction is uneven and takes the extensive form: entire industries disappear, one after another. The relevant unit is the city: industries are nested by size - the hierarchy property of industrial location - each viable only above a minimum population. Necessity industries' thresholds bunch at the low end, so a city's industry count - and its jobs - is sharply concave in size (concavity on jobs). A modest loss pushes a small city below many thresholds at once; a large core sheds a few specialized industries, one at a time. Lost industries consolidate upward to the next city large enough to host them; for the worker it means a step down to a lower-paid local job if one is left, and a fall to the bottom of the hierarchy if none is. To recover the lost wage, workers move up to the apex - the only city hosting the full industry range. In Japan - two decades ahead of the OECD, Tokyo at its apex - a wage regression in real, housing-inclusive wages, on worker-level panel data for the young workers who carry the migration, finds a Tokyo-bound migration incentive that varies across origins exactly as concavity on jobs predicts.

items.title: Shrink Responsibly: Empirical Bayes in Economics
items.summary: Empirical researchers are often interested in the relative causal impact of individuals or institutions such as teachers, schools, hospitals, or neighborhoods. Regression-based estimates of such unit-specific parameters are often noisy; empirical Bayes (eB) methods can help isolate the signal from the estimation noise. This article provides an overview of eB methodology, showing how eB shrinkage can improve compound decisions---such as selecting individuals with the highest causal impacts---even when the working model motivating the shrinkage is misspecified. Not all analyses benefit from eB shrinkage, however, and we discuss which types of causal summaries are best estimated directly and how to do so robustly. We illustrate practical takeaways with a running analysis of public elementary and middle school value-added.

items.title: Bayesian Model Comparison for Nonlinear State Space Models without Posterior Sampling
items.summary: Marginal likelihoods are central to Bayesian comparison of nonlinear state space models, but commonly used estimators require posterior simulation for each model, with computational costs that grow with the sample size $T$. We propose a deterministic estimator that requires no posterior simulation. A grid filter integrates out the latent states, and a Laplace approximation with a second-order correction integrates over the static parameters. Under derivative-growth and posterior-concentration conditions, the corrected Laplace approximation has error $O(T^{-2})$, and the size of the correction indicates the error that remains. In stochastic volatility experiments, the estimator is more accurate than Chib's method, the Gelfand--Dey estimator and importance sampling with a fitted proposal at equal computing time for $T\geq 2{,}000$. Applications to two exchange rates and to $T=19{,}266$ five-minute stock returns provide the strongest support for heavy-tailed observations and a transitory volatility factor.

items.title: Stationarity with Occasionally Binding Constraints
items.summary: This paper studies a class of multivariate threshold autoregressive models, known as censored and kinked structural vector autoregressions (CKSVAR), which are notably able to accommodate series that are subject to occasionally binding constraints. We develop a set of sufficient conditions for the processes generated by a CKSVAR to be stationary, ergodic, and weakly dependent. Our conditions relate directly to the stability of the deterministic part of the model, and are therefore less conservative than those typically available for general vector threshold autoregressive (VTAR) models. Though our criteria refer to quantities, such as refinements of the joint spectral radius, that cannot feasibly be computed exactly, they can be approximated numerically to a high degree of precision.

items.title: Partially identified heteroskedastic SVARs
items.summary: This paper presents new results on the identification of heteroskedastic structural vector autoregressive (HSVAR) models. Point identification through heteroskedasticity alone fails when two or more structural shocks have identical population relative variance shifts across regimes. This paper proposes a new strategy that allows researchers to continue using HSVAR models in this empirically relevant case. We show that a combination of heteroskedasticity and zero restrictions can recover point identification in HSVAR models even in the absence of heterogeneous variance shifts. We derive the identified sets for impulse responses and show how to compute them. We perform inference on the impulse response functions, building on the robust Bayesian approach developed for set-identified SVARs. To illustrate our proposal, we present an empirical example based on the literature on the global crude oil market, where standard identification is expected to fail under heteroskedasticity. A set of Monte Carlo experiments complements the analysis and investigates the properties of our methodology.

items.title: Trade Tensions Meet the Gig Economy: Evidence from the 2025 Halving of Chinese Travel to Japan
items.summary: How do geopolitical shocks to services exports reach local labor markets? Using China's November 2025 Japan travel advisory and postings on Japan's largest spot-work platform, we provide the first such evidence for the gig economy. Posted hourly wages fall immediately and persistently in prefectures more dependent on Chinese visitors, relative to others, whereas postings, hours, and employment show no robust change. Wages fall more for early morning and daytime shifts, when hotels and shops hire, than for evening and night shifts. Where each shift is priced anew, a services-trade shock lowers the price of labor in the hours it hits.

items.title: The Narrow Corridor of Stable Solutions in an Extended Osipov--Lanchester Model with Constant Total Population
items.summary: This paper studies a modification of the classical Osipov-Lanchester model in which the total population of the two sides, $N=R+B$, stays constant. In this model the ratio $y=R/B$ obeys the Riccati equation $\dot y=αy^2-β$, which is solvable in elementary functions for all values of the parameters. The main result is a complete classification of the stable regimes. An asymptotically stable invariant set in the quadrant $R,B\ge 0$ exists only in three cases: $α<0,\ β<0$ gives a stable interior equilibrium; $α=0,\ β<0$ makes the boundary $B=0$ stable; $α<0,\ β=0$ makes the boundary $R=0$ stable. If $α>0$ or $β>0$, every solution except one unstable equilibrium reaches a boundary of the quadrant in finite time, where the model stops being applicable. If the parameters vary in time, a fixed distance from the boundaries is kept when $α(t)$ and $β(t)$ obey buffer dynamics that push them away from zero. Finally, in the case $α<0,\ β<0$ the original system grows exponentially, while in the two degenerate cases it grows at most linearly. Growth demanded of a given cost, the sum of the two channels, bounds their imbalance and, with the perturbation bound, confines the parameters to an explicit wedge about $|α|=|β|$ truncated near the origin: the narrow corridor of the model.

items.title: Do Hierarchical Networks Actually Learn? Insights from Word-of-Mouth Estimation
items.summary: We study recursive estimation of a constant state vector by a hierarchical network of asymmetrically informed linear estimators, modeled as a directed tree. Only the leaves observe the regression signal, whereas every other estimator learns by word of mouth from noisy signal estimates relayed by its children. Authority within the hierarchy is expressed through common prior information: after each round, every estimator adopts the estimate and error covariance broadcast by the root. The more accurate this common information, the larger the effective noise variance on local observations, which makes estimation intrinsically self-defeating. The resulting performance is the subject of this paper. We show that recursive least-squares (RLS) estimators do learn the state in mean square, albeit slowly. Under strong persistency of excitation, the broadcast error covariance decays polynomially in time, at a rate that we characterize by upper and lower bounds of matching order. The exponent is determined by the smallest number of relays between a leaf and the root, and it decreases exponentially with this number.

items.title: Testing Clustered Equal Predictive Ability with Unknown Clusters
items.summary: We develop tests of clustered equal predictive ability (C-EPA) in panels where the clusters are unknown and estimated by Panel Kmeans. Since the hypotheses depend on data-driven clusters, we adopt a selective conditional inference framework. We show that the square root of a Wald statistic for the equality of two estimated cluster centers is asymptotically a truncated $χ$ variable, conditionally on the selected clusters and their number, with multiple random initializations, and that the truncation set is a finite union of intervals that can be computed exactly. Unlike existing methods of selective inference for Kmeans, this holds under serial and cross-sectional dependence and heteroskedasticity. For the C-EPA hypothesis, we combine the pairwise $p$-values with a test of overall EPA. In Monte Carlo experiments, the proposed tests control size where naive tests severely over-reject. An application to exchange rate forecasting with time series and machine learning methods illustrates the procedure.

items.title: TTC Domains
items.summary: The Top Trading Cycles (TTC) rule is fundamental to object reallocation: it is the only rule that is individually rational, pair efficient, and strategyproof on the unrestricted domain. Despite its desirable properties, at some profiles, TTC precludes longer trading cycles that could lead to more appealing allocations. We explore restricted preference domains as an avenue for finding alternative rules satisfying the three axioms. Our main contribution is to introduce a richness condition on domains, the top-two condition, and show that it characterizes TTC domains: domains to which the above characterization of TTC extends. The condition requires that, within every subset of objects, any two objects that can each be ranked first can also be ranked as the top two, in both possible orders. For every domain that fails the top-two condition, we construct a rule distinct from TTC that is individually rational, Pareto efficient, and strategyproof, and that executes longer trading cycles that TTC precludes.

items.title: When Better Artificial Intelligence Widens the Adoption Gap in Health Care
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist healthcare providers in clinical practice or replace services for which they are paid. We model how provider influence shapes two policy choices. The first is adoption, the share of cases in which coverage is switched to care using AI. The second is the review requirement, the number of paid reviews that must accompany AI when it is used in clinical care. Assistance can lower providers' costs and increase their profits while leaving paid reviews unaffected. However, increasingly capable AI may support autonomous use that can replace reviews and reduce providers' profits. Provider gains from adoption first rise and subsequently fall as AI capability improves. Hence, providers oppose sufficiently autonomous AI if their lost income from reviews exceeds savings from better assistance. Opposition to AI adoption arises earlier for AI that displaces more reviews. When providers can influence adoption but not the review requirement, their opposition causes under-adoption. The patient value forgone at the margin grows as AI improves. At interior policies, provider influence over both decisions widens adoption and raises review requirements above the patient optimum.

items.title: Sequential algorithm for structural estimations with equilibrium constraints
items.summary: This study examines sequential algorithms with the Zero Jacobian Property (ZJP) for estimating structural models subject to equilibrium constraints. For Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM), the current study shows that these algorithms attain fast (near-quadratic) local convergence in large samples to the solution of the constrained optimization problem. If consistent initial estimates of the parameters satisfying a suitable rate condition are available, the algorithms yield an asymptotically efficient estimator even after one iteration. It then proposes a novel algorithm called the Sequential Linearly Constrained (SLC) algorithm, which is applicable to a broader class of structural models than existing methods. A key advantage of the SLC algorithm is that it can be implemented without explicitly computing the Jacobian of the equilibrium constraints and can be several times faster than the Nested Fixed Point (NFXP) approach. The current study illustrates its performance through two numerical experiments: a dynamic discrete game with time-varying unobserved heterogeneity and a dynamic demand model.

items.title: Debiased Conditional Independence Tests for Causal Effects
items.summary: We propose robust tests for causal effects on potentially high-dimensional outcomes where there may be selection into treatment. These tests measure conditional independence of outcomes from treatment assignment by asking whether treatment can be predicted from outcomes more accurately than from covariates alone. We design three such tests of conditional independence. First, we propose a conditional randomization test based on an inverse propensity weighted mean squared error test statistic. If the propensity score is known, the test controls size in finite samples. Second, we propose a double-residualization approach, where we partial out covariate effects from both treatment and outcome-based treatment predictions, and test whether the correlation between the residuals is zero. Third, we propose a test based on an augmented inverse propensity weighted estimator built around doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal population moments that are necessary and sufficient for conditional independence. Simulations show that all three tests improve power over a joint Wald test based on a seemingly unrelated regression across many non-linear settings, particularly under heavy tails, outliers, mixtures, heterogeneous effects, and effects with opposite signs.

items.title: That Time of the Year Again: Government Pay Revisions in the Aggregate Economy
items.summary: Public pay is set by law in nominal terms, so inflation erodes its real value between legal acts until the government revises it. I model each revision as the choice of a forward-looking government, shaped by two costs that push in opposite directions. A fixed cost of acting makes revisions large and rare, whereas a convex cost of financing the increase at once makes them small and frequent. Through the budget, each revision also moves debt and the risk of fiscal stress under which the next one is made. In the documented pay decisions of eleven countries, pay set at discretion erodes against prices and private earnings and is restored in discrete steps, every cut was decided during market stress or an adjustment program, and court rulings drove a wedge between the cuts legislated, the cuts paid and the cuts that lasted. Estimated on the legal acts, the model reproduces the documented paths of pay in most countries when data and simulations are measured the same way. In Portugal's estimated model, the savings that the Treasury requires once spreads rise produce the cuts, the debt overhang holds pay down after the crisis, and a court that strikes cuts after they take effect invites cuts it will strike. Review of cuts before they took effect would have lowered the social cost of Portugal's crisis relative to review after the fact, and partial indexation would have paid in Bangladesh unless its automatic increases were costly to finance.

items.title: Self-Employment as a Career Investment
items.summary: This paper studies self-employment as an investment in future employment. Workers know their ability and choose between a safe wage and a risky independent project whose outcome becomes public. Employers pay the mean productivity of their applicants. In a two-period model with uniform ability and square-root utility, we establish a range of discount factors on which greater concern for future income increases independent production in both periods and lowers all employment wages. Some workers sacrifice current expected utility to produce a record, then accept employment after either outcome. The record is most valuable to a worker of intermediate ability; the highest types remain independent. We distinguish current income insurance from the cost of giving up this record opportunity. Identifying employers' recruitment cohorts reduces the payment needed to attract some applicant pools, but leaves the equilibrium unchanged on the established range.

items.title: The Anatomy of Value Creation: Input-Output Linkages, Policy Shifts, and Economic Impacts
items.summary: This paper describes the construction of high-resolution 7-digit product-level Supply-Use Tables (SUTs) and symmetric Input-Output Tables (IOTs) for the Indian economy from 2016-17 to 2022-23, primarily utilising microdata from the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI). It outlines the intricate methodology for generating comprehensive input and output flows, reconciling data from registered and unregistered manufacturing sectors using NPCMS-NIC concordance, and transforming SUTs into analytically robust IOTs via the Industry Technology Assumption. The paper demonstrates the application of this framework through an in-depth case study of India's mobile phone manufacturing sector (NPCMS 4722200), analysing its economic impact, particularly on Domestic Value Added (DVA) and employment. The findings reveal significant structural shifts, including output growth, import substitution, export surges, and evolving labour dynamics. These detailed tables represent a valuable advancement for analysing sectoral interdependencies, the efficacy of industrial policy, and enhancing India's National Accounts Statistics, resonating with the NSS's legacy of data-driven policymaking.

items.title: Knowing Less After a Diagnostic Test: Dilation in Clinical Decision-Making
items.summary: Dilation (Seidenfeld and Wasserman 1993) occurs when conditioning on new information \textit{only} increases uncertainty regardless of what the information reveals. Often viewed as an undesirable feature of models of ambiguity, dilation has sparked sustained debate about belief updating. This paper shows that following established clinical guidance can induce dilation, even for diagnostic tests that meet conventional performance benchmarks. We characterize when a test is dilation-inducing and show that a ubiquitous feature of performance studies -- evaluating tests against an imperfect reference -- creates scope for dilation. To facilitate detection before clinical use and inform regulatory standards, we develop a finite-sample valid hypothesis test of the null that a diagnostic test is dilation-inducing in this context. Applying the method to an influential study that preceded and contributed to the clinical adoption of chest CT screening for COVID-19, we find that the data are consistent with dilation.

items.title: Paying Creators for Training Data Can Increase AI Displacement
items.summary: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out. We study how such policies affect creator displacement in a model of a platform where creators choose whether to contribute training data and consumers choose between purchasing from creators and prompting generative AI trained on their content. When compensation is required, the low-quality creator chooses to remain solely as a training data supplier while AI fully displaces her demand, despite AI quality and the price the platform charges for AI-generated content being identical with and without compensation. Without compensation, the risk of losing creators and their training data constrains the platform to set the price of creators' content to preserve their demand. This constraint also prevents further AI displacement as AI improves, with the platform raising AI prices while keeping creators' prices and demand unchanged to prevent exit. Compensation increases creators' payoffs and total surplus but reduces consumer surplus. Our findings highlight how compensation policies for training data can shape creators' economic roles in a future with more capable generative AI.

items.title: Testing Sign Agreement
items.summary: This article studies the problem of testing sign agreement among a finite number of parameters, with applications to dynamic treatment effects, instrument validity, and labor-market discrimination. We propose least favorable and two-step tests that accommodate correlated estimators. Both have parametric and nonparametric bootstrap implementations and uniform asymptotic validity. Although neither test dominates the other in general, local power analysis shows that the two-step test can gain power when several parameters provide strong directional information. Simulations show substantial power gains for the two-step test over the least favorable and competing procedures. Empirical applications examine unilateral divorce laws and the college-proximity instrument.

items.title: Who Observes Whom: Network Rationalizability and Its Complexity
items.summary: Nash equilibrium and rationalizability sit at opposite informational extremes: the former presumes that each player knows all opponents' strategies, the latter that players reason from common knowledge of rationality alone. When visibility is partial and asymmetric, we study the solution concepts induced by a directed \emph{observation network} $G$ in which an edge $i\to j$ means that $i$ observes $j$'s strategy. A set of profiles is \emph{self-sustaining} if every profile in it can be justified, for every player, by conjectures from the same set that agree with everything the player observes. We consider \emph{point} conjectures (single profiles) and \emph{belief} conjectures (distributions over profiles). Both range from Nash equilibrium on the complete network to point- and correlated rationalizability on the empty network, and shrink monotonically as links are added. Network topology governs both behavior and complexity. A predicted profile can be found in polynomial time on the empty network, whereas a single link makes search $\mathsf{PPAD}$-hard: under one-sided two-player monitoring, the observed player's strategies are exactly her Nash equilibrium strategies. On hierarchical networks (transitive tournaments), membership reduces recursively to smaller games and admits polynomial-size certificates, placing verification in $\exists\mathbb{R}$, and in $\mathsf{P}$ for two players. On the directed three-cycle, however, iterated elimination may never terminate under either variant, and under point conjectures interior predictions may admit only infinite witness sets, a pathology that belief conjectures avoid in the same game. Finally, when only realized pure actions are observed, the solution set is guaranteed to be non-empty exactly when the network has no edges, and is computable in time $O(n|A|^2)$.

items.title: Revisiting the ABCs of Working with AI: Evidence from Radiologists
items.summary: I examine the relationship between the benefits of working with AI and two baseline traits - ability and belief calibration - among all 227 radiologists available in Collab-CXR, a dataset from an experiment where AI assistance was provided during X-ray diagnosis. When analyzed jointly, both lower unassisted accuracy and smaller miscalibration, measured by the absolute gap between average confidence and accuracy, are associated with greater improvements in accuracy with AI. In addition, the association between unassisted accuracy and improvement with AI becomes more negative and statistically significant when controlling for calibration.

items.title: High-Dimensional Approximate Factor Models with Score-Driven Dynamics: Estimation and Inference
items.summary: We propose a factor model for high-dimensional time series where the dynamics of the latent factors is generated by a multivariate score-driven model, thus allowing to model nonlinearities and heavy tails in both the conditional mean and the conditional variance. Estimation is in two steps: first the factors are extracted via Principal Components and then the parameters of the score-driven model are estimated via Quasi Maximum Likelihood based on the estimated factors. Since factors are not identified, we first establish set-consistency and asymptotic normality for the estimated parameters governing their dynamics, as both the number of time series and the sample size diverge to infinity. Then, we construct valid asymptotic prediction intervals, which do not depend on the chosen identifying constraints for the factors. Numerical results confirm the goodness of our estimator.

items.title: Economic Power in International Trade
items.summary: Economic power is a country's capacity to harm another more than itself by withdrawing from a trading relationship. This paper develops a general equilibrium model of the world trade network to measure that power through counterfactual sanctions. Using a world input-output table of eighty economies and fifty industries, we solve for $3{,}160$ such sanction equilibria, one for each bilateral severance of a trading relationship. We read the asymmetry between the two sides' losses as power. Our results show that mutual trade dependence is anything but mutual. The distribution of power in world trade is highly skewed. In the median trade relationship, one country inflicts on its trading partner more than four times the loss it bears. Only one pair in seven is close to balanced. The United States is more powerful than all seventy-nine of its partners and China against all but one. Economic power is not determined by the bilateral trade balance.

items.title: A choice-based axiomatization of Nash equilibrium
items.summary: An axiomatization of Nash equilibrium is provided for games of complete information in normal form. The Nash equilibrium correspondence is shown to be the unique solution concept that satisfies four simple and intuitive axioms. Two axioms reflect a mild form of individual rationality: one states that any profile of dominant strategies in a game must be a solution, whereas the other says that any solution to a game should not depend on strictly dominated strategies. The remaining two axioms are adaptations to non-cooperative games of standard choice-theoretic axioms about contraction and expansion consistency.

items.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
items.summary: When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, like Australia's switch to five minute electricity settlement on October 1, 2021, intervals calibrated before it can stop covering at their stated level. Whether a forecaster needs the next interval to cover or a finished period's share of misses on target decides the restart. We recompute the next conformal interval from post-break forecast errors, and for n independent ones from the same continuous law, its expected coverage error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, the optimal order in a fixed class among methods told the date. For a finished period's share of misses to match its target, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI), which on bounded errors brings that share within $O(n^{-1})$ of target if its corrections at a lower limit stay bounded in total, for that period only. After a simulated mean jump of 5.0 standard deviations, recomputed 90% intervals lie an expected 3.5 percentage points from target at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five adaptive methods. Of 9 announced changes in Texas, Australian and PJM power markets and a Federal Reserve decision, only Australia's switch moves the errors enough for a 5% test at 80% power to resolve a gain from restarting ACI, and dates help restarted ACI only after large changes.

items.title: Finding pure Nash equilibria in large random games
items.summary: Best Response Dynamics (BRD) constitute a family of strategy update rules designed to identify Pure Nash Equilibria (PNEs) in strategic games. In each iteration, a player is selected uniformly at random and adopts a best response strategy, maximising their payoff given the current strategies of the other players. If no improvement is possible for the selected player, another is chosen. The process terminates upon reaching a state where no player wishes to deviate, corresponding to a PNE. However, convergence is not guaranteed as either PNEs may not exist, or the dynamics may become confined within substructures of the game, which we call traps, that admit no PNEs. We investigate this behaviour in the context of random games with $N$ players, each choosing between two actions and receiving independently and identically distributed payoffs. The payoff distribution is permitted to have atoms, allowing for the possibility of ties. The induced dynamics define a class of random walks on the $N$-dimensional hypercube, where the landscape includes two types of absorbing sets: PNEs and traps. Our analysis encompasses BRD, simple random walks, and a broad class of nearest-neighbour processes. We prove that, with high probability, these dynamics reach a PNE before encountering any trap. Our results complete and generalise the ones by Amiet, Collevecchio, Scarsini and Zhong (2021), using a different approach.

items.title: Comparing Two-Sample IV Estimators under Weak Instruments
items.summary: We compare three estimators in a two-sample summary-data instrumental variables (IV) model: inverse-variance weighting (IVW), debiased inverse-variance weighting (dIVW), and the profile score (PS) estimator. The framework assumes independent samples and instrument-specific summary estimates, with two-sample Mendelian randomisation as a leading application. We compare existing fixed- and many-weak-instrument results and the sufficient conditions for the three estimators. Under the variance scaling used in the profile-score literature, the principal collective-strength conditions for PS and dIVW are equivalent, although their additional restrictions on instrument concentration and growth differ. We then compare their asymptotic variance formulae for fixed and diverging numbers of instruments. For fixed $L$, IVW and dIVW have the same first-order asymptotic variance. Under a common variance-ratio condition, the PS variance formula exceeds the IVW variance by a positive term of order $n^{-2}$, compared with the order-$n^{-1}$ leading variance. For diverging $L$, we establish variance orders across instrument-strength regimes and the exact ordering $\mathsf{V}_{\mathtt{IVW}} < V_{\mathtt{PS}} \leq \mathsf{V}_{\mathtt{dIVW}}$ under the same variance-ratio condition. Absolute variance gaps vanish when $\sqrt{L}κ\to\infty$, whereas relative equivalence holds if and only if $κ\to\infty$. These comparisons concern asymptotic variance formulae rather than finite-sample efficiency or mean squared error.

items.title: Identifying Time Preference Shocks: Stated and Revealed Preferences after an Italian Earthquake
items.summary: Identifying time preference shocks is challenging: shocks large enough to shift survey-elicited stated impatience also tighten financial resources, confounding the interpretation of stated time preference. Jointly examining stated and revealed preferences resolves this identification problem: impatience shocks and reductions in financial resources generate opposite consumption responses, even though both raise stated impatience. Applying our identification framework to the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, we combine panel data with spatially granular seismic and damage data in a difference-in-differences design that compares undamaged households that experienced the earthquake with a spatial control group at similar distances from the epicenter. Treated households report greater impatience and increase nondurable consumption by 11 percent relative to controls. Effects are consistent with a psychological stress channel, concentrated among the most vulnerable to stress, and persist as households deplete their liquid wealth buffer over time.

items.title: Team Stability: Theory and Evidence
items.summary: Teams emerge organically when individuals decide on their own their activities and collaborators. I develop and test a theory in which teams form with consent, interactions reflect team composition, and payoffs feature externalities and several forms of congestion. Stability constraints concern group interactions and require each team member to be willing to remain rather than withdraw or pursue a project alone. Empirical analysis of research collaborations among economists at the Federal Reserve Board suggests that: (i.) these constraints help explain observed teams beyond the payoffs to collaboration; (ii.) estimated violations point to large teams of entrants that appear to be assigned; (iii.) a compensatory mechanism mitigates the effects of variation in policy workload, which appears to affect team composition more than total research output; and (iv.) shifting workload toward experienced economists increases entrants' research output and collaboration, at the cost of lower output among experienced economists who compensate for this shift in policy workload with increased interactions with entrants.

items.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
items.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

items.title: Cluster-Robust Inference in Small Samples Using Bias Corrections
items.summary: This paper derives an exact expression for the bias of the linearized estimator of the variance for cluster-robust inference, which generalizes an earlier result derived by Bell and McCaffrey (2002). Both cases of continuous and binary treatments are discussed. Under the former it is shown that the bias of the linearized variance estimator and its jackknife variant are of order $G^{-1}$ relative to the true variance, where $G$ denotes the total number of clusters. A bias-corrected variance estimator (BCCV) is then proposed and shown to have a relative bias of order $G^{-2}$. In the case of models with binary treatments the orders of the bias of standard estimators and the proposed bias-corrected one are shown to be $\max (G_{1}^{-1},G_{0}^{-1})$ and $\max (G_{1}^{-2},G_{0}^{-2})$, where $G_{1}$ and $G_{0}=G-G_{1}$ are the numbers of treated and untreated clusters. Scale and degrees of freedom adjustments to the $t$-statistic computed using bias-corrected standard errors are also proposed. Small sample properties of the proposed BCCV test are investigated using Monte Carlo experiments. It is shown that the proposed test generally outperforms tests based on conventional and jackknife cluster standard errors, and performs comparably to wild bootstrap inference and the recent jackknife distribution-adjusted testing procedure by \cite{hansen2026jackknife}. The utility of the proposed test is illustrated\ using three empirical applications from the literature.

items.title: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment?
items.summary: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.

items.title: Complements or Substitutes? Technology Adoption and Clinical Care Utilization: Evidence from Automated Insulin Delivery
items.summary: Whether medical technology reduces or increases demand for professional care is central to understanding its effects on healthcare utilization and costs. We study automated insulin delivery (AID) adoption among 1,608 adults with type 1 diabetes treated in four specialist clinics of the Italian National Health Service, 283 of whom adopt AID. Because adoption is clinically targeted and staggered, we combine risk-set coarsened exact matching with a staggered event-study design. Matching retains 181 adopters with comparable untreated controls. We further adjust for differential pre-adoption trends by extrapolating the untreated trajectory in event time. After adjustment, AID adoption is associated with greater routine outpatient engagement. The estimated effect on the probability of a diabetologist visit is 16.3 percentage points one semester after adoption and 39.3 percentage points four semesters after adoption, relative to a 55.2% visit probability in the semester before adoption. HbA1c testing and a broader process-of-care index show similar positive patterns, although the evidence is less precise. The visit estimates remain sensitive to the trend-extrapolation assumption and should therefore be interpreted conditionally on that restriction. The findings are consistent with a task-based view in which automation substitutes for routine dosing decisions while complementing clinical labor through interpretive, adjustment, and supervisory tasks. Patient-facing automation may therefore reorganize rather than simply reduce healthcare use.

items.title: Probabilistic Causal Panel Analysis
items.summary: Many causal panel estimators construct counterfactuals using weights or latent structure estimated directly from observed outcomes, making their estimates sensitive to observation noise. Bayesian hierarchical models can account for this noise and pool information across related observations. Existing Bayesian approaches to causal panel analysis, however, typically specify counterfactual imputation within the probabilistic model, so changing estimators may require a new formulation. We develop a framework that learns the latent untreated panel with a probabilistic model and applies established causal estimators to its posterior draws. The model accommodates non-Gaussian observations and structured pooling, while re-estimation across draws propagates uncertainty through counterfactual imputation. We establish conditions for posterior consistency and characterize how pooling affects imputation risk. Under correct posterior specification, we show that the excess Bayes risk of our approach is bounded by the causal estimator's expected squared imputation error when given the true latent outcomes in observed untreated cells. We also develop a fast cross-validation approach for model selection and calibration of predictive uncertainty for treatment effects. We use simulations to examine when pooling helps or harms imputation and cross-validation to assess whether probabilistic modeling improves accuracy in multiple empirical applications.

items.title: Robust Trust
items.summary: An agent chooses an action based on her private information and a recommendation from an informed but potentially misaligned adviser. With a known probability, the adviser truthfully reports his signal; with the remaining probability, he can send any message. We characterize robustly optimal decision rules that maximize the agent's worst-case expected payoff. Every optimal rule is equivalent to a trust-region policy in belief space: the adviser's reported beliefs are taken at face value if they fall within the trust region but are otherwise projected onto the trust region's boundary. We derive alignment thresholds above which advice is strictly valuable, explicitly characterize the solution in binary-state environments, and develop a procedure for computing the trust region numerically.

items.title: Unit-Level Conformal Inference for Panel Counterfactuals
items.summary: We develop conformal inference for panel counterfactual estimators using the exchangeability of prediction errors across units rather than over time. Existing conformal methods for panels with few treated units rely on temporal properties of treated-unit residuals, which are vulnerable to strong temporal heterogeneity such as nonstationarity. We instead hold out each control unit, hide its relevant outcomes, and predict them using the same rule applied to the treated unit. Target-date estimators, including difference-in-differences and synthetic control, use controls' pre-treatment and target-date outcomes to construct the counterfactual, allowing both full conformal confidence sets and Jackknife+ intervals. Full-path estimators, including factor-model imputation and matrix completion, also use controls' outcomes at other post-treatment dates; for these, we use the Jackknife+. Both procedures yield finite-sample, period-wise confidence sets under this across-unit exchangeability, without requiring stationarity or random assignment. We characterize when the coverage holds and show why a common prediction rule alone does not ensure it. For multiple treated units, a block Jackknife+ covers their average effect, while a relabeling test is exact for sharp nulls over all treated cells. We show that the synthetic control placebo test is a full conformal test of no effect that extends to full-path estimators. We also relate our procedures to a parametric bootstrap and classify common estimators by the inference they allow. We illustrate our procedures in three empirical applications.

items.title: Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations
items.summary: This paper develops computational algorithms for testing discrete-choice random utility models (RUM). The set of RUM-consistent choice probabilities forms a polytope, and existing computational methods rely on its vertex representation. We exploit alternative half-space (Block--Marschak inequalities) and network-flow representations to develop two methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers and a flow-based column-generation algorithm. Compared with current vertex-based methods, our algorithms are better suited to GPU implementation. We establish convergence guarantees and provide optimality certificates for all three algorithms. The resulting algorithms achieve $100$--$600\times$ speedups over existing methods. The solver based on our methods is publicly available on Github at \href{https://github.com/mingxiz/d-rum-testing-gpu}{\texttt{d-rum-testing-gpu}}.

items.title: Identification and estimation for matrix time series CP-factor models
items.summary: We propose a new method for identifying and estimating the CP-factor models for matrix time series. Unlike the generalized eigenanalysis-based method of Chang et al. (2023) for which the convergence rates of the associated estimators may suffer from small eigengaps as the asymptotic theory is based on some matrix perturbation analysis, the proposed new method enjoys faster convergence rates which are free from any eigengaps. It achieves this by turning the problem into a joint diagonalization of several matrices whose elements are determined by a basis of a linear system, and by choosing the basis carefully to avoid near co-linearity (see Proposition 5 and Section 4.3). Furthermore, unlike the generalized eigenanalysis-based method which requires the two factor loading matrices to be full-ranked, the proposed new method can handle rank-deficient factor loading matrices. Illustration with both simulated and real matrix time series data shows the advantages of the proposed new method.

items.title: A General Theory of Dynamic Mechanism Design: Joint Optimization of Contracting, Information-Production Technology, and Disclosure
items.summary: We develop a general theory of dynamic mechanism design that jointly optimizes contracting, information-production technology, and disclosure across a broad class of economic environments with general allocation constraints. Hidden actions, endogenous information acquisition, learning, and disclosure interact through dynamic incentives. We accommodate correlated private information, interdependent preferences, and potentially infinite-dimensional allocations. We introduce joint perfect Bayesian equilibrium, establish the Dynamic Revelation Principle, and recursively characterize incentive compatibility. Under private values with informational interdependence, we characterize joint incentives through choice obedience, reporting-envelope first-order conditions, and global integral monotonicity. We derive an exact dynamic information-rent identity, dynamic revenue equivalence, and dynamic virtual surplus. Comparing first-best, two second-best, and third-best contracts distinguishes information rents, hidden-action implementation costs, and direct information-production expenditures, revealing nonadditive interactions of either sign and branched outcomes. Applications show Milgrom-Weber revenue-ranking reversal with endogenous acquisition, no efficient first-price equilibrium under Gaussian signals, and absent, interior, or full financial-contract disclosure.

items.title: Affirmative Action in India with Hierarchical Reservations
items.summary: We study the design of affirmative action mechanisms, focusing on India's system of horizontal reservations within vertical reservations. We consider a one-to-all policy, under which an applicant eligible for multiple horizontal categories simultaneously contributes toward each category's minimum guarantee. When horizontal reservations have a hierarchical structure, we introduce a choice rule that selects the unique merit-optimal set of applicants subject to these guaranties, satisfies the substitutes condition and size monotonicity. In a matching-with-contracts framework, we show that the generalized deferred acceptance mechanism is stable, strategy-proof, and eliminates justified envy under aggregate choice rules using the hierarchical choice rule in each vertical category. We establish a fundamental trade-off between merit and affirmative action between the one-to-all and one-to-one counting policies.

items.title: Predictive Uncertainty with Revised Economic Data
items.summary: Data revisions create uncertainty that outlives the first publication of an economic indicator. We develop a framework that turns an existing point forecast of the first release into a predictive distribution for a later release. The framework combines forecast-error records with official-release histories, including periods without recorded forecasts. We establish identification conditions and, from the component distributions, construct sharp bounds for directional probabilities and dependence-robust prediction intervals. We also show when additional revision records strictly improve estimation precision for a fixed rare-tail bound. Monte Carlo simulations quantify the predictive gains from longer release histories. Across four US inflation series, full histories improve interval scores relative to forecast-matched histories, with the largest gains in PCE. The conditional procedures lower pooled interval scores by 27--28 percent relative to a joint stochastic-volatility benchmark. With recency weighting, they match its observed coverage using intervals 34--36 percent narrower.

items.title: Aggregating Rankings of Coalitions to Rank Individuals
items.summary: We develop an ordinal framework for aggregating a profile of rankings of coalitional performances to determine the ranking of individuals. From university ratings to the assessment of team-sports players, we often evaluate individuals based on their coalitional performances. Although such evaluation has been addressed by cooperative game theory, it is only recently that its ordinal counterpart, social ranking theory (Moretti, 2015), has emerged. As most of the literature considers a single coalitional ranking (which corresponds to a real-valued characteristic function), we extend the model to allow a profile of coalitional rankings (which corresponds to a multidimensional characteristic function). We tackle the aggregation problem by introducing three families of inter-profile axioms, each representing how the rankings should interact or contribute to the output. After revealing fundamental impossibilities concerning the reconciliation of different families, we characterize a new solution, Pareto-extension Lex-cel (PEL), via some weaker versions of the inter-profile axioms. PEL extends Lex-cel, which is a central solution in social ranking theory, by analogy with Sen's Pareto extension rule. Our results develop the connection between classical Arrovian aggregation, cooperative game theory, and social ranking theory.

items.title: Hidden Eligibility and the Credibility of Adoption
items.summary: Subsidies encourage adoption, but they also change what others can learn from it. We study a government that chooses the amount and coverage of an early-adoption rebate and the information released about eligibility. Both early and late adoption create positive externalities. When eligibility is hidden, expanding the programme makes adoption less informative. As the benefit of early adoption rises, the optimal programme jumps from a small one that preserves imitation to a larger one that gives it up. We show that partial disclosure can support intermediate coverage and strictly improve on both optimally chosen opacity and full disclosure. An optimal report certifies the eligibility of some users, leaving the remaining adoptions sufficiently persuasive to induce imitation. We characterise the conditions for this policy and compare coverage under the alternative reporting rules. Analytical extensions allow delivery failures, private information, and heterogeneous adoption costs. The discontinuous change in optimal coverage can persist even when cost heterogeneity makes welfare continuous in coverage.

items.title: How optimistic inflow forecasts distort dispatch, prices, and contracts in hydro-dominated power systems: evidence from Brazil
items.summary: Centralized hydrothermal planning models determine generation schedules and electricity spot prices based on inflow forecasts in audited-cost power systems, such as those prevalent in Latin America, and provide operational benchmarks and decision support in hydro-dominated competitive electricity markets. Consequently, biased forecasts can propagate directly into both operational decisions and market outcomes. This paper studies how persistent optimistic inflow forecast bias can propagate through a hydrothermal power system, from system operation to market outcomes. For a stylized hydrothermal model, we show that optimistic bias weakly reduces water values and weakly increases first-stage hydro discharge relative to the unbiased optimum, thereby lowering reservoir storage and postponing thermal commitment. Using official Brazilian planning and operational data, we provide empirical evidence consistent with this mechanism. We then conduct controlled SDDP experiments to compare policies trained under biased and bias-corrected inflow-forecast processes, evaluating both under the same bias-corrected inflow scenarios. The policy based on biased forecasts produces lower reservoir levels, delayed dry-season thermal dispatch, sharper spot-price peaks, higher reliability risk, and higher expected operating costs. Finally, a stylized contracting exercise indicates that these distortions increase the price-quantity risk of a representative hydropower producer and reduce its willingness-to-contract. The results indicate that inflow-forecast bias can be a source of operational inefficiency, reliability risk, and distorted market incentives in hydro-dominated power systems. The insights and policy implications drawn in this paper may be relevant to hydro-dominated systems and electricity markets that are increasingly reliant on energy storage.

items.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
items.summary: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. We identify two reversal phenomena in the optimal mechanism. First, the principal's expected payoff is strictly higher in the first period than in the second, even though she is better informed after the review. Second, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but less funding following a bad review, and may receive less funding following a good review as well.

items.title: When AI Improves Answers but Slows Knowledge Creation: Matching and Dynamic Knowledge Creation in Digital Public Goods
items.summary: Generative AI helps users solve problems more efficiently, but can also replace exchanges between people with private conversations with chatbots. When more problems are solved privately, fewer problem-solving episodes are converted into reusable public knowledge for others. We build a dynamic model of public good provision where agents post and answer questions on a public platform. AI can shrink the platform's archive through two margins. Private diversion can reduce the posted volume of knowledge-enhancing questions (the flow margin), while contributor exit can lower conditional resolution (the resolution margin). Low-archive traps can arise with or without AI, because a thin archive makes public answering too costly to sustain; AI can narrow the viable region. The model gives conditional empirical predictions that distinguish demand-side diversion from supply-side pool thinning under explicit identifying restrictions. Logging private solutions adds archive inflow, while rewards for answering strengthen contribution incentives.

items.title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
items.summary: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information. In a competitive market with resource-constrained forecasting, more capable algorithms can substitute analysis of public records for private observations, reducing the private information aggregated into prices. The same trades can convey sophisticated public-data analysis to investors unable to perform it themselves. We establish conditions under which these effects coexist and the private benefit of further computation falls. Numerical equilibrium calculations and finite-data neural-market experiments exhibit corresponding patterns. Out-of-sample earnings forecasts and controlled language-model tasks show related patterns of information substitution. In the neural experiment, wider adoption increases the predictive value of price for limited observers, reduces it for advanced observers, and lowers the benefit of upgrading by 44\%. Retraining by investors who did not upgrade can amplify the loss of private-information precision. The informational consequences of AI trading depend on what prices reveal and who can use them.

items.title: Local Asymptotic Power of Honest Confidence Intervals
items.summary: Honest or bias-aware confidence intervals, conservative against untestable bias, are now standard in DiD, IV, RD, and factor models. This paper characterises the local power of their tests, which has three regimes set by the bias bound's rate relative to the sampling rate. A bound vanishing faster than the standard error costs nothing, one of the same order costs a bounded amount, and a dominating bound, typical at the parametric rate, leaves zero local power. This loss is intrinsic to honesty, and the standard bias-aware interval is rate-optimal. The paper recommends reporting the power ``dead zone'' half-width alongside bias-aware intervals.

items.title: Estimating a Rational Inattention Discrete Choice Model: A Semiparametric Approach
items.summary: People's choices depend on both the payoffs of the available options and what they learn about those payoffs before deciding. This paper shows how choice data identify both unobserved payoff heterogeneity and the cost of information acquisition in a rational inattention discrete-choice model. I establish conditions for semiparametric point identification using exogenous payoff and information-cost shifters, without imposing parametric forms on the taste-shock distribution or on how the unit cost of information varies with observed characteristics. In the model with binary choice, I construct an unobserved choice threshold whose cumulative distribution function is the choice probability as a function of the payoff shifter. Moments of this threshold identify the payoff coefficients and the unit cost of information at each value of the information-cost shifter. A deconvolution argument then identifies the taste-shock distribution. I then extend identification to the model with multinomial choice.
